E.1 Additional Spend–Performance Curves E.2 AHC025 Scoring License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.05334v1 [cs.AI] 04 Oct 2026 AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding Mahdi Farahbakhsh Ilan Sela Fatemeh Doudi Vishnu Teja Kunde Affiliation: Krishna Narayanan, Jean-Francois Chamberland, Dileep Kalathil Affiliation: Texas A&M University Email: {mahdi.farahbakhsh,isela1,fatemehdoudi,vishnukunde,krn,chmbrlnd,dileep.kalathil}@tamu.edu Abstract Frameworks that use large language models for scientific discovery typically rely on a fixed, human-designed algorithm that decides what the model sees at each step, leaving the model only the role of proposer. The model knows nothing of the search beyond what it is shown. As models grow more capable, a question arises: does a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scale better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search? The Bitter Lesson suggests that choosing the strategy in advance is the kind of hand-designed structure that general methods eventually outscale. We introduce AgentDiscover, in which a coding agent plans the search using its context as working memory, runs experiments, and records every attempt in a database of ideas, candidates, and their relations. This database serves as the agent’s long-term memory and is structured so that the selection rules of classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and Monte Carlo tree search each reduce to a single query, which the agent is free to use, combine, or replace. A server maintains the database and steers the agent after every submission, keeping it on course over long runs. In our experiments, AgentDiscover is more cost-efficient than existing frameworks, reaching better scores at lower cost. On tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks. Its programs would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder heuristic contests, and on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks it matches or exceeds every baseline that uses the same model. Our code is available here . Figure 1: On the kernel builder task, AgentDiscover reaches 960 cycles, the lowest count among the frameworks we compare against, and it reaches comparable cycle counts at lower model spend (more tasks in Appendix E ). All platforms run on Claude Opus 5 with the same budget. 1 Introduction Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly capable problem solvers, but their solutions must be verified. Returning each verdict to the model lets it improve its solutions, closing a loop of proposal and verification. When both the candidate solution and its evaluator are programs, this loop needs no human intervention: the model writes a program that either encodes a solution or searches for one, and an evaluator program runs it and scores the result. This recipe, typically run as an evolutionary search, has already produced genuine mathematical and scientific discoveries. For instance, FunSearch ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ) found new constructions in extremal combinatorics, and AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) improved the best known results on roughly a fifth of more than fifty open mathematical problems. A growing family of open systems follows the same recipe ( Sharma, 2025 ; Lange et al., 2026 ; Cemri et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) , and some go further by training the model on each problem at test time ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ) . These systems share a common architecture with three roles. A search algorithm selects past candidates for the model’s context, a proposer , a language model, writes a new candidate from them, and an evaluator scores it; the result will then be recorded, typically in an archive of past candidates. In most implementations, the selection rule is designed by humans and fixed before the run: AlphaEvolve combines MAP-Elites ( Mouret and Clune, 2015 ) with island models, ShinkaEvolve ( Lange et al., 2026 ) extends a prescribed population loop with novelty filtering, and MCTS-AHD ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) organizes candidates in a tree and selects among them with the upper confidence bound for trees (UCT) ( Kocsis and Szepesvári, 2006 ) . More recent systems adapt this rule during a run, but only within a space prescribed beforehand by their designers ( Cemri et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) . In every case, the search is run by a human-designed algorithm and the LLM only proposes: it sees the candidates that the algorithm puts in its context, but has no say in which ones those are. Leaving the search to a fixed human-designed algorithm becomes harder to justify as LLMs improve. In The Bitter Lesson , Sutton observes that methods built on human knowledge are eventually overtaken by general methods that exploit growing computation ( Sutton, 2019 ) . Choosing the search strategy before the run is such a use of human knowledge; it bets that the designer understands the problem better than the language model will. The LLM, meanwhile, could run the search itself: classical algorithms such as MAP-Elites and UCT are well documented in the text it is trained on, and coding agents , which let an LLM write and run code with tools, can implement them when needed. Knowing the alternatives matters because no single search strategy is best across problems ( Wolpert and Macready, 1997 ) . In automated evolutionary discovery specifically, a budget-matched comparison of 30 fixed search strategies (“harnesses”) found none reliably better than a simple baseline across models and problems, and the full OpenEvolve recipe ranked last ( Gupta et al., 2026 ) . The best strategy can also change within a run ( Cemri et al., 2026 ; Liu et al., 2026a ) ; fixing one for the whole search leaves the model’s knowledge of the alternatives unused. This raises a natural question: can coding agents fill both roles, one planning the search and another proposing candidate solutions with minimal human-engineered search heuristics? Handing the search to a coding agent is not enough on its own. The agent must remember what it has tried long after those attempts have left its context, retrieve the relevant part of that history cheaply, stay on course over hours of work, and do all of this without being able to tamper with the evaluator that scores it. Without a structured memory, the agent must reconstruct the state of the search from raw logs before it can apply any strategy to it. Storing such a memory is cheap; reading it is not. Every attempt can be recorded, with its score, its lineage, and the ideas it builds on, at negligible cost next to the compute a run already spends, but an agent pays in context for every record it reads. Databases have long addressed this: a query states what is wanted, and indexes and a query planner find it, so the reader receives only the answer. This raises a second question: can the history of a search be kept so that the agent retrieves only what it needs, at the cost of a query? We answer these questions affirmatively by developing AgentDiscover, a novel framework for scientific discovery in which a coding agent both directs the evolutionary search and proposes its candidates, with every past attempt one query away in a graph database (Figure 2 b, § 3 ). A coding agent works on the problem inside a sandbox, and its context is its working memory: it runs experiments, writes candidates, and decides what to try next. Each agent session eventually ends and a fresh one takes over, for two reasons: a fresh agent is not conditioned on its predecessor’s reasoning; and beyond some length, re-reading an ever longer context at every step costs more than starting over. What a session learns outlives it in a long-term memory: a graph database of ideas and candidates. Because the graph makes each candidate’s ideas and lineage explicit, the selection rule of a classical algorithm becomes a single query: the best candidate per idea for MAP-Elites, or visit counts and values over the candidate lineage for Monte Carlo tree search. The agent can use these rules, combine them, or replace them. Because the search strategy is not fixed in advance, a stronger model improves not only the candidates but also the search that produces them, whereas under a fixed search algorithm it can improve only the candidates. A server mediates all access to this memory, evaluates submitted candidates in isolation from the agent’s sandbox, and returns each score with a message that keeps the agent on course within and across sessions. A meta agent reads past sessions and writes skills that later sessions draw on. We evaluate AgentDiscover on tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ) (Table 1 ), on five further AtCoder heuristic contests ( Imajuku et al., 2025 ) (Table 2 ), on eleven mathematical and systems optimization tasks ( Qu et al., 2026 ) , run with the same LLM as the published baselines (Table 3 ), and on the kernel builder task ( Anthropic, 2026 ) (Figure 1 ). In the course of this evaluation we found that several evaluators used by prior work admit reward hacking; we correct them and describe the common vulnerabilities. Figure 2: AgentDiscover lets a coding agent direct the evolutionary search. (a) A fixed algorithm decides what the LLM sees in prior systems; in AgentDiscover, the agent queries its memory itself. (b) The agent’s loop: (1) query the graph database, (2) experiment, (3) submit a candidate, (4) receive its score and a steering message. New sessions start with a fresh context and the same memory. In summary, our contributions are: 1. We present AgentDiscover, a framework for scientific discovery that replaces the fixed evolutionary search algorithm with a coding agent that directs the search and proposes candidates, and that manages its context efficiently through a database of past attempts in which the selection rules of classical search algorithms are single queries the agent can use, combine, or replace (§§ 3.1 and 3.2 ). 2. We show that AgentDiscover outperforms prior discovery frameworks on tasks in kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics, would have placed first against human competitors in seven past AtCoder contests, matches or improves the best published result on all of the eleven standard tasks, and improves the best published bound on the first autocorrelation inequality, while being more cost-efficient than the frameworks we compare against (§ 4 , Appendix E ). 3. We identify reward-hacking vulnerabilities in evaluators used by prior work and correct them (Appendix C ). 2 Related Work LLM-based evolutionary search. A first line of work couples an LLM with an evolutionary search loop for scientific and algorithmic discovery. FunSearch ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ) established the recipe, evolving programs inside a fixed island-based loop and discovering new constructions in extremal combinatorics. AlphaEvolve ( Novikov et al., 2025 ) then shifted the landscape, improving the best known results on roughly a fifth of more than fifty open mathematical problems with a fixed archive and population policy combining MAP-Elites and island models. ShinkaEvolve keeps a prescribed population outer loop but adds novelty filtering and bandit-based model selection, while MCTS-AHD replaces population evolution with a fixed UCT-organized tree ( Lange et al., 2026 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . SimpleTES designs parallel trajectories, refinement, and history selection, and sets new best-known values with an open model ( Ye et al., 2026 ) . Fine-tuning variants keep the same loop: ThetaEvolve and TTT-Discover update the model parameters themselves at test time ( Wang et al., 2025 ; Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ) . In all these systems the search algorithm is designed in advance and stays fixed; they differ mainly in which algorithm they fix. A few go a step further and adapt the algorithm at runtime: AdaEvolve adjusts within-island exploration, cross-island allocation, and stagnation-triggered guidance through a prescribed three-level controller ( Cemri et al., 2026 ) ; Gupta et al. (2026) run several fixed harnesses side by side and shift the remaining compute to those whose early scores lead; and EvoX evolves an explicit parent-selection, inspiration, and variation policy, but only when a fixed progress monitor triggers replacement ( Liu et al., 2026a ) . Even here, adaptation remains confined to a predefined space. Coding agents as proposers. A few systems instead hand the search to a coding agent. AlgoEvo lets an agent decide when to inspect, diagnose, edit, or evaluate code, but a fixed upper-confidence rule still chooses which earlier design guides each step ( Qiu et al., 2026 ) . Vesper gives repository-level coding agents direct database access, but its fixed island-model policy samples the parent and seeds the worktree before the agent is invoked ( Ishibashi et al., 2026 ) . Meta-Harness removes the selection rule entirely: a coding agent reads every earlier harness with its scores and traces and decides what to change next, though its object is the harness around a model rather than the solution to a discovery task ( Lee et al., 2026 ) . CORAL is the closest work to ours: its long-running agents control retrieval and search direction across shared persistent state ( Qu et al., 2026 ) . AgentDiscover differs mainly in how it manages context, which lowers its cost. First, AgentDiscover periodically resets the agent’s context, which avoids paying for an ever longer history and helps the agent find new ideas. Second, where CORAL shares attempts, notes, and skills as file-system artifacts, AgentDiscover keeps its long-term memory in a graph database of ideas and candidate lineage: a fresh agent re-explores the search cheaply through queries, and the selection rule of a classical algorithm is a single query. Third, AgentDiscover lets the agent write its own tools and run experiments before it submits a candidate, and an optional meta agent turns past sessions into skills for later ones. Finally, CORAL interrupts and restarts the session on a heartbeat, whereas AgentDiscover’s server steers the running session with a message after every submission. Adapting prompts, scaffolds, and memories. A third group adapts artifacts other than the candidate program. With frozen weights, GEPA adapts prompts, BES searches over reasoning trajectories at inference time, SICA recursively edits its coding-agent scaffold, and SkillOpt applies bounded updates to skill documents ( Agrawal et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Robeyns et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2026 ) . Others persist semantic search state: SeaEvo clusters and retrieves strategy descriptions and PACEvolve decouples idea generation from code evaluation ( Luo et al., 2026 ; Yan et al., 2026 ) . Autonomous research agents. A fast-growing line of work gives LLM agents autonomy over research itself. The AI Scientist automates the cycle from idea to paper ( Lu et al., 2024 ; Yamada et al., 2025 ) ; the AI co-scientist and the Virtual Lab organize agents as a research group ( Gottweis et al., 2026 ; Swanson et al., 2025 ) ; and long-running systems combine literature search and data analysis to reach new findings ( Ghareeb et al., 2026 ; Mitchener et al., 2025 ) . Agents are also changing how research is shared: Paper2Agent turns papers into agents ( Miao et al., 2025 ) , AgentRxiv lets agents build on each other’s reports ( Schmidgall and Moor, 2025 ) , and concurrent projects run coding agents autonomously on optimization targets ( Karpathy, 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . These systems target open-ended research judged by humans or experiments. AlphaEvolve-style methods instead perform verifier-driven program evolution, but the LLM only proposes candidates inside a fixed, human-designed search loop. AgentDiscover combines the two: an autonomous agent that owns the search, scored by a verifier. 3 Methodology 3.1 Problem Formulation and Motivation LLM-driven scientific discovery casts a research problem as a search over programs. The problem is stated in natural language, and each candidate is a program x x : a representation the LLM can read and revise, and a machine can execute and score. A fixed evaluator E E scores each candidate with a scalar fitness E ⁡ ( x ) E(x) , oriented so that higher is better, and reports any auxiliary metrics the problem defines. The goal is a candidate of high fitness within a budget of evaluations, found by an LLM that revises candidates iteratively in light of what has already been tried. Existing systems ( Romera-Paredes et al., 2024 ; Novikov et al., 2025 ; Lange et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2024 , e.g.,) fix this iteration before the run: an evolutionary algorithm decides which past candidates the LLM sees, and the LLM only proposes the next one. This design is ironic: these systems aim to surpass human design, yet their search procedure is human-designed, and the LLM, the one component meant to outdo human design, has no say in it. Committing the whole run to one such procedure is hard to justify when no single strategy is best across problems (§ 1 ). We therefore replace the LLM proposer with a coding agent. The agent queries past attempts to build its own context, runs its own experiments, and records what it tries in a memory that outlives its context. Which candidates to revisit, which directions to abandon, and which strategy to follow become decisions the agent makes, and revises, during the run; in the terms of metacognition, it takes over the monitoring and control of its own search ( Flavell, 1979 ) . This flexibility pays off only if it remains safe and efficient over the long horizons these tasks demand; AgentDiscover is the infrastructure that provides it. 3.2 The AgentDiscover Framework Figure 3: AgentDiscover on a toy task: place 15 circles in a square to maximize the sum of their radii. A coding agent does the search. An MCP server stores all past ideas and candidates in a graph database and scores new candidates. (0) The agent starts in its folder (worktree). A CLAUDE.md file there describes the task and a summary of the database. (1) The agent explores the database with any read-only query. (2) It runs experiments, using available tools or new ones it writes first. (3) It submits a candidate. The server scores it with the task’s evaluator and replies with a steering message. The agent repeats steps 1–3 for each new candidate (inner loop). After the last one, a new agent with a fresh context starts on the same database and keeps all tools written so far (outer loop). AgentDiscover has three components. The search agent is a coding agent that studies previous attempts, plans, runs experiments, and proposes new candidates. The long-term memory is a graph database that keeps every idea and candidate tried so far. The optional meta agent is another coding agent that reflects on the search agents’ reasoning logs and writes what it learns as skills for them. We designed these components with two properties in mind, and show below how they achieve them. First, flexibility : no search strategy is hard-coded, and the agent decides what to read, what to try, and when to change course. Second, efficiency over long horizons : a search runs for hours, so the agent must stay on course, retain what it learns beyond its context, and keep its token cost under control. Search agent: The search agent is a coding-agent CLI, such as Claude Code, sandboxed in a version-controlled worktree. It starts from an instruction file that describes the task, summarizes the database, and explains how to access it through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server; the worktree also holds tools and skills folders, both empty in the first session. At each step, the agent chooses whether to query the database, plan, write or run tools, or submit a candidate, and it reflects on each evaluation and plans further. When the agent finds that it has stalled, or that carrying its context costs more than starting afresh, it records a lesson in the database, including experiments that never became candidates, and terminates, ending the session . A new session then starts a fresh search agent that inherits the long-term memory, tools, and skills. Figure 3 walks through a session on a toy task. Long-term memory: The long-term memory is a graph database of all ideas, candidates, sessions, and lessons, and the relations among them. It sits on the MCP server alongside the evaluator: the agent reads it with any query but writes only through MCP tools that validate their input arguments, keeping the database consistent. The server scores each submitted candidate and sends the agent a steering message that reports the fitness and the number of candidates left, keeping the agent on course over the long horizon. The graph also makes classical strategies native: MAP-Elites, which keeps the best candidate per niche, is one query returning the best candidate for each idea. Meta agent: The meta agent is another coding-agent CLI, but with a different task and a different view of the database. It runs after each search-agent session and focuses on how the search was done rather than on what it found. It reads the session transcripts, including the search agents’ reasoning traces, and relates them to the outcomes recorded in the long-term memory to find which ways of reasoning paid off and which did not. It then consolidates its conclusions into skill files that later sessions draw on. The agent accumulates a long context, which causes three problems. (i) Each LLM call re-reads the full context, so past some length a new session is cheaper than continuing, even with the reduced cost of cached tokens. (ii) The agent also becomes anchored to its earlier reasoning, which makes it harder to change ideas and more likely to get stuck in a local optimum. (iii) It is more likely to lose track of the task. Fresh agents and the database together address the first two problems. The new agent explores the database from scratch and can form a new perspective on the search; we expect this to produce new ideas more reliably than prompting the old agent to try something else while its context stays the same. Restarting is cheap because retrieval is a query. Without the database, the agent would read past attempts from files: the Meta-Harness ( Lee et al., 2026 ) , for example, reads a median of 82 files per iteration, each read costing an LLM call and consuming context the agent cannot get back. For the third problem, the server answers every submission with a steering message that tells the agent where the search stands and keeps it on course. 4 Experiments We evaluate AgentDiscover on 24 problems spanning five systems tasks, six mathematical optimization tasks, seven AtCoder heuristic contests, the first and second autocorrelation inequalities (AC1 and AC2), two GPU kernel engineering tasks, single-cell denoising, and Anthropic’s kernel builder task. We compare solution quality with existing search frameworks and published test-time finetuning results, including comparisons at matched model spend. We also study the effects of context resets, parallel search agents, and meta-agent guidance. We provide hyperparameters and run configurations in Appendix D . Benchmarks and baselines. We organize the evaluation into four settings: TTT-Discover’s multi-domain discovery tasks ( Yuksekgonul et al., 2026 ) , AtCoder heuristic contests, systems and mathematical optimization, and Anthropic kernel builder (Tables 1 – 4 ). AgentDiscover outperforms both TTT-Discover and CORAL on every task in Table 1 . On AHC039 and AHC058, its programs would have placed first in both original contests. Its AC1 upper bound of 1.50274 1.50274 ranks first on the public Einstein Arena leaderboard ( Bianchi et al., 2026 ) at the time of writing (Appendix E ). AtCoder heuristic contests. AgentDiscover achieves scores that would have placed first in all five original AtCoder contests (Table 2 ). It also outperforms the compared search frameworks on four of the five tasks; CORAL scores higher only on AHC006. When post-contest submissions are included, AgentDiscover remains in the top five on every task, ranking first on two. For AHC025, we report the relative score from a fixed standings snapshot and provide absolute scores in Appendix E . Systems and mathematical optimization. AgentDiscover matches or outperforms every baseline on all eleven tasks in Table 3 , leading on seven and tying for best on four at common reporting precision. It achieves the best score on four of the five systems tasks: EPLB, LLM-SQL, transaction scheduling, and Cloudcast; and it reaches the known optimum on PRISM. On the mathematical tasks, it achieves the best score under the corrected signal-processing evaluator and improves on all baselines for both Erdős overlap and the third autocorrelation inequality. It matches the strongest results on circle packing, MMD-16-2, and MMD-14-3. These gains are obtained using the same backbone model across all methods. Anthropic kernel builder. AgentDiscover achieves the lowest cycle count at every reported budget (Table 4 and Figure 1 ). With just $25 of model spend, it reaches 1,016 cycles, outperforming every baseline even at their full $118 budget. By $100, it reaches 960 cycles, compared with 1,098 for the strongest baseline, EvoX, a 12.6% reduction in execution cycles. This corresponds to a 153.9 × 153.9\times speedup over the naive kernel. Appendix E shows the same pattern of performance against model spend on more tasks. 4.2 Additional Experiments We study three components of AgentDiscover: context resets, parallel search agents, and meta-agent guidance. Figure 4: Context resets. (a) Without a reset, the input cost per call keeps growing. (b) After a reset, the agent sees the search afresh, making new ideas more likely. (c,d) After a stall of over five candidates, a reset raises the chance and size of an improvement; a meta pass raises them further. Context resets. AgentDiscover resets the context when the agent realizes that it has stalled, or when carrying a long cached context costs more than the input tokens of a fresh one. This helps in two ways (Figure 4 ). First, without a reset, the cost of each call keeps increasing (Figure 4 a). Second, after a reset the agent explores again, gains a new perspective, and is more likely to escape a local optimum, as in the Cloudcast run of Figure 4 b, where every improvement comes right after a reset. Figures 4 c and 4 d show that this holds on average across all our experiments: when the search has stalled for more than five candidates, a reset raises both the chance of improving the best score and the size of the improvement. The meta agent raises both further. Parallel search agents. AgentDiscover also supports several search agents in parallel, all reading from and writing to the same candidate database through one MCP server. We compare one search agent with four on transaction scheduling with Claude Haiku 4.5, using five runs per setting. With four agents, the search converges faster in wall-clock time (Figure 5 a), since the agents propose and evaluate up to four times as many candidates in the same time. At equal model spend, however, we do not see a clear difference between the two settings (Figure 5 b). Thus, parallel agents shorten the time to a good solution without reducing its cost, which makes them useful when wall-clock time matters more than model spend. Lines show the mean over five runs, bands the standard error, and faint lines individual runs. (c) With meta guidance, a new search agent beats the best score so far sooner: within two candidates in 73% of cases, against 33% without meta guidance. Meta-agent guidance. To isolate the effect of the meta agent, we run transaction scheduling five times without a meta agent. We then fork each run three times, after its first, second, and third iteration. A fork copies the run’s database and workspace at that point, adds a single meta pass, and continues for two more iterations with no further guidance; the original run continues from the same point without guidance. A fork and its original therefore start from the same state, and the only difference between them is whether the next search agent has read the meta agent’s guidance. This removes most of the run-to-run randomness from the comparison. Across the 15 forks, guidance helps the new agent make progress sooner: it beats the best fitness found before the fork within its first two candidates in 73% of the forks, against 33% without guidance, and within ten candidates in 87% against 53% (Figure 5 c). Guidance also raises the quality of what the agent proposes, not only of its best candidate: across all candidates proposed in the two iterations after the fork, the median fitness rises from 0.801 to 0.832 (Figure 5 d). At the end of these two iterations, the guided run has the higher best fitness in 10 of the 15 forks, the same in 2, and a lower one in 3. We use Claude Haiku 4.5 as the search agent and Claude Opus 4.6 as the meta agent, with ten candidates per iteration and five iterations per run. 5 Conclusion We asked whether a search strategy chosen by a human before the run scales better than promoting the model from proposer to planner and letting it own the search. Our results favor the agent. The agent reached better scores at lower cost than the frameworks we compared against, would have placed first among human competitors in seven past AtCoder contests, and improved the best published bound on the first autocorrelation inequality. The improvement over fixed search algorithms comes, in our view, from the agent seeing the whole search rather than the few candidates a fixed algorithm would hand it, and from reasoning and experimenting over many steps rather than proposing each candidate in one shot. The improvement over CORAL, where an agent also runs the search, comes from managing context more efficiently over the long horizon. We showed that resetting the agent’s context kept the cost of each call low and made it more likely to escape a stall, and that a meta agent helped further. A graph database let each fresh agent re-explore the search cheaply, while the agent wrote its own tools and ran experiments before submitting. Together, these made AgentDiscover more cost-efficient than CORAL and other frameworks we compared against (see Appendix E for more tasks and figures). Along the way, we found that several evaluators inherited from prior work admit reward hacking, and corrected them (Appendix C ). Limitations. Each entry in our main tables is a single run, so we report no variance; small margins between methods should be read cautiously. Additionally, we ran AgentDiscover with Claude models and, on some tasks, GPT-6 Sol; the framework supports other coding agents, but we have not varied the backbone model on a fixed task. Finally, we have not analyzed which search strategies the agents actually use: whether they rediscover classical rules such as MAP-Elites and UCT from the provided queries, or synthesize new ones. 6 Acknowledgments Portions of this research were conducted with the advanced computing resources provided by Texas A&M High Performance Research Computing. Appendix A Implementation Details This appendix adds implementation details to the components of § 3.2 . Prompt templates and tool descriptions are in Appendix B , and the settings of our experiments in Appendix D . A.1 Architecture and Run Lifecycle Processes and setup. The trusted side is the orchestrator, a Neo4j database whose data persists between runs, and the MCP server, a host process. Only this trusted code holds the database password, and the database and the server listen on loopback only. Containers are started through one sandbox module that supports Docker, Podman, Apptainer/Singularity, and Enroot. Before any agent starts, the orchestrator starts the database and the MCP server and builds the evaluation environment. Each branch takes its starting iteration from the database, so a new invocation continues a branch where it stopped. A new branch’s worktree (its workspace in § 3.2 ) is a fresh git repository, not connected to the main repository’s history, holding a copy of the problem’s solution.py and empty tools/ and skills/ folders. Iterations. Each branch runs its sessions in sequence in its own loop, in parallel with the other branches; iterations are grouped into blocks, and all branches wait at a barrier at the end of a block before the meta pass. To open a session, the orchestrator renders the instruction file from a template with the branch’s current guidance last, builds a short briefing from fixed queries (Appendix B ), and creates the Session node. The coding-agent CLI then runs non-interactively ( claude -p or codex exec ) in the branch’s container. The session ends when the CLI exits or its wall clock expires; a crash or timeout is recorded and the run continues. On close, the orchestrator stores the reasoning text from the transcript on the Session node, writes the exposure edges (§ A.2 ), and commits the worktree. State across sessions. A branch keeps its worktree (with solution.py as the last session left it, tools/ , and skills/ ), the worktree’s git history, its guidance, the tools the meta agent wrote for it, and the shared graph. Each session is a new CLI process with a re-rendered instruction file. One exception: a session cut off because the model provider’s usage window ran out is resumed with its transcript once the window resets. A.2 Knowledge Graph Schema Tables 5 and 6 list the node labels and relationships. Every key has a uniqueness constraint. A candidate’s key is the SHA-256 of its program text, so a resubmitted program never becomes a second node; its fitness is the evaluator’s score, and each further metric the evaluator reports is a property of its own. A.3 Meta Pass The optional meta pass runs at the barrier between blocks; a single meta agent serves all branches, and if the pass fails, the next block keeps the guidance already in place. Its container mounts each branch’s transcripts read-only and gets neither the evaluator, the database password, any solution.py , nor any git history. Besides the skill files of § 3.2 , it writes through three tools of its own: write_meta_lesson stores its judgment of one session on that Session node; add_tool stores a read-only saved query for one branch, which the branch’s later sessions are offered as an MCP tool; and write_strategy stores a branch’s new strategy as a Guidance node that supersedes the previous one and is rendered into the branch’s next instruction file. A.4 Execution Safeguards • Evaluator isolation. The evaluator is never mounted into an agent’s container, and a worktree’s git history cannot contain it. The server reads solution.py from the agent’s worktree itself and evaluates a copy in a separate container, under limits set per problem and without network access (except on the Enroot and none backends, which cannot disable it). Hidden evaluation data is fetched before any candidate exists, into a cache no agent can see. • Agent containers. A search agent’s container holds its own worktree and the problem’s public files, and never the database password. The CLI’s web tools are removed by default, and the prompt forbids looking up results online (Appendix B ); the container keeps the network access the CLI needs to reach its model API. • Read-only queries, typed writes. read_graph runs in a Neo4j read transaction, so the database itself rejects any write; all writes go through the fixed tools. • Attribution. The server attributes every call to a session itself, never trusting what an agent says about itself, and offers each caller only its own tools. Appendix B Agent Prompts and Tools The search and meta agents receive different instructions and tool sets. The boxes below preserve the wording of the consequential passages while condensing long lists. B.1 Search-Agent Instructions At the start of each search session, the orchestrator creates CLAUDE.md or AGENTS.md by substituting {{PROBLEM}} , {{SCHEMA}} , {{FOLDER_LISTING}} , and {{STRATEGY}} in one template. Box B.1 selects the parts that define the agent’s objective, interface, persistent state, and search loop. Box B.1: Selected search-agent instructions (abridged) AgentDiscover You are working on an evolutionary search over solution.py , building on work that is already done. A shared database holds every candidate submitted so far, the ideas behind them and the lessons written about them; your working directory holds tools/ and skills/ left by earlier work. Explore the database and those folders first, then either build on what you find or pursue your own idea. Problem {{PROBLEM}} What you are judged by Your briefing names a target . Beating it, preferably by a clear margin, is what this run is for. Your job is to push the best number in the database past it, as far past as you can get within this session’s cap. The target is also your yardstick. After each candidate you see your score and the distance still to go: judge from that whether your current idea can realistically reach the target, or whether it is levelling off short of it. If it is levelling off, change idea rather than refine it further. Your tools read_graph(cypher) —run any read-only Cypher query and get rows as JSON. add_idea(name, description, related_to) —record the idea a candidate will use, or reuse an existing idea by exact name. submit_candidate(idea, linguistic_prediction, fitness_prediction, parents, resources) —submit the current solution.py ; the server evaluates it in a locked sandbox and returns the score. write_lesson(text) —after your last candidate, write one lesson for the whole session. Your whole working directory persists and is committed after every session. Put reusable code in tools/ ; skills/ contains notes, written from the evidence so far, on how the search on this problem has gone. The graph you can read This is a graph database, not a table: read_graph takes any read-only Cypher, so follow relationships across several hops rather than only listing nodes. {{SCHEMA}} The session loop Your prompt names the maximum number of candidates for this session. It is a cap, not a quota. Push the fitness with every candidate. If your improvements look like they are levelling off short of the target, switch to a different idea rather than tweak the same one further. 1. Explore —briefing first, then read_graph . Before your first candidate, read the most recent lessons; explore beyond that as much as is useful. 2. An idea (mandatory)— add_idea a new one, or pick an existing idea’s exact name to reuse. 3. A candidate (mandatory)—edit only the marked evolve block of solution.py ; test locally; decide its parents; write both predictions before submitting; then call submit_candidate and read the score it returns. 4. Loop back, building on what the scores taught you. When you stop—at the cap, or earlier because different ideas all failed—call write_lesson with one lesson covering the whole session. Then stop; the orchestrator takes over from there. Honesty rules Your declared parents, idea, and resources are recorded as your claims about how the candidate was made. What you actually retrieved and read is recorded separately, by the platform, from your session log. Persistent artifacts and current strategy {{FOLDER_LISTING}} {{STRATEGY}} B.2 Meta-Agent Instructions After each block, the orchestrator renders the meta template by substituting the problem and graph schema, the block and session sizes, branch paths, and a block summary. The meta agent sees the search traces and outcomes but not the evaluator. Box B.2 selects the instructions that define its evidence, outputs, and boundary with the search agent. Box B.2: Selected meta-agent instructions (abridged) Role You are the meta-learning step, not one of the search branches. You run after all search agents have paused for this block. Search agents are short-lived: each is spawned fresh with no memory, proposes a few candidate solution.py programs, and stops. Your job is to find which ways of thinking paid off , and to make them cheap for the next fresh agents. Whatever you write for a branch stays in force for {{META_EVERY}} sessions, each proposing {{PROPOSALS}} candidates. That horizon tells you how long your claims must keep being true; it is not a budget for you to allocate. What you can reach The shared history graph through read_graph ; each branch’s raw session logs (read-only); and each branch’s skills/ directory (writable). You do not have any genome, solution.py , the evaluator, or database credentials. You shape how branches search, never the genomes directly. Branches: {{BRANCHES}} Briefing for this block: {{BRIEFING}} What to read The useful material is always pairs —thinking joined with outcome, because thinking alone is stories and fitness alone is numbers. Compare session reasoning with candidate fitness, predictions with results, idea and lineage reuse, tool use, and performance under earlier guidance. What you write—per branch 1. write_meta_lesson(session_id, text) —for each session you reviewed: your judgment of how well it searched, independent of the score it got. 2. add_tool(...) —a saved query , and only that: a read-only Cypher template exposed to later sessions as a named tool. 3. Skills —short Markdown files of methodological guidance from behavioural evidence: how the branch tends to fail, what exploration paid for, and what need not be re-derived. 4. write_strategy(...) —what ways of thinking pay off for this branch and what ways do not, written to the next fresh agent. The line between your job and theirs Deciding what to try next is the search agent’s job. Deciding how to think about the problem is yours. Do not write candidate allocations, ranked lists of approaches, or implementation into a strategy. A test before you write: would this still make sense to an agent that finds something you did not anticipate? B.3 Session Briefing and Feedback The orchestrator’s command-line prompt for the search agent adds a candidate cap, the internet policy, and a briefing built by fixed database queries. With web access off (the default), the internet rule reads “Never reach out to the internet in any way (web search, curl, wget, git clone, or otherwise) to look up other results for this problem.”; otherwise “You may search the internet if you want.” Each submission returns a code-generated steering message from the MCP server. Box B.3 shows their stable forms and the cost note; angle-bracketed fields are runtime values, and other optional variants are omitted. Box B.3: Search-session prompt and server feedback (abridged) Invocation prompt Submit up to ⟨ \langle proposals ⟩ \rangle candidates with the submit_candidate tool. Do not reply with a plan or a summary of what you intend to do: a reply that calls no tool ends your session immediately, and a session that submits nothing is wasted. Explore as much as you need, then edit solution.py and submit. ⟨ \langle internet rule ⟩ \rangle Briefing Best fitness in your branch: ⟨ \langle value ⟩ \rangle Best in the database: ⟨ \langle value ⟩ \rangle Best ⟨ \langle objective name ⟩ \rangle in the database: ⟨ \langle value ⟩ \rangle (target to beat clearly: ⟨ \langle target ⟩ \rangle ) The database holds ⟨ \langle n ⟩ \rangle candidates and ⟨ \langle m ⟩ \rangle ideas. ⟨ \langle k ⟩ \rangle search agents are running in parallel. This whole session is capped at ⟨ \langle wall ⟩ \rangle s (approximately ⟨ \langle hours ⟩ \rangle h)—budget your candidates against it; a session cut off at the cap loses its lesson. Now write the lesson for this session with write_lesson —include the work that never became a candidate, since only submitted ones are in the graph—then stop. B.4 Tools Table 7 lists the MCP interface. The “saved query” in the meta prompt is a named, branch-specific, read-only Cypher query registered with add_tool ; we call it a meta-written query tool below. Later search sessions see its name, description, and argument schema, but not its Cypher implementation. Table 7: MCP tools available to search and meta agents. Tool Caller Arguments Effect read_graph both cypher Runs a read-only Cypher query and returns rows as JSON. add_idea search name , description , related_to Creates or reuses an idea and records its relations to existing ideas. submit_candidate search idea , predictions, parents , resources Evaluates the current solution.py , records its provenance and result, and returns steering feedback. write_lesson search text Stores the session’s final lesson. write_meta_lesson meta session_id , text Stores the meta agent’s assessment of one session’s search process. add_tool meta branch , name , description , code , params Registers a read-only Cypher query as a tool for one branch. write_strategy meta branch , strategy , diff_summary Replaces a branch’s guidance for later sessions. meta-written query tool search arguments declared by its schema Runs the branch-specific query registered by the meta agent. Appendix C Evaluator Failure Modes and Corrections The evaluation sandbox (Appendix A.4 ) keeps the evaluator and its private files outside the agent’s workspace. The submitted program must nevertheless run somewhere, and the evaluator must determine whether its output is a valid solution. While porting the benchmark evaluators, we repeatedly encountered the following failure modes. We report these recurring patterns rather than attempt an exhaustive audit of every evaluator or upstream version. Incomplete output validation. Affected tasks: Signal Processing, LLM-SQL. An evaluator may compute a favorable score for an output that does not satisfy the constraints of the stated task if it checks only that the output can be parsed. On Signal Processing, the required output length was never enforced: a candidate that returned only two samples, with no slope reversals and near-perfect correlation, scored 0.9259 0.9259 on the evaluator, although it is not a solution to the task at all. Even with the length enforced, the metric rewards smoothness and penalizes the hidden clean signal for its own oscillations, so an oversmoothed output can score above the exact ground truth, which scores 0.727 0.727 . We leave the metric itself unchanged, so that our scores stay comparable with the evaluator used in prior work. On LLM-SQL, the returned table was never checked to be a rearrangement of the input rows: a candidate that discarded the input and returned one long constant row n n times made every row after the first a full prefix-cache hit and scored 0.994 0.994 , against 0.737 0.737 for the best honest reordering we found. We therefore check the output’s shape, contents, completeness, and resource constraints against authoritative task data before scoring it. Candidate-controlled scoring. Affected tasks: Signal Processing, 3rd-Autocorr., PRISM, and LLM-SQL result loading. If candidate code runs in the process that computes the score, it can rebind the metric functions, inspect scorer state, or simply print a result in the evaluator’s name. On Signal Processing, a candidate that replaced pearsonr with a function returning 10 9 10^{9} was scored 2 × 10 8 2\times 10^{8} , and one that printed {"score": 1e9} and exited had that value reported at face value. Loading a candidate-controlled serialized object into the scoring process creates the same boundary failure: on LLM-SQL the returned DataFrame was exchanged via pickle , whose deserialization executes code the candidate chooses. We run candidate code separately, exchange only the proposed solution, restrict deserialization to the expected data types, and compute the score in a process the candidate did not enter. Information leakage across the boundary. Affected task: EPLB. EPLB scores a placement on the next recorded workload, so the workload data must stay hidden: a candidate that sees the future no longer has to predict it. The agent nevertheless found two ways to obtain it. First, although the agent’s own sandbox blocks the data, the candidate program it submits ran where the file was readable, and candidates that read it raised the balance score from 0.25 0.25 to 0.44 0.44 ; a keyword blocklist did not stop this, since a file path can be built indirectly. Second, whatever a candidate prints was returned to the agent as feedback, and the same workloads are replayed in the same order on every evaluation. Candidates printed their inputs, and later candidates hardcoded the answers, lifting the score from a best honest 0.153 0.153 to 0.201 0.201 in our strongest run. Candidate processes therefore receive only public task inputs (the private data is replaced by an empty directory), and their stdout and exception messages are withheld from search feedback. Appendix D Experimental Details This appendix records the model and run configuration for each evaluation setting in § 4 . All AgentDiscover runs use the Apptainer/Singularity backend of the sandbox described in Appendix A ; only settings that vary by experiment are listed below. D.1 Models, Access, and System Budget Table 8 reports the model, access policy, and system-level budget. The reasoning-effort setting is shared by the search and meta agents; Table 10 reports the meta model and schedule. For the multi-domain tasks, TTT-Discover retains its published training and compute setting, while CORAL and AgentDiscover run under the same model-spend cap: with GPT-6 Sol on TriMul, MLA-Decode, and denoising, and with Claude Opus 5 on AHC039, AHC058, AC1, and AC2. All five kernel methods use Claude Opus 5 at low reasoning effort and the same evaluator. For baseline runs we conduct ourselves, OpenEvolve, ShinkaEvolve, and EvoX run through SkyDiscover ( Liu et al., 2026b ) with their default configurations, and CORAL uses its default configuration. Candidate budgets count submitted programs, including those whose evaluation fails or times out; only valid candidates can be reported. Model spend is computed consistently for every method (Appendix D.4 ). It is not a raw token count, and includes meta-agent calls when enabled. D.2 Search Schedule and Stopping Rules Table 9 reports the maximum scheduled search work. Every setting runs a single search branch, except the parallel-agent ablation, which compares one branch with four. Each iteration runs one search session on every active branch. Runs continue until the shared system-level budget in Table 8 is exhausted. The maximum-iterations setting in Table 9 is a non-binding safety ceiling, not the comparison budget. A session ends when the agent finds that it has stalled, or that carrying its context costs more than starting afresh. Each session also has a candidate cap and a time cap; these are upper limits that control context length, not the comparison budget, and reaching the candidate cap starts another session when one remains. The launcher may raise the configured search timeout when it cannot accommodate the candidate cap and evaluator’s per-candidate limit. Candidate evaluation has a separate task-specific timeout. Each main-table entry is the best valid candidate from one run, so the main comparisons report no variance. One meta pass runs after each completed search iteration. Table 10: Meta-agent configuration by evaluation setting. D.4 Model-spend accounting We estimate model spend from the token usage recorded in the coding-agent transcripts (Claude Code or Codex) for each task. For every assistant message, we price input, output, cache-read, and cache-write tokens at the published rates for the model used, accounting separately for 5-minute and 1-hour cache writes on Claude models. We sum message costs across all search and meta agents in a run to obtain cumulative model spend. These values are estimates at list prices, not invoice charges, because the runs used subscriptions. Appendix E Additional Results and Spend–Performance Curves Official submissions. The AC1 construction is submitted to the Einstein Arena leaderboard , where it ranked first with a bound of 1.50274353 1.50274353 on October 3, 2026. AgentDiscover finishes highest on all five, and its lead is clear on AHC015, AHC025, and AHC041. On AHC006 and AHC012, AgentDiscover and CORAL finish within rounding of each other, and on AHC006 CORAL’s program scores higher on the official system test (Table 2 ). Describe the issue below: Description: Submit without GitHub Submit in GitHub arXiv is now an independent nonprofit! Learn more × Back to arXiv Why HTML? Report Issue Back to Abstract Download PDF Abstract 1 Introduction 2 Related Work 3 Approach 3.1 ARC-AGI-3 and the level as a task 3.2 Memory as prose 3.3 Memory as executable code 3.4 Measurement at a task boundary 4 Results 4.1 Rewritten scripts 4.2 Scripts reused by reference, reused by copying, or abandoned 4.3 Updates to the notes 4.4 Negative transfer from stale memory 5 Conclusion References License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.11450v1 [cs.AI] 08 Oct 2026 \workshoptitle Continual Learning in the Era of Foundation Models and Embodied Agents Tracing the Thoughts of a Coding Agent Playing ARC-AGI-3: Lessons for Continual Learning Chen Wu Affiliation: AWS Email: wuc@amazon.com Josh Passenger Affiliation: AWS Email: jospas@amazon.com Yin Song Affiliation: AWS Email: yinsong@amazon.com Abstract We study how a coding agent learns across a sequence of abstract reasoning tasks. The agent runs on a frozen foundation model inside a fixed harness and acts by writing and running Python and shell scripts. The agent retains no state across turns other than its written artifacts, so every thought it forms, carries, corrects or abandons leaves a trace, where a thought is any belief, rule or plan committed to a file. We let the agent play ARC-AGI-3, a set of interactive reasoning games that provide no instructions. Each game is a sequence of levels, and a strategy that clears one level can fail on the next, so every new level is in effect a new task. The agent records what it learns about each game as Python scripts and text notes, while the harness keeps a complete log of every action and observation. Our contribution is a measurement protocol that traces each thought through these files, from the task where it forms to the task where it is corrected or abandoned, applied to seven evaluation runs with three backbones from two model families. We find that scripts written for one task are almost never called again in a later task (33 of 630 references cross a task boundary), because most scripts embed the state of the current level and become invalid when the level changes. Instead, the agent rewrites its knowledge into new scripts, retyping most of each version while keeping the general rules and dropping the level-specific details, and abandons 74% of the scripts it wrote before a boundary. The notes, which only the model reads, are never revised. The agent appends to them without removing earlier claims, and the contradictions that accumulate are settled against the log. Because the log preserves everything, the agent can discard scripts freely and reconstruct their content when needed, so it forgets selectively, not catastrophically. The most costly error is a hard-coded value carried into a task where it no longer holds. The fix the agent found was to turn the constant into a parameter that must be supplied afresh for each new task. The above findings were obtained from the files the agent wrote, without access to the model, and constitute a white-box analysis of how a coding agent continually learns. 1 Introduction Continual learning is usually framed as updating a parametric model over a sequence of tasks without catastrophic forgetting of earlier competence, and the difficulty is attributed to a tension between stability and plasticity ( Parisi et al., 2019 ; De Lange et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023b ) . An agent built on a frozen foundation model, on the other hand, tackles the same continual learning problem without weight updates: it must decide where knowledge is kept and what happens to that knowledge when the task changes. To study that question, we develop a coding agent whose knowledge resides entirely in a directory, building on the programmatic-memory design of PRO-LONG ( Fox et al., 2026 ) . The harness appends every interaction to logs.txt and provides the agent only the path to that file. Any fact about the environment must therefore be established by a script the agent writes. The memory of the agent consists of these scripts and its notes, and both are directly readable. We evaluate the agent on ARC-AGI-3 ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026b ) , the interactive benchmark designed to test general intelligence as the efficiency of acquiring skills on novel tasks ( Chollet, 2019 ) . The rules of every game must be discovered by playing it. Each game is a sequence of levels that share one interface yet differ enough that a solution to one can fail outright on the next (Section 3.1 ). A level boundary is therefore a task boundary inside a single episode, and it arrives unannounced. At each one the agent must decide what to carry, what to rebuild and what to abandon. Our contribution is a measurement protocol . Every script is assigned to the task that was open when it was written, which yields 4,786 scripts across 689 boundaries (Section 3.4 ). The protocol needs no access to the model that produced the memory, so it applies to any agent that writes its knowledge to a file system. It makes retention and transfer directly countable where both were previously inferable only from task performance. Applying the protocol to seven deliberately varied runs across three backbones from two model families, which clear between 34 and 183 of the 183 available levels, we report two findings. The first is an empirical characterization of cross-task update (Sections 4.1 – 4.3 ). Transfer occurs by re-derivation rather than by reference: an agent carries the rule it has learned and discards the script that established it. The moment it writes the rule out again is the moment it separates what the environment always does from what belonged to the task it has just left. All backbones respond to a boundary by partitioning memory rather than by reconciling it and differ only in the partition key. The second finding is negative transfer from stale memory, and its repair (Section 4.4 ). A false belief is eventually corrected by the interaction record, so the most costly failure is a belief that is true of one task and false of the next, which we find in three runs of one game. The one repair that works changes how the belief is stored: the value fixed inside a script becomes an argument the script must be given, an operation the scripts allow and the notes lack. 2 Related Work Surveys of continual learning group methods by the mechanism that protects earlier tasks while a new one is learned: regularization of parameters, replay of stored data, and parameter isolation ( Parisi et al., 2019 ; De Lange et al., 2021 ) . The field asks how much a learner retains, how much it can still acquire, and whether earlier learning helps later ( Wang et al., 2023b ) . Task-free formulations drop the assumption that boundaries are announced ( Aljundi et al., 2019a ) . Regularization methods protect the parameters that earlier tasks depend on ( Aljundi et al., 2018 ) , and replay methods make the question of what to keep explicit, fixing a budget and selecting into it by the gradients a sample constrains ( Aljundi et al., 2019b ) . Our setting inherits the question but removes the budget, because a file system imposes none, so what to discard is decided free of the pressure of a full buffer. Studies of continual learning in agents differ in what changes during learning. In-context learning changes nothing persistently and is bounded by the context window. Even so, CL-Bench ( Asawa et al., 2026 ) finds that keeping the full context outperforms several purpose-built memory systems, a baseline any memory architecture must beat. Memory systems change an external record ( Park et al., 2023 ; Packer et al., 2023 ) , eliminating parametric forgetting but replacing it with a retrieval bottleneck and with consolidation error. Skill libraries change a set of reusable procedures ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) , on the premise that the collection only grows, the premise our boundary counts contradict. Harness and loop engineering change the scaffold around a fixed model ( Seong et al., 2026 ; Wei et al., 2026 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Agrawal et al., 2026 ) . These approaches require a predefined space of admissible edits and a corpus of prior trajectories, and neither exists on first contact with a single unseen environment. Test-time training changes weights transiently ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , and memory written as code is its non-parametric counterpart: the state is a directory of scripts and the update rule is the agent writing code. Common to these families is that the representation in which knowledge is held is chosen in advance rather than by the agent, and that retention and transfer are estimated from task performance rather than read from the stored knowledge itself ( De Lange et al., 2021 ; Wang et al., 2023b ) . Interpretability research answers opacity inside the model with instruments: circuit tracing recovers a graph of the internal computation at substantial cost per prompt ( Ameisen et al., 2025 ; Lindsey et al., 2025 ) . In this work, by contrast, the agent holds its state in files, which provide a complete trace of what it keeps, revises and discards across tasks. 3 Approach 3.1 ARC-AGI-3 and the level as a task ARC-AGI-3 ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026b ) gives an agent a 64 × 64 64\times 64 grid of colored cells and seven actions named ACTION1 to ACTION7 together with RESET , and nothing else. There are no instructions, no statement of the objective, no account of what any action does and no key to the colors. The only feedback is a score that increases when a level is cleared. The agent can learn a mechanic only by acting and observing how the grid changes. The public demo dataset has 25 such games. A game is a sequence of levels, and clearing one loads the next inside the same episode. The grid size, the action names and the scoring are constant across a boundary. The layout, the objects present and the winning condition change, often enough to invalidate the rules the agent learned on the previous level. Our first agent cleared level 1 (L1) of wa30 on a theory of “pushable boxes” and then failed L2 by exploiting the same theory. ARC Prize gives the same warning ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a ) : without a check on why a level was won, a model carries its misconception forward. We therefore treat each level as a task. A boundary arrives unannounced, with no signal beyond the score, and at each one the agent must decide which of the things it has learned is a law of the game and which was only a fact about the level it has left. Everything measured in Section 4 happens at one of these transitions. 3.2 Memory as prose Our first agent, a predecessor of the runs in Table 1 , kept its memory as prose in the manner of Park et al. (2023) and Packer et al. (2023) , summarizing the interaction history and retrieving fragments of it into the prompt. That design has two weaknesses. First, summarizing discards information. Second, a rule written in prose cannot be executed, so it cannot be checked against the recorded history. Both weaknesses showed in the run. The agent compressed 2,416 memory entries into 106 through as many consolidation passes. Having inferred a movement budget from an on-screen bar, it filed that budget under a section titled CONFIRMED MECHANICS and treated it as ground truth thereafter. Had the rule been a transition function, the recorded episode could have been replayed against it. The runs studied here retain one prose component, the notes. Sections 4.3 and 4.4 show that the same pattern, correction by addition rather than by deletion, persists in them. 3.3 Memory as executable code The runs studied here keep the remainder of their memory as executable code, the scripts, whose outcomes at a task boundary are reported in Sections 4.1 and 4.2 . A rule written as a script can be run against the recorded history, and a mismatch tells the agent that its model needs revision. The memory then accumulates as a set of artifacts (parsers, state reconstructions and simulators) that persist in a directory and can be read from outside, which is the trace this paper follows. Figure 1: The loop, taken unmodified from PRO-LONG ( Fox et al., 2026 ) , with runs differing only in backbone, prompt and operating mode (Table 1 ). The analyzer, the only component that makes a decision, reads logs.txt and writes its intended actions to actions.json . The runner issues one action at a time, appends each action and the returned board to logs.txt , and invokes the analyzer again once its queue empties, discarding any queued plan when the score changes. Figure 1 shows the loop that writes this memory. Because the analyzer receives the path to the log rather than the board itself, establishing the current or any past state requires writing and running a script. Over an episode logs.txt reaches tens of megabytes, 24.9 MB at the largest, while the prompt stays a fixed size. The analyzer therefore keeps its model of the game in its memory, the files it writes. A turn is one call to the analyzer. The model is called once, works, and emits a plan of up to the action cap, after which the runner executes the plan and calls the analyzer again. Each turn runs the analyzer as a Strands agent ( Strands Agents, 2026 ) , a ReAct loop ( Yao et al., 2023 ) of roughly ten tool calls that searches the log, writes a parser, runs it, inspects the output, revises and emits the plan. Six tools run inside a sandbox with no network and writes confined to the workspace of that game, so the agent can neither consult outside information nor see the files of another game. The system prompt describes only the interface, naming the actions without saying what they do and asserting no structure, not even that a controlled entity or an objective exists. One prompt serves all 25 games. Only the actions sent to the game are counted, while reasoning, tool calls and retries are not ( ARC Prize Foundation, 2026a ) . Every action spent probing a mechanic therefore costs score, and every script run against the log is free, so the agent is rewarded for running its scripts on logs.txt , the record of every action already taken, rather than probing again. The setting is also close to task-free ( Aljundi et al., 2019a ) , since the agent is told nothing about task identity and receives no reward during the episode, so it alone decides when to change its model. 3.4 Measurement at a task boundary A task is one level of one game, and a boundary is the transition between two consecutive levels, the instant at which one is cleared and the next loads into the same episode. Figure 3 summarizes the four subsections. 4.1 Rewritten scripts Rewriting is frequent and its unit is a single script. In R4, 230 of the 734 scripts are a new version of an earlier one, 101 scripts reach two or more versions and one reaches twelve. The three Opus 5 runs write each new version as a separate script and never call the file-editing tool. Across the seven runs, 2,319 scripts were written before a boundary, and 523 of them were rewritten after it. In R4 the figures are 565 and 117. New versions are largely retyped rather than extended. When a script is rewritten, the new version drops 56% of the functions of the old one in R4, 62% and 61% in R2 and R3, 38% in R1, and 73%, 74% and 52% in R5, R6 and R7. What survives a rewrite is the part that does not depend on the level. The game su15 splits cleanly. The L6 simulator keeps five functions of the L5 simulator unaltered and replaces four, the disc the player moves, the pieces on the board, the chasing units and the winning condition. The five kept functions encode the rules of the game, the four replaced ones the layout of L5. Writing a new version is the moment the agent must separate the rules of the game from the contents of a level. 4.2 Scripts reused by reference, reused by copying, or abandoned Reuse by reference stays inside a level and almost never crosses one. Across the seven runs a script imports or exec s another 630 times. In 597 of these cases both scripts belong to the same level, so the reuse is within a task and is not a boundary outcome. In the remaining 33 the imported script belongs to an earlier level. A referenced script is not a library, because it runs code the moment it is imported. Of the 273 referenced scripts, 263 do this and 229 embed five or more numbers in that code, such as the dimensions of the current level. The L5 simulator in the R4 game sp80 opens with ROWS=19 and COLS=19 , fixing the board size as it loads. All four scripts that import it were written during L5. L6 has a different board, so on L6 the script is invalid on import, before any of its functions is called. Reuse by copying is the more common route across a boundary. A function body recurs across two or more scripts 562 times, and 72 of those pairs span a level change against the 33 spanned by reference. Figure 2 shows both routes. Only the three Opus 5 runs (R2–R4) reuse any script across a level change. R1 and the three Qwen runs (R5–R7) reuse none, neither by reference nor by copying. R1 does copy 137 bodies within levels, more than any other run, so it reuses scripts but never across a level. What the Opus 5 runs move into a later level is a copied function rather than a retained artifact. These runs accumulate versions rather than the growing library of reusable procedures that skill-library designs assume ( Wang et al., 2023a ; Tang et al., 2026 ) . Abandonment is the remainder and the most common outcome. Of the 2,319 scripts written before a boundary, 1,726, or 74%, are neither rewritten nor reused after it. Per run, the abandoned share is 60% in R3, 73% in R2, 74% in R4 and 88% in R1, and 84% in R5, 93% in R6 and 100% in R7. In R1, R5 and R6, which reuse nothing across a level, every script that is not abandoned was rewritten. R7 passed few levels, so only 17 of its 169 scripts were written in a level the agent later passed, and none of the 17 was rewritten. 4.3 Updates to the notes Table 3: How the notes of each run accommodate a task change. In sb26 , R2 and R3 each add a section titled CORRECTION and leave the false sentence standing above it. The agent works around a contradiction rather than settling it, which is workable because logs.txt lies outside the memory and decides between the claims the memory cannot reconcile. The notes are a dated record of past beliefs rather than a statement of current ones, which is what makes them traceable. Every thought the agent held about a game, including the ones it later abandoned, is still there in the order it was formed. 4.4 Negative transfer from stale memory The failure that recurs in both model families is negative transfer from stale memory, a belief that is true in one task and false in the next. The log of the first task cannot expose it, because it is true there. Both kinds of memory carry it into the next task, each rewrite by retyping the constant into the new version (Section 4.1 ) and the notes by restating it (Section 4.3 ). The clearest case is the game m0r0 , whose horizontal control is mirrored. The action that brings the two markers together in L4 is reversed in L5 and reversed again at the next boundary. All three Opus 5 runs carry the L4 direction into L5. They differ in the repair, which in every run is made in the scripts. Two runs changed the form of the belief, replacing the fixed value with a parameter ( def solve(polarity, ...) in one and S3 = int(sys.argv[1]) in the other), so the direction must be supplied at run time. R4 kept the value in a dictionary and edited it. It carried the wrong value into L5, corrected it there, carried the correction into L6 where it was wrong again, and restored the original. The parameter is the repair that works. At L6, R2 and R3 tried both values and settled the direction within a few actions, whereas R4 carried its L5 value across and failed again. The notes of all three runs restate the direction as a fact under each level heading, and at L5 record the reversal as a correction, but none of them records the direction as a quantity to be re-established at every level. That representation exists only in the scripts, as the parameter. The same failure appears in the Qwen runs, and in R6 the repair runs backwards. In the game tu93 the L2 simulator takes the step size as an argument, def move(r, c, mv, n=2, ...) . The L3 rewrite replaces the function with a table of fixed offsets, DIRS={’ACTION1’:(-2,0), ’ACTION2’:(2,0), ...} , so the value that L2 had left open is closed again. The pattern holds across R6, whose scripts hold almost one hard-coded number per line of code. The cases in both families share one structure. A value that changes from level to level is written into the script as a constant, and the repair, where one was made, turns that constant into a parameter. Solid arrows are actions on live scripts and the dashed arrow is content copied into a different script, as in Figure 2 . 5 Conclusion We traced how a coding agent learns across the abstract reasoning tasks of ARC-AGI-3 by reading the scripts and notes it writes and the log the harness keeps, and the same outcomes appeared, in different proportions, in all three backbones. The agent reuses scripts within a task, and across tasks it rewrites a few, copies a function from fewer, and abandons most, keeping the general rules and dropping the level-specific details. The notes only grow, and the log settles what they cannot. In the taxonomy of continual learning this is the isolation strategy ( De Lange et al., 2021 ) , adopted without instruction. The agent discards only beliefs, never evidence, so a wrong disposal costs a re-derivation rather than a competence, and forgetting is selective rather than catastrophic. The most costly error is a hard-coded value carried into a task where it no longer holds, and the fix the agent found, turning the constant into a parameter, is as visible in the trace as the error. Learning in this agent takes place in its memory, proceeds by selecting what to keep and what to discard, and every step of it leaves thoughts that can be traced, making the continual learning of a coding agent transparent from the first task to the last. Six tools run inside a sandbox with no network and writes confined to the workspace of that game, so the agent can neither consult outside information nor see the files of another game.
What survives a rewrite is the part that does not depend on the level.
A value that changes from level to level is written into the script as a constant, and the repair, where one was made, turns that constant into a parameter.
