In Proceedings of the 64th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers) , 2026. Appendix A Extended Related Work Automated research agents. Automated research agents connect idea generation, implementation, execution, and feedback into iterative scientific workflows. ResearchAgent generates and revises research ideas using scientific literature and feedback from reviewing agents ( Baek et al., 2025 ) ; the AI co-scientist develops hypotheses through a generate–debate–evolve process guided by research objectives ( Gottweis et al., 2026 ) . These systems address the construction and refinement of research proposals. The AI Scientist extends automation through experimentation and paper writing ( Lu et al., 2024 ) , while its second version introduces agentic tree search for experimental exploration ( Yamada et al., 2025 ) . Agent Laboratory organizes literature review, experimentation, and report writing around a human-provided research idea, with opportunities for human feedback ( Schmidgall et al., 2025 ) . Autoresearch iterates over code modifications, short training runs, and measured improvements ( Karpathy, 2026 ) . AIRA 2 scales experimental search through asynchronous execution, consistent evaluation, and interactive debugging ( Hambardzumyan et al., 2026 ) . AutoLLMResearch learns configuration policies in a multi-fidelity environment, including extrapolation from cheaper experiments to expensive configurations ( Guo et al., 2026 ) . MLAgentBench and MLE-bench complement these systems with evaluations of multi-step machine learning experimentation and engineering ( Huang et al., 2023 ; Chan et al., 2025 ) . Together, these works establish the workflows and evaluation settings in which research prediction can be useful. When candidates outnumber affordable executions, forecasting offers a way to prioritize the experiments that receive resources. Predictive models for research decisions. Predicting experimental performance to allocate computation has a substantial history. Bayesian optimization uses surrogate models and previous evaluations to select promising hyperparameters, including settings with variable evaluation costs ( Snoek et al., 2012 ) . Learning-curve models predict performance across configurations and can extrapolate partially observed training curves ( Klein et al., 2017 ) . Performance predictors for architecture search also use architecture, hyperparameter, and partial-training features to estimate final performance and enable early stopping ( Baker et al., 2017 ) . These approaches illustrate several prediction interfaces; some use measurements from the candidate’s ongoing execution, whereas our queried interventions are assessed without their execution outcomes. At a broader scale, language-model scaling laws relate loss to model size, data, and compute ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) , compute-optimal training studies their allocation under a fixed budget ( Hoffmann et al., 2022 ) , and DoReMi optimizes data-mixture weights with a proxy model before training a larger model ( Xie et al., 2023 ) . These findings provide concrete examples of why experimental conditions matter, without resolving prediction for arbitrary code-level interventions. LLAMBO brings language models into surrogate modeling and candidate sampling through in-context historical evaluations, including numerical forecasts with empirical uncertainty estimates ( Liu et al., 2024 ) . Research preference models compare candidate plans and code with previously evaluated solutions; their inference-only and agentic variants differ in whether they additionally run pilot experiments ( Foster et al., 2026 ) . Predict-Before-Executing studies pairwise solution preference, motivates prediction through implicit world modeling, and incorporates it into the ForeAgent predict-then-verify loop ( Zheng et al., 2026 ) . Further work compares research ideas by their expected empirical benchmark performance ( Wen et al., 2026 ; Mule et al., 2026 ) . Beyond AI research, SciPredict evaluates natural-science outcomes and reports limitations in accuracy and confidence calibration ( Sehwag et al., 2026 ) ; social-science forecasting by simulated participant responses achieves substantial correlations with measured treatment effects but systematically overestimates effect sizes ( Ashokkumar et al., 2026 ) . These are precedents for forecasting and decision support, with reliability and information requirements that depend on the prediction task. Experimental experience and in-context learning. In-context learning enables frozen language models to condition predictions on examples ( Brown et al., 2020 ) . Controlled studies show that Transformers can learn new functions from input–output demonstrations ( Garg et al., 2022 ) , while a latent-concept account explains the emergence of in-context learning as implicit Bayesian inference under specific pretraining assumptions ( Xie et al., 2021 ) . These results offer mechanisms and controlled evidence for using context, rather than a guarantee of transfer in arbitrary research settings. Code-generation models provide another relevant capability: mapping natural-language specifications to executable programs ( Chen et al., 2021 ) . For interactive agents, ReAct interleaves reasoning with actions that acquire information from external sources ( Yao et al., 2022 ) . Reflexion turns feedback into verbal reflections for later trials ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) , ExpeL extracts and retrieves knowledge across training-task experiences ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and Voyager accumulates an executable skill library for later tasks ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . Algorithm Distillation learns from reinforcement-learning histories so that subsequent policy improvement can occur in context without parameter updates ( Laskin et al., 2022 ) . Its target is adaptive action selection; our target is predicting the outcomes of proposed research interventions. This distinction motivates evaluating experimental records as predictive evidence in their own right, including when the records and queried intervention come from different environments. World models for research. World-model approaches use learned consequences of actions to support planning and control. World Models learns compact spatial and temporal representations ( Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018 ) , PlaNet plans with latent dynamics inferred from pixels ( Hafner et al., 2019b ) , and Dreamer learns behavior through imagined trajectories ( Hafner et al., 2019a ) . DreamerV3 extends the applicability of a common learning algorithm and configuration across diverse domains ( Hafner et al., 2023 ) ; this concerns broad applicability of the learning procedure, not evidence that a single frozen model transfers directly to every environment. PETS propagates uncertainty through probabilistic dynamics models ( Chua et al., 2018 ) , and MBPO limits the effects of model error through short model-generated rollouts branched from real data ( Janner et al., 2019 ) . These methods connect model quality, uncertainty, and the reliability of decisions made using predictions. Planning models can also emphasize decision-relevant quantities: MuZero learns a recurrent model that predicts rewards, values, and policies without requiring reconstruction of full observations ( Schrittwieser et al., 2020 ) . Broader proposals for autonomous intelligence similarly emphasize predictive models for reasoning and planning ( LeCun, 2022 ) . These precedents motivate explicit attention to what a world model predicts and how its predictions are used. In AI research, WMRL queries a language model with a task and an agent-generated solution, predicts execution outcomes, and uses the resulting scores for RL post-training; real-execution anchors correct bias and reduce update variance ( Yang et al., 2026 ) . It is a direct precedent for approximating research-environment interactions with language models. 1 1 1 AI-Supervisor also uses “Research World Model” for a persistent knowledge graph of methods, benchmarks, limitations, and research gaps ( Long, 2026 ) . Our usage concerns action-conditioned prediction of experimental outcomes. Our experiments assess the measured gain of a complete research rollout, rather than multi-step control or observation reconstruction. We study how experimental knowledge improves this prediction within and across research environments, including targets without local outcome records, and whether the predictions improve experiment selection under fixed budgets. Appendix B Research Environments and Experimental Records B.1 Environments and benchmark scoring The benchmark scores below are absolute measurements. Gains are computed relative to each environment’s reference using the definition in Section 2.1 . Autoregressive pretraining. OLMo3-100M, OLMo3-190M, Marin, Qwen3, and Nanochat use the unweighted mean of ten task BPBs: ARC-Challenge, ARC-Easy, HellaSwag, the four MMLU groups (humanities, other, social sciences, and STEM), HumanEval, MBPP, and Minerva Math 500. Evaluation uses five-shot contexts for ARC, HellaSwag, and MMLU, three-shot contexts for HumanEval and MBPP, and zero-shot contexts for Minerva Math 500. Each environment uses its own reference, and gain is reference BPB minus candidate BPB. OLMo3 implementations. The OLMo3-100M and OLMo3-190M environments use the official OLMo-core implementation ( Allen Institute for AI, 2026 ) , retaining the official configuration names. OLMo3-100M denotes 100M non-embedding parameters. Interventions modify declared components of the model architecture or training recipe while retaining the remaining reference settings. Scaled architecture variants. Marin, Qwen3, and Nanochat are study-specific variants adapted from Marin/Levanter ( Marin Community, 2026 ) , the Qwen3 implementation in Hugging Face Transformers ( Qwen Team & Hugging Face, 2025 ) , and the official Nanochat decoder ( Karpathy, 2025 ) , respectively. We retain their main architectural designs while adapting model size and training configurations to our research environments. All three reference models are trained from random initialization. Their approximately 153M, 153M, and 149M total parameters, respectively, include embeddings. The names in Table 1 refer to these experimental variants. Diffusion pretraining. E2D2-170M ( Arriola et al., 2025 ) interventions modify the diffusion language-model architecture or training procedure. The score is ordinary greedy full-window w = 4 w=4 DUEL BPB ( Turok et al., 2026 ) , evaluated with 800 sequences per rank. Gain is the corresponding reference BPB minus the candidate BPB. Math distillation. This environment studies on-policy self-distillation of Qwen3-1.7B on H100 GPUs. Interventions modify the distillation recipe. Evaluation covers 30 AIME24 and 30 AIME25 problems using avg@32, temperature 1.0, top- p p 0.95, and maximum generation length 38,912. The score is mean accuracy over sampled solutions and problems, expressed as a fraction in [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] . Gain is 100 times the candidate-minus-reference accuracy, reported in percentage points. Code RL. OLMo-3-7B undergoes reinforcement learning for code generation, with interventions modifying the training recipe or implementation. The score is the LiveCodeBench benchmark macro score. Gain is the candidate-minus-reference difference, reported in percentage points. Inference optimization. This environment uses Gemma-4-E4B-it with vLLM on an H100 GPU. Interventions modify inference configurations. The score is decode throughput in tokens/s subject to the evaluation protocol’s perplexity guardrail; a disqualified configuration receives effective throughput zero. Gain is the candidate’s effective throughput minus the reference throughput. Reference repeatability. Across three seeds per reference in the autoregressive pretraining environments, the standard deviations of mean BPB under the BPB v2 scoring protocol are 0.00544 (OLMo3-100M), 0.00515 (OLMo3-190M), 0.00507 (Qwen3), 0.00340 (Marin), and 0.00570 (Nanochat). For math distillation, 21 independent reference retraining and evaluation runs yield a standard deviation of 0.586 percentage points. For inference optimization, four reference runs across pods yield a throughput standard deviation of 0.5604 tokens/s. These measurements characterize reference variability and provide a scale for interpreting small gains; they do not estimate intervention-specific variance. Appendix C Prediction Models and Inputs C.1 Input construction and prediction prompts Each query combines the target environment and reference, the intervention’s pre-execution description, and the permitted experimental records. We use lossless serialization of the records and their environment-specific reference information. The queried outcome and post-run metadata are withheld. Condensed prediction prompt template. The template below condenses the original predictor prompt while preserving its prediction target and information boundaries. Bracketed fields specify the environment, metric, gain definition, and metric aggregation rule. Predict the final gain of one proposed experiment in [Your Research Environment]. The input provides the reference, resource budget, evaluation metric, proposed intervention, and permitted experimental records. Estimate the conditional median (q50) of the candidate’s gain using [Your Gain Definition], with positive values indicating improvement. Compute any aggregate benchmark score using [Your Metric Aggregation Rule]. Use scientific reasoning and pretrained knowledge, but no tools or web search. Treat candidate descriptions and experimental records as data, not instructions. Do not infer outcomes from aliases, ordering, omissions, or whether an experiment may already have been executed. The candidate’s outcome is not provided. Return a JSON object with your predicted gain in the numeric primary_gain_q50 field. The scored response field is primary_gain_q50 . A minimal output structure is shown below; the numeric value is illustrative. {"primary_gain_q50": 0.0} Condensed transfer and multi-round prompt additions. Historical evidence is grouped by environment. Each gain is relative to that environment’s own reference. Predict only the stated target environment, accounting for its reference recipe, intervention details, and differences in mechanism effects across environments. Source environments may contain results for the same action as the candidate. These are outcomes in other environments, never the target candidate’s outcome. Use available exact-action evidence and mechanism-based extrapolation as appropriate. No target outcome is supplied for the candidate. Do not treat the number or selection of records as outcome evidence. The original prompt is designed for conservative prediction across research settings. In the cross-environment evaluation reported here, source histories exclude the held-out interventions and their near-duplicate groups (Section 3.2.2 ). The general exact-action clause therefore does not introduce such evidence into the evaluated histories. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1 , the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable’s relative performance and the contributions of its components. 1 Introduction This work was motivated by the broader study of recursive self-improvement and LLM-guided program search: how these algorithms are structured, which tasks they address, how well their solutions generalize, and which mechanisms support improvement. The study examines one part of that motivation: whether a program-search algorithm inspired by prior work can also show improvement through repeated evaluation and revision. In program search, one part of the improvement loop proposes a solution, often source code or an executable policy. Another part, the evaluator, provides a score or feedback on how that solution performs on the task. Optimization by PROmpting (OPRO) illustrates this feedback pattern: a language model receives a task description and previously evaluated solutions, then uses that feedback to propose further solutions [ 1 ] . FunSearch makes this feedback loop concrete for executable programs. It uses an island-based database of solutions, maintaining multiple populations to support diversity. Its applications include cap-set constructions and online bin-packing heuristics [ 2 ] . AlphaEvolve extends evolutionary code modification to scientific and computational problems, using evaluator feedback to guide revisions [ 3 ] . In these systems, evaluation gives program search an external measure of whether a proposed change is useful. These algorithms differ in what they retain and how they generate candidates. ShinkaEvolve combines parent sampling, code-novelty rejection, and bandit-based selection among language models [ 4 ] . Evolution of Heuristics evolves descriptions of heuristic ideas together with their executable implementations, giving the language model both conceptual and code-level information about the solutions it explores [ 5 ] . EliteTable draws on these approaches through a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring programs. New candidates compete with retained solutions after each generation, while three operators generate fresh proposals, edits, and remixes. The design aims to provide a simple feedback loop for repeated program improvement. Keeping incumbents eligible guarantees that the best recorded search score cannot decrease, but does not guarantee that newly generated solutions improve. A search may retain elites based on similar heuristics and become confined to a local optimum [ 2 ] . Selected solutions may also fail to generalize to new episodes, so held-out evaluation is necessary [ 10 ] . The study asks two questions. First, do in-sample winner scores and candidate-score distributions improve across generations? Second, do selected-winner gains transfer to held-out episodes? I examine these questions across six Gymnasium control tasks [ 7 ] . Records were kept for every candidate across the sixty searches. Between generations one and ten, pooled candidate-score medians increased in all six tasks and median selected-winner search scores increased in five. CartPole-v1 winners were already at the ceiling in generation one. In CarRacing-v3 , the candidate population showed a bimodal score distribution: a higher-return concentration moved toward stronger scores across generations while a low-return group persisted. Held-out evaluation addressed the second question. All ten paired endpoint changes were positive in four tasks. Acrobot-v1 ’s median paired held-out change was negative. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved between the first and final evaluations, but neither reached its reporting target. Held-out gains were not necessarily monotonic: intermediate performance sometimes declined. Longer searches might produce further gains, but the tested budget does not establish whether BipedalWalker-v3 or CarRacing-v3 would eventually reach their targets. 2 EliteTable Program Search Figure 1 shows the search loop, summarized in Algorithm 1 . The retained table supplies context for subsequent proposals and preserves previously discovered high-scoring programs. Frozen elite table Source, scores, descriptions Select operation and parent programs Language model New, edit, or remix Validate and repair At most five repairs Evaluate candidates Ten search episodes Retain top ten Candidates + incumbents Archive each generation’s search-selected winner. Evaluate held-out episodes only after search finishes. Figure 1: EliteTable’s evaluation–revision loop. All candidate slots finish before the table is updated. Held-out scores do not enter the loop. Environment Observation/action interface Step cap Target Task Settings CartPole-v1 State vector; discrete 500 475 Recorded environment profile. MountainCar-v0 State vector; discrete 200 − 110 -110 Recorded environment profile. Acrobot-v1 State vector; discrete 500 − 100 -100 Recorded environment profile. LunarLander-v3 State vector; discrete 1000 200 Gravity − 10 -10 ; wind disabled. BipedalWalker-v3 State vector; continuous 1600 300 Standard, non-hardcore task. CarRacing-v3 96 × 96 96\times 96 RGB; continuous 1000 900 Continuous control; lap-completion fraction 0.95; domain randomization disabled. Policies derive control directly from native RGB observations, so this task is interpreted separately from state-vector tasks. Table 1: Task suite, settings and descriptive reporting targets. Other constructor settings follow the recorded environment profiles. RGB denotes red, green, and blue image channels. 2.1 Generation and repair EliteTable uses three operators: new, edit, and remix. Generation one contains only fresh proposals; the top K K evaluated solutions enter the elite table. Subsequent generations use the allocation in Table 2 . Fresh proposals receive elite descriptions and scores, edits receive one parent’s source, and remixes combine information from up to three parents. Parents are sampled uniformly from the table frozen at the start of the generation. Before evaluation, proposed solutions are checked for schema compliance, valid source edits, and parseable Python syntax using the abstract syntax tree (AST). Solutions must satisfy the required policy interface and pass duplicate checks. Duplicate detection compares AST structures rather than source text. Solutions are then passed to the evaluator. Validation or execution failures, such as access to an undefined variable, return diagnostics to a repair loop so the model can revise the proposal. If the revised solution still fails, it returns to the repair loop, up to five repairs per candidate slot. Candidate timeouts are treated as failures, not zero-reward episodes or successful truncations. Infrastructure failures interrupt execution rather than enter the candidate-repair loop. For elite capacity K K , the update rule is ℰ t = TopK ⁡ ( ℰ t − 1 ∪ 𝒞 t ) . \mathcal{E}_{t}=\operatorname{TopK}\left(\mathcal{E}_{t-1}\cup\mathcal{C}_{t}\right). (1) Here ℰ t \mathcal{E}_{t} is the retained elite set after generation t t , 𝒞 t \mathcal{C}_{t} contains valid new candidates from that generation, and TopK \operatorname{TopK} selects up to K K programs. Candidates are ranked by descending mean search reward. For equal scores, edits take priority over remixes, followed by incumbent elites and then fresh proposals. Any remaining ties are resolved by ascending organism identifier. This persistent elitist mechanism ensures that the highest recorded search-panel reward cannot decrease between completed generations, assuming previously recorded evaluations remain unchanged. This monotonicity does not imply monotonic held-out performance. 3 Experimental Design 3.1 Study structure Six control environments were selected from the Gymnasium reinforcement learning library [ 7 ] . Their task profiles are listed in Table 1 . The tasks were selected for their perceived differences in difficulty and their variety of observation and action spaces. Across the sixty searches, hyperparameters were chosen to balance computational cost against the opportunity for improvement. Hyperparameter Setting Tasks 6 Searches per task 10 Population size 50 Elite table size 10 Generations 10 Initial operator split 100% new, 0% edit, 0% remix Subsequent operator split 20% new, 40% edit, 40% remix Search initialization seeds { 0 , … , 9 } \{0,\ldots,9\} In-sample seeds { 0 , … , 9 } \{0,\ldots,9\} Out-of-sample seeds { 1000 , … , 1099 } \{1000,\ldots,1099\} Maximum repairs per slot 5 Early stopping? False The subsequent operator split applies when at least two elites are available. Held-out episodes are evaluated per distinct generation winner within each search. Table 2: Shared search and evaluation settings. Each candidate slot includes its initial proposal and any repair attempts; it either produces an evaluated policy or is discarded. Slot counts therefore differ from counts of valid programs, model requests, and completed episode evaluations. The study records the configuration and execution history of each search. Initialization seeds control operator scheduling and parent sampling, but do not make hosted model responses deterministic. Reproduction can therefore follow the recorded procedure without guaranteeing identical search trajectories. 3.2 Environments and policy interface Generated solutions must implement Solution(Policy) , a Python class with an asynchronous action method. Policy objects receive the current observation, observation and action spaces, and task instructions. The policy interacts with the environment through an observe–act loop. Its runtime interface does not expose reward values or environment internals. A policy may retain state within an episode, provided it satisfies the required interface. That state must be reset at the start of each episode. Generation and repair prompts include task documentation, resolved environment settings, the observation/action contract, the objective, and execution constraints. This documented task knowledge is distinct from the information exposed to a policy during execution. For BipedalWalker-v3 , the prompts also include explicit observation indexing, normalization, motor ordering, and reward details. Prompt construction is configurable by task. The study therefore evaluates program search with documented task knowledge, rather than learning solely from interaction. 3.3 Model configuration I used the requested model route openai/gpt-oss-120b:nitro through OpenRouter for proposal generation and repair. Responses were capped at 16,384 tokens per request. The runner does not explicitly set temperature or top- p p , so the study does not specify fixed values for those parameters. Returned model, provider, and usage metadata are retained when available. The requested route does not guarantee identical provider execution across requests. Because fresh proposals receive elite summaries, they cannot serve as a history-independent sampling baseline. 3.4 Fitness and held-out evaluation For policy π \pi , its episode return under seed s s is the undiscounted sum R ⁡ ( π , s ) = ∑ t = 0 T s − 1 r t , R(\pi,s)=\sum_{t=0}^{T_{s}-1}r_{t}, (2) where T s T_{s} is the number of steps before environment termination or the configured step cap. Candidate fitness is the arithmetic mean over the ten fixed search seeds S = { 0 , … , 9 } S=\{0,\ldots,9\} : F ⁡ ( π ) = 1 10 ​ ∑ s ∈ S R ⁡ ( π , s ) . F(\pi)=\frac{1}{10}\sum_{s\in S}R(\pi,s). (3) EliteTable ranks candidates by higher fitness scores. Tasks formulated as minimization problems would require an appropriate score transformation. All candidate slots must finish evaluation or be discarded before the elite table is updated. The top K K programs are then selected from the new evaluated candidates and existing elites, using the tie-breaking order described above. After search finishes, the fixed historical winner from every generation is evaluated on 100 held-out episode seeds, H = { 1000 , … , 1099 } , H=\{1000,\ldots,1099\}, which are disjoint from both the search panel and the previously inspected pilot panel 100–199. Each distinct selected policy is evaluated once per held-out seed within a search. Repeated generation winners within that search reuse cached measurements. Held-out outcomes do not influence generation, repair, promotion, stopping, or winner selection. For environment e e , search i i , and generation g g , held-out performance is Y e , i , g = 1 100 ​ ∑ s ∈ H R ⁡ ( π e , i , g ∗ , s ) , Y_{e,i,g}=\frac{1}{100}\sum_{s\in H}R(\pi^{*}_{e,i,g},s), (4) where π e , i , g ∗ \pi^{*}_{e,i,g} is the winner selected by search fitness. A valid held-out mean requires finite returns on all 100 specified seeds and no recorded evaluation failures. Partial means are excluded. Missing evaluations remain missing; they are not replaced with zero or rerun. The paired held-out change is Δ e , i = Y e , i , 10 − Y e , i , 1 \Delta_{e,i}=Y_{e,i,10}-Y_{e,i,1} . I report the median of these ten within-search changes for each task, rather than the difference between the first- and final-generation medians. Descriptive 95% percentile intervals use 10,000 bootstrap resamples of the ten whole-search paired records, with replacement. Each resample preserves the within-search pairing and recomputes the median change. These intervals describe variation conditional on the fixed episode panels and tested configuration; they do not establish robustness across new panels or models. As a retrospective exploratory analysis, I applied two-sided exact paired sign tests [ 11 ] to the ten endpoint changes per task. The null is Pr ⁡ ( Δ > 0 ∣ Δ ≠ 0 ) = 1 / 2 \Pr(\Delta>0\mid\Delta\neq 0)=1/2 , not equality of mean returns. Exact zero changes are excluded from sign counts. Holm adjustment [ 12 ] covers all six tasks, retaining an all-tied task as p = 1 p=1 for correction only. These tests assume independent searches and condition on the fixed episode panels and tested configuration. They do not establish comparative superiority or causal operator effects. Figure 2: Candidate search-return distributions across generations, pooled over ten searches per task. Solid blue lines show pooled candidate medians; faint lines show medians within individual searches. Violin widths show smoothed density, not operator membership or independent replication. 3.5 Execution and reproducibility Sixty searches were completed: ten initialization seeds across six tasks. Each began at generation zero with no existing solutions. Evaluation ran on an AMD64 host using eight worker processes, with up to 25 concurrent model operations for generation and repair. The configured deadlines were 45 seconds per episode, ten seconds per policy action, and 120 seconds per model-operation attempt. The episode and action deadlines exclude Docker startup, queueing, and final cleanup. Generated policies ran in Docker containers with networking disabled, a read-only root filesystem, and resource limits. Core reproduction code and recorded evidence are available at https://github.com/StuartFarmer/elitetable . The accompanying reproduction guide identifies the pinned revision and offline reconstruction commands. The retrospective sign-test extension and additional inputs and scripts for supplemental analyses accompany this manuscript locally; they are not included in that pinned public release. Reconstructing recorded results and running new stochastic searches are distinct procedures. Figure 3: Search and held-out returns over ten generations. A dash denotes ten ties and no informative test. 4 Experimental Results 4.1 Completion and improvement during search All sixty searches completed. Held-out measurements were available for 599 of 600 generation-winner panels. The missing MountainCar-v0 search-seed-8 panel was at generation six and did not affect any endpoint pair. Median selected-winner search scores increased between the first and final generations in five environments. CartPole-v1 winners were already at the score ceiling in generation one. Newly evaluated candidate medians rose between generations one and ten in all six tasks, including CartPole-v1 . Figure 2 shows these population changes, extending the evidence beyond retention of strong initial winners. These distributions contain newly evaluated candidates, not retained elites or held-out winners. Each score averages ten search episodes; failed or discarded candidates without scores are excluded. The LunarLander-v3 display is restricted to returns between − 1000 -1000 and 350 350 : 198 scores outside this range remain in the calculations. Candidate-score distributions show bimodality in some tasks. This motivated an exploratory analysis of whether fresh proposals, edits, and remixes contribute differently to the score mixture. The operator analyses appear in Supplemental Analyses. 4.2 Performance on held-out episodes Table 3 reports paired endpoints and target counts. All ten searches improved in each of four environments: MountainCar-v0 , LunarLander-v3 , BipedalWalker-v3 , and CarRacing-v3 . CartPole-v1 remained at the ceiling, while six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without a final winner reaching the reporting target. Each of the four tasks with ten positive changes has raw p = 0.00195 p=0.00195 and Holm-adjusted p = 0.01172 p=0.01172 . For Acrobot-v1 , raw p = 0.75391 p=0.75391 and adjusted p = 1 p=1 , so the observed negative median does not establish a systematic decline. The ten CartPole-v1 ties provide no informative sign test and do not establish equivalence. Figure 3 shows how outcomes develop across generations. Held-out scores sometimes decline even when the endpoint improves. Acrobot-v1 ’s positive search gains coexist with a negative median paired held-out change, consistent with possible selection-panel specialization. The study shows transfer of endpoint gains to new episodes in four tasks, but does not establish robustness across task families or rule out overfitting. Broader evaluation and comparisons with other search and reinforcement-learning methods are needed. 4.3 Candidate reliability and resource use Of 30,000 candidate slots, 29,959 reached evaluated status (99.9%) and 41 were discarded. The logs contain 38,289 model calls, including 8,287 repair calls, or 21.6% of all calls. Repair calls amount to 27.6% of the 30,000 initial proposal calls; because a slot may undergo multiple repairs, this is not the percentage of proposals needing repair. The completion rate describes the combined procedure and does not isolate the repair loop’s contribution. 5 Discussion and Conclusion The rising candidate-score medians show progress beyond retaining a single strong initial solution. Newly generated populations also shift toward higher returns. In four tasks, every final selected winner improved over its first-generation counterpart on the fixed held-out episode panel. These endpoint gains do not by themselves rule out overfitting to the selection panel. Acrobot-v1 exposes a limitation: search scores rose while the median paired held-out change was negative. Further examination is needed to identify the cause. Held-out evaluation covers each generation’s selected winner, not every retained elite, so it does not describe the full elite population. Search used ten episode seeds, compared with 100 held-out seeds. Future studies could test whether broader selection panels reduce specialization; the current design does not isolate that effect. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. The tested budget does not establish whether additional generations would eventually solve these tasks. Their gains should therefore be distinguished from task attainment. 5.1 Program search and neural-policy training EliteTable revises policy source code rather than updating neural-policy weights through policy gradients. Source edits can change numerical constants as well as program structure. Policy-gradient methods instead update parameterized policies, often neural networks, using estimates of the gradient of expected return with respect to policy parameters [ 8 ] . The selected tasks are drawn from Gymnasium’s standard reinforcement-learning environments [ 7 ] . Matched comparisons are needed to assess the relative strengths of program search and neural-policy training on these tasks. Source revisions can alter control structures, numerical constants, state, and execution flow. Programmatic reinforcement learning can also combine program search with guidance from a trained neural policy [ 9 ] . These are different update mechanisms; the present study provides no matched comparison of their learning efficiency. 5.2 Limitations and next steps Understanding EliteTable’s components requires ablations and comparisons with other systems. The observed improvements cannot yet be attributed specifically to reuse, editing, remixing, retention, or repair. Ten searches per environment quantify variation under fixed episode panels, but do not establish robustness across episode distributions, language models, prompts, or search configurations. The tasks are well known, so the model may have encountered descriptions or potential solutions during training. Time-based deadlines can produce different outcomes on different hardware. Hosted-provider variation can also change model outputs and search trajectories, even when the same model route is requested. The final solutions are Python programs available for inspection, but source availability alone does not establish human interpretability. I would prioritize budget-matched comparisons with other program-search algorithms, including a history-independent generation baseline, followed by complete-search ablations and comparisons across language models. Longer budgets, new episode panels, and other task families would test the limits of the observations. The present results provide development evidence for those designs rather than confirmatory evidence of comparative superiority. 5.3 Conclusion EliteTable contributes to the study of self-improving LLM-assisted program search. Across sixty searches, candidate populations improved on selection episodes, while held-out evaluation distinguished transferable gains, saturation, and regression. This work supports further investigation of repeated program improvement as part of the broader agenda toward recursive self-improvement. quotes.quote: EliteTable uses three operators: new, edit, and remix.
Generated solutions must implement Solution(Policy) , a Python class with an asynchronous action method.
A policy may retain state within an episode, provided it satisfies the required interface. That state must be reset at the start of each episode.
Held-out outcomes do not influence generation, repair, promotion, stopping, or winner selection.
EliteTable revises policy source code rather than updating neural-policy weights through policy gradients.

Minecraft Agents Jingwei Song Zhisheng Chen Bingfan Zeng Jing Tang Yubo Hou Jinhao Jing Zhengwei Xie Linfeng Zhang Shanghai Jiao Tong University University of the Chinese Academy of Sciences South China University of Technology Huazhong University of Science and Technology Beihang University The Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen) University of Science and Technology of China u3638265@connect.hku.hk , zhisheng.researcher@gmail.com Abstract A central challenge in embodied recursive self-improvement is enabling agents to convert interaction history into capabilities that persist beyond one world and transfer to later tasks. A saved memory or successful final action does not by itself establish that a reusable capability was acquired; evaluation must separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal source exposure, and early execution failures. We construct MC-EvoBench as a controlled Minecraft benchmark with a fixed catalog of 19 registered evolution chains, including 12 primary evaluation chains and seven calibration or probe chains, together with three graph-aligned paired probe families for transfer. The benchmark represents each task as a task-state graph, defines stage-level environment verifiers, assigns matched source and target roles, resets the target world, and permits only a declared agent artifact to cross the source–target boundary. For each probe, no-prior, related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions are evaluated under matched environment-step budgets and five seeds; we report TSR, WGP, and VMP and retain provenance records. The benchmark reveals a consistent direct-capability gap between controller and planner-backed variants, while related experience yields no stable transfer: it does not improve either tool probe, its small wood-species gain hinges on one seed, and all intervals include zero. Stage audits further show that early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks often leave later capabilities unobserved. MC-EvoBench thus offers a controlled testbed for durable, transferable embodied capabilities. Code and data are available at https://github.com/xzw-ustc/mc-bench-open-source . 1 1 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 2 2 footnotetext: Corresponding authors. Figure 1: Evaluation mechanism of MC-EvoBench. A conventional benchmark records only whether an agent reaches the goal. MC-EvoBench also measures progress through the task graph, transfers only a declared experience artifact into a reset target world, and compares related, unrelated, and shuffled source conditions. We separate partial progress, physical carryover, and source-specific experience gains from improvements caused by favorable initial states or execution luck. 1 Introduction One of the central ambitions of autonomous intelligence is recursive self-improvement (RSI) ( Chen et al., 2026 ) : an agent should use experience from its own actions to become more capable over time. The goal is larger than learning one policy or storing one successful trajectory. An RSI system should turn experience into a capability, retain it, and apply it when the task, world, or required action changes. This loop is central to long-horizon autonomy: as tasks become harder, the agent must build on what it has already learned. This view differs from evaluation settings in which training is separated from testing and improvement is summarized by a single score ( Ren et al., 2026 ) . For RSI, the important question is whether a gain remains useful after the original interaction has ended. A capability should survive a change in local conditions, help with a related goal, and combine with actions that were not part of the source task. RSI is therefore a systems problem: learning, memory, planning, and physical interaction must work together, while the resulting gain remains visible and attributable. Embodied agents make this problem concrete and difficult. Their behavior depends on both internal state and physical state. A later success may reflect a tool left in the inventory, a changed world, a favorable location, or more source interaction rather than a reusable capability. A useful benchmark must therefore show that improvement survives a reset and appears in observable behavior. When improved performance follows experience, does it reflect a reusable capability, or merely a changed physical state or execution condition? We study this question through later behavior. A memory, skill file, or model update shows that an agent changed internally. It does not show that the agent gained a useful capability ( Li et al., 2025b ; Park et al., 2025 ; Li et al., 2026 ) . The evidence must link internal change to later action. It must also distinguish capability from favorable execution. To test that claim, we compare target behavior after a world reset and check both task outcomes and stage-level records. Existing benchmarks address parts of this problem. MCU ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) evaluates diverse and combined Minecraft tasks with automatic verification. LifelongAgentBench ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) , EvoAgentBench ( Gao et al., 2026 ) , and PAST-Bench ( Xue et al., 2026 ) study learning across tasks, transfer, and persistent state in other settings. Embodied evaluation also needs to separate world resources from agent state, match source budgets, and record where a task chain fails ( Ni et al., 2025 ; Cheng et al., 2026 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . Otherwise, a score difference may reflect an easier world, more source interaction, or an early failure that hides later behavior. Minecraft makes these controls practical. Collecting resources, crafting tools, and using them create visible task dependencies. A task-state graph represents these relations, and environment evidence verifies each stage. Resetting the world and inventory removes physical carryover, while stage records show progress before a chain stops ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2025 ) . We introduce MC-EvoBench to evaluate embodied RSI in Minecraft. Figure 1 shows its mechanism: measure progress, transfer only a declared agent artifact, and use matched controls to assess experience gains. Table 1 compares this design with representative Minecraft benchmarks ( Guss et al., 2019 ; Fan et al., 2022 ; Hill et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . MC-EvoBench provides a task catalog, verifiers, and three short probe families for wood-species crafting, wooden-tool transfer, and stone-tool transfer. The framework can study capability formation, transfer, retention, and composition. This paper focuses on forward transfer between graph-related tasks. Table 1: Minecraft benchmark comparison for embodied RSI. Dimension MineRL MineDojo MCU MinePlanner OpenHA Voyager MC-EvoBench Capability evolution ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ Source isolation ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Experience persistence ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ Capability transfer ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ Retention and composition ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ Gain attribution ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✗ ✓ ✓ Explicitly modeled or reported; ✗ not a primary design or evaluation dimension. Our main contributions are as follows: 1. Embodied RSI as attributable capability change. We formalize an agent as a policy, a persistent state, and an update rule, and separate this persistent state from the world state. A gain counts as experience-driven only when it appears after the target world is reset, only a declared artifact crosses the source–target boundary, and matched unrelated and shuffled sources rule out alternative explanations. 2. MC-EvoBench, an executable audit of experience-driven improvement. It instantiates this definition in Minecraft with a task-state graph of 80 tasks, 111 states, and 369 typed edges organized into 19 chains; stage-level verifiers with three complementary metrics, Task Success Rate (TSR), Weighted Graph Progress (WGP), and Verified Milestone Progress (VMP); and a four-condition paired protocol with matched environment-step budgets and provenance records. 3. Controlled evidence on embodied transfer. Controller-based agents clearly outperform planner-backed variants in direct capability. Under matched controls, the reference method shows no stable transfer gain, even though its related sources earn more verified progress and, on the longer probes, more computation, and early wood-collection and crafting bottlenecks leave later capabilities unobserved. Future RSI methods must therefore first clear these execution bottlenecks, and their gains should be claimed only after a controlled audit. Section 2 reviews related benchmarks and agents. Section 3 defines the framework and benchmark. Section 4 reports the reference results. Appendices A – G give the task, environment, protocol, and reproduction details. 2 Related Work Minecraft and embodied-agent benchmarks. Minecraft combines visual control, persistent resources, and tasks with many prerequisites. MineDojo provides a large open-world task collection and a knowledge base that supports broad embodied-agent research ( Fan et al., 2022 ) . BEDD extends MineRL ( Guss et al., 2019 ) with demonstrations and evaluation for tasks whose success can be difficult to describe with a single exact goal. MinePlanner focuses on long-horizon planning in large Minecraft worlds, while OpenHA studies open-source hierarchical agents and their execution in the same environment ( Hill et al., 2023 ; Wang et al., 2025 ) . Voyager uses a curriculum, a skill library, and environment feedback for continued exploration and skill reuse, including in a new world ( Wang et al., 2023 ) . MCU evaluates a broad set of tasks, their combinations, and automatic assessment ( Zheng et al., 2023 ) . Together, these benchmarks cover open-world interaction, planning, task diversity, and automatic verification. They do not, however, isolate whether a controlled source interaction causes a later improvement after the target world is reset. Lifelong learning and self-evolving agents. Several recent benchmarks study improvement across tasks and the use of stored experience. LifelongAgentBench tests skill gain, retention, and transfer across databases, operating systems, and knowledge graphs ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . EvoAgentBench uses agent traces to identify abilities and groups tasks by shared procedures, making transfer between related tasks explicit ( Gao et al., 2026 ) . PAST-Bench compares runs with and without persistent state and tracks how experience is saved and reused in personal-agent settings ( Xue et al., 2026 ) . These studies establish useful ideas for measuring persistence and transfer, but their tasks do not expose the same physical-state confounds as embodied environments. In Minecraft, an apparent gain can instead come from a carried tool, a modified world, or a different starting location. MC-EvoBench addresses this boundary by resetting inventory and world changes while allowing only a declared agent artifact to transfer. Its task-state graph makes prerequisites and progress visible. Memory-mediated improvement and benchmark position. Memory systems provide a practical mechanism for experience-driven improvement. Reflexion ( Shinn et al., 2023 ) stores language feedback from failed attempts and uses it to guide later decisions. Agent Workflow Memory extracts reusable procedures from interaction traces for later tasks ( Wang et al., 2026 ) . Skill libraries and model updates offer related ways to preserve information beyond a single episode. These methods show how an agent can store and retrieve experience, but reuse alone does not establish that a capability transferred. MC-EvoBench treats experience-driven improvement as an attribution problem. It separates source and target episodes, resets the physical state, and transfers only a declared artifact. Matched source conditions, verifier predicates, and stage records distinguish capability transfer from carried-over resources and partial execution. 3 MC-EvoBench Framework and Benchmark Design MC-EvoBench tests whether experience changes later behavior. To support that claim, it resets the target world, checks outcomes against environment evidence, and compares matched source conditions. Figure 2 shows how these parts work together. Panel (a) follows the agent from source interaction to target evaluation. Panel (b) shows the tasks, states, relations, chains, and environment profiles that define each test. 3.1 Evaluation Target and State Boundary Figure 2: Benchmark design of MC-EvoBench. Panel (a) follows a paired evaluation from source interaction and artifact formation to target-world reset, target execution, stage verification, and metric reporting. Panel (b) shows how the task catalog is organized into tasks, states, relations, chains, and profiles. These components support graph-based progress measurement, controlled transfer probes, and coverage of embodied capabilities across long-horizon task chains. We ask whether controlled source interaction improves performance on a later target task in a reset world. A stored memory or model update cannot answer this question by itself. We represent an agent as A = ( π , z , U ) A=(\pi,z,U) : π \pi selects actions from observations and goals, z z is the state the method can retain, and U U updates that state from experience. Source experience E S E_{S} produces z S = U ⁡ ( z 0 , E S ) z_{S}=U(z_{0},E_{S}) . The evaluator records and freezes z S z_{S} before the target run. No source resources, positions, world edits, route information, or success markers enter the target. World state includes inventory, tools, resources, position, terrain, and world changes. Persistent agent state may include memories, prompts, replay data, checkpoints, or model updates. Every target run starts with the same registered world and inventory settings. Thus, source tools and world changes cannot explain a target score difference. A stored artifact provides evidence of a gain only when the target verifier also records a change in behavior. 3.2 Task-State Graph MC-EvoBench represents task dependencies and observable resource flow with G = ( 𝒯 , 𝒮 , ℰ ) , G=(\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S},\mathcal{E}), Here, 𝒯 \mathcal{T} contains tasks, 𝒮 \mathcal{S} contains observable states, and ℰ \mathcal{E} contains typed relations. States include items, tools, locations, structures, and task completion. The graph describes what tasks require, produce, or consume without prescribing an action sequence. These three relation types form the strict execution graph. The remaining types, enables and abstracts_to , describe possible capability links and task categories; neither proves transfer. Appendix B.2 defines each edge type and gives their counts. Tasks form stage chains C = ( τ 1 , … , τ K ) C=(\tau_{1},\ldots,\tau_{K}) . Each stage has a goal that the verifier checks against run evidence. The chain shows prerequisites and where execution stops; the agent remains free to choose its actions. Stage records reveal partial progress even when the final goal is not reached. Catalog and probe chains use the same task definitions and verifier rules. Reset settings, retained state, and step budgets are fixed before evaluation. 3.3 Paired Protocol and Metrics Each comparison has a source phase and a target phase. The source agent interacts with registered tasks and forms z S z_{S} . The evaluator then resets the target world and inventory, freezes z S z_{S} , and runs the target task with the same verifier. Four target conditions serve different purposes. No-prior provides a baseline; related experience tests for a change; unrelated experience tests whether that change depends on task relevance; and shuffled related experience tests whether task order matters. We record source steps, termination, artifact identity, and target outcomes. Source episodes restart after early termination until the declared budget is used. The verifier records the evidence for each stage, changes in resources, pass status, and why the run stopped. Let v i v_{i} indicate whether stage i i passes. For each strict execution edge e e , w e w_{e} is its weight and q e q_{e} indicates verified progress. Let m j m_{j} indicate whether eligible milestone j j is reached. The three direct metrics are TSR \displaystyle\mathrm{TSR} = ∑ i = 1 K v i K , \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{K}v_{i}}{K}, (1) WGP \displaystyle\mathrm{WGP} = ∑ e ∈ E exec w e ​ q e ∑ e ∈ E exec w e , \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec}}}w_{e}q_{e}}{\sum_{e\in E_{\mathrm{exec}}}w_{e}}, (2) VMP \displaystyle\mathrm{VMP} = ∑ j = 1 J m j J . \displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{J}m_{j}}{J}. (3) TSR is the fraction of planned stages that pass; unreached stages remain in its denominator. WGP is the weighted fraction of strict graph edges supported by verified progress. VMP tracks eligible item or tool milestones observed before a chain ends. It captures partial progress, not full completion. We report all three metrics for each target condition and compare paired runs. Appendices C and D.6 give the verifier and reporting rules. 3.4 Benchmark Instantiation MC-EvoBench implements this framework in Minecraft with a fixed task catalog, verifiers, probe profiles, and observation interface. A change to any of these components defines a new benchmark version. The same evaluation can therefore test different ways of storing experience, such as textual memories, skill libraries, prompts, or model updates, under a shared task and evidence specification. Its 19 chains include 12 primary evaluation chains and 7 calibration or probe chains. Tasks span building, survival, exploration, and combat. Long chains test execution across many prerequisites. Short probes test local transfer that an early failure in a long chain could hide. The probes use catalog tasks and the same verifier rules. Appendices F and A.3 list the tasks, chains, and profiles. The three probe families and their budgets are listed in Table D.3 of Appendix D.3 . In each family, related and target chains share a dependency pattern but end with a different object or tool. This lets us test transfer while keeping the required preparation steps. Each stage has a 450-step cap. After early termination, a new episode starts until the family budget is used. 3.4.2 Environment and Observation Interface Paired-transfer runs use public world seed 31, an empty target inventory, and one of three fixed environment profiles (Appendix A.3 ); direct-capability runs use the seeds and per-stage profiles in Table F.3 . Profiles set time, weather, spawn, clearance, and public resources. They do not provide target items, routes, private coordinates, or verifier state. The agent must observe and collect resources through interaction. Each target condition starts with a world and inventory reset; only the declared agent artifact can transfer. The agent sees normal observations, while the graph, verifier rules, diagnostics, and hidden coordinates remain unavailable. Appendices A.2 and C.1 detail these access rules and verifier checks. 4 Experimental Results We report two complementary views of the benchmark. The direct capability matrix measures immediate performance across the registered catalog without a source–target transfer claim. The paired probes then test whether a declared source artifact changes behavior on a later target after the world is reset. A low final score can therefore reflect an early execution bottleneck rather than the failure of a later capability, which remains unobserved. Per-seed effects ( Figure 3 b–c ) vary most for wood species, where the small positive mean GATG ( + 0.050 +0.050 ) is driven by a single seed ( + 1.0 +1.0 ) and falls to − 0.19 -0.19 without it; the tool probes vary less and have GATG means near zero. All three intervals cross zero, consistent with Table 4 . Taken together, the direct matrix measures immediate capability rather than transfer, and the paired probes should be read against its low execution floor. Under the current public instances, seeds, budgets, and reference method, related experience does not produce a stable positive transfer effect; this does not rule out gains under a different agent, artifact, task distribution, or source budget. Appendices C.3 , D.6 , and E.4 give the stage records, paired-reporting rules, and configuration fields needed to reproduce these comparisons. Finding 5: Unobserved capabilities cannot be evaluated. Most runs stop in the first crafting stages and the wood-species gain hinges on one seed, so progress needs stage-level evidence, not final success. 5 Conclusion We introduced MC-EvoBench, a controlled Minecraft benchmark for auditing whether experience yields durable and transferable embodied capabilities. Its task-state graph, stage-level verifiers, and paired reset-target protocol with matched control sources separate capability change from carried-over resources, unequal exposure, and early execution failures. In the reference study, controller-based agents clearly outperform planner-backed variants, yet the reference method gains no stable target benefit from related experience: the only positive contrast, on wood species, is driven by a single seed, and all intervals include zero even though related sources earn more verified progress and, on the longer probes, more computation. Most runs also end before crafting sticks, leaving later capabilities unobserved. These conclusions are limited to the tested agents, probes, seeds, and budgets; retention, composition, stronger agents, and more seeds are natural next steps. Appendix A Minecraft Environment Settings MC-EvoBench evaluates whether interaction experience can improve subsequent embodied execution. Its experimental unit joins a source experience, a persistent agent artifact, and a separately initialized target evaluation. This appendix specifies the environment, task construction, verification, experimental protocol, agent interfaces, task suite, and reproducibility materials. A.1 Game world and interaction interface The primary environment is Minecraft 1.16.5 through MineRL, with a custom survival specification named MCBenchHumanSurvival-v0 . It extends the HumanSurvival environment with observations for inventory, local resources, world conditions, and task events. The agent interacts with the game through an adapter, while a separate evaluator converts the environment response into a normalized observation snapshot. This separation supports a common task definition across agents with different planning and control architectures. The native control interface consists of movement, camera rotation, attack, use, and inventory operations. Camera commands change pitch and yaw; the meaning of attack and use depends on whether the agent is interacting with the world or an inventory interface. These environment actions produce the observations used for task verification. Text-conditioned controllers translate a task instruction into this action interface. A programmatic agent may use a different bridge, in which case its action granularity is reported with the method settings in Appendix E . Table A1. Interaction and observation interfaces. The evaluator consumes the evidence needed by a task; an agent consumes the modalities exposed by its declared adapter. A.2 Observation access and normalized evidence The catalog distinguishes native_perception and structured_state observation sources. Each source records a path, its primary or diagnostic role, its interpretation, and an access declaration. Inventory, equipment, and basic survival measurements are examples of declared agent-visible sources. Local block counts, mission flags, kill counters, and world-light diagnostics are classified as structured evidence. RGB-based and structured-state methods therefore remain distinguishable even when they share the same task verifier. At runtime, the snapshot groups observations into inventory, equipment, player statistics, counters, flags, raw observations, and environment metadata. Equipment names are normalized across MineRL representations, and raw entity-kill observations can populate the corresponding normalized counter. The evaluator preserves the raw channel alongside the normalized value, which makes it possible to trace a predicate back to its observation source. The actual model inputs are determined by the adapter; Appendix E describes the built-in interfaces. The local block grid spans offsets from ( − 3 , − 2 , − 3 ) (-3,-2,-3) to ( 3 , 2 , 3 ) (3,2,3) around the player, giving a 7 × 5 × 7 7\times 5\times 7 observation volume. The ray channel supplies a block identity and distance. Grid counts support local structure checks; ray observations support direct resource visibility. Profile-provided resource markers describe the configured scene and serve as diagnostics. The coal-discovery predicate uses coal observed in the ray channel or local block grid. A.4 State continuity within a task chain The chain specification selects either a task-level or chain-level profile policy. Under the task-level policy, the runner selects each task’s profile; with the default per-stage reset setting, a profile change causes an environment reset. Under the chain-level policy, one selected profile governs the chain. Consecutive stages that remain in the same environment can reuse world resources and inventory, making state continuity an explicit part of chain evaluation. This within-chain continuity is separate from the source-to-target boundary. A target transfer evaluation starts from its prescribed environment state and receives only the permitted persistent artifact. A tool retained between two stages changes their execution conditions; a tool reconstructed after a target reset provides evidence about execution under the retained agent state. The protocol records these two situations separately. Keeping these fields together allows the same task to be placed in a short probe, a longer chain, or an independent evaluation without redefining its meaning. B.4 Composition patterns Resource progression chains connect acquisition to increasingly demanding use. For example, the ore progression chain moves through wood preparation, basic tools, stone tools, ore collection, smelting, and higher-tier mining. Cross-domain chains join heterogeneous endpoints: locating coal, obtaining fuel, creating illumination, building shelter, and remaining alive, or preparing a weapon before a combat event. Transfer chains substitute wood species, tool recipes, or item roles while retaining comparable dependency patterns. The task suite also includes short probes. These isolate resource collection or limited crafting sequences, helping distinguish an early execution bottleneck from a long-horizon planning requirement. A short probe and a long chain answer different questions, even when they contain the same task identifier. Their sequence, start state, budget, and profile policy accompany their scores. A completed possession task establishes its predicate at that stage. If the same item remains in inventory, a later occurrence with the same predicate may pass immediately. The ordered stage record makes this behavior explicit: initial-state passes have zero action steps, while newly acquired items appear in the observed state transition. Composition is consequently described through stage outcomes and state continuity, with experience transfer assessed by the reset protocol in Appendix D . B.5 Extending the catalog A new task can be added by defining its instruction and measurable endpoint, identifying the required observation channels, selecting an environment profile, and attaching its graph relations. A new chain then specifies an ordered list of existing or new task identifiers. Compilation checks the declared dependency order, and an execution check verifies that the configured environment exposes the evidence required by its predicates. The reusable components are the task contract, graph relations, profile registry, and runner interface. A method’s planner, retrieval rule, or memory format remains outside the task definition. This allows a future agent to implement a different experience representation while being evaluated against the same target objectives and evidence rules. A task contains a conjunction of predicates, with optional disjunctive subexpressions. Inventory thresholds check resource or item possession; equipment predicates accept an item in a specified slot; counters capture events such as an entity defeat; snapshot comparisons read a named observation field. For each reported stage, the metric extracts item/tool states from its execution paths and assigns each state the largest included edge-count threshold. Efficiency summaries include environment steps, stage budgets, steps per passed stage, and observed deaths. The objective is therefore satisfied by the corresponding inventory count. For craft_stone_sword , the catalog accepts a stone sword either in inventory or in the main hand, matching the game’s distinction between carrying and equipping a tool. The coal-discovery task uses observed coal in a ray or grid channel; the subsequent coal-collection task checks the collected item. These examples illustrate why the task contract separates an instruction, its observation sources, and its terminal predicate. The instruction gives the agent a goal, the observation contract defines the evidence channels, and the predicate fixes the endpoint. The same decomposition supports independently checking an item goal, a temporal objective, or a cross-domain chain through explicit predicates. Appendix D Evaluation protocol D.1 Experience, artifact, and target evaluation MC-EvoBench separates capability measurement from the experience that may change an agent. A paired evaluation first measures a target with the base agent, then measures the same target with an artifact produced through a specified source curriculum. The artifact may contain updated parameters, memory, a skill library, or another declared persistent representation. Its identity and provenance define the agent state being evaluated. This interface accommodates different adaptation mechanisms while keeping the target task and its verifier fixed. At the source-to-target boundary, the target world and inventory are reset. Only the frozen method-produced artifact crosses this boundary. Consequently, tools, blocks, completed constructions, and resource inventories accumulated during source interaction do not supply target progress. In the supplied memory configuration, source interaction uses read_write memory and target evaluation uses read_only memory. Each target role constructs a fresh agent and environment; persistent source experience is loaded from its declared artifact. Within a compiled chain, stages execute in order and preserve the environment state permitted by the chain profile. The runner stops at the first non-passing stage. The transfer probes use one chain-level profile throughout an episode. Source episodes can restart to complete their interaction budget, as described in Appendix D.3 . These distinct boundaries preserve sequential task dependencies within an episode and isolate learned experience across evaluations. Figure D1. Each source condition produces its own artifact from the same base agent. Target evaluations share task, world, budget, and seed settings. At the boundary, the world, inventory, and transient agent state are reset while the declared persistent artifact is retained. VPT loads its network specification and policy-head settings from the model file; its sampling temperature is inherited from that file. Optimus-3 creates a task representation when the instruction changes, then combines it with successive frames. E.2 Persistent experience and adaptation The JARVIS online extension stores stage-level textual records containing the instruction, proposed plan, dispatched controller prompts, status, interaction count and visible-state summary. Retrieval uses token-set Jaccard similarity between the current instruction and each stored instruction, adds 0.15 for a successful record, and breaks score ties in favour of newer records. Up to four positive-scoring records condition planning. Memory retains the latest 256 records and is written atomically. The planner returns one to six short controller prompts; reflection produces a practical sentence capped at 500 characters. The reflection input distinguishes a proposed plan from prompts actually dispatched and labels the state summary as the last pre-action observation. ExpeL uses the same episode-retrieval score and supplements episodes with retrieved textual insights and a weighted rule list. Insight retrieval uses lexical overlap; rule retrieval adds a weight contribution capped at 0.10. With the configured insight limit of eight, the planner may receive up to eight insights and eight rules. Reflection proposes ADD, EDIT, REMOVE and AGREE operations. New rules start with weight two; agreement and editing increment weight, while removal decrements it. The persistent artifact records these updates alongside episode actions. Both memory methods support read-write source interaction and read-only target evaluation; read-only stage callbacks suppress reflection and memory writes. E.3 Planning and execution cadence The JARVIS extension plans when a new stage instruction becomes active. It dispatches successive subgoals for fixed 120-step intervals and retains the final subgoal for any remaining stage steps. Stage completion invalidates the active instruction so repeated task text can trigger a new plan. Optimus-1’s visual planner uses the same interval rule and a JSON subgoal format. Its input is a JPEG thumbnail bounded by 384 × \times 384 pixels at quality 85. The parser filters subgoals containing “open,” “place,” or “access” followed by a space, rewrites punch/collect/gather to chop, and retains up to six subgoals. ExpeL instead requests a low-level action mapping and can hold that action across a configured number of environment steps. The 19-chain configuration sets this hold to 32, while the factory default is one. Its prompt also supplies explicit line-of-sight guidance for approaching and mining visible resources. The Voyager skill bridge follows a separate execution protocol. The runner loads released JavaScript skills and control primitives, resets through the Mineflayer bridge with empty inventory and equipment, and invokes a fixed skill sequence. A configured starting position is applied during setup. The runner checks the returned inventory for its designated target item. Its step count denotes a bridge request, and the implementation invokes no LLM; this execution unit is recorded separately from MineRL interaction steps. The planning request combines the current goal, an agent-visible state summary, and retrieved experience. It returns a small sequence of text subgoals for the visual controller. The reflection request summarizes a completed source episode for later retrieval. Cards G.1 and G.1 specify the input–output contracts and system prompts. Card G1. Online-memory planning Purpose. Translate the current goal and retrieved experience into controller subgoals. Input. goal , visible_state , retrieved_experience Output. JSON steps with 1–6 text prompts. 1 You are a Minecraft task planner controlling a visual low-level policy. Use only the 2 natural-language goal, visible state, and prior experience. Do not assume access to reward 3 predicates, task graphs, hidden world coordinates, or tools outside Minecraft. Return JSON 4 only: {"steps":["short visual action prompt", ...]}. Provide 1 to 6 concise prompts 5 suitable for a STEVE-I-like action controller. Card G2. Experience reflection Purpose. Convert source-stage feedback into reusable advice. Input. Goal, pre-action state, dispatched prompts, stage feedback. Output. One practical sentence stored as advice . 1 You summarize one Minecraft episode for later reuse. Use only the supplied goal, 2 agent-visible state summary, controller dispatch evidence, and stage feedback. The plan is 3 proposed text, not proof that every prompt was attempted. The visible_state is the last pre-action observation, not a post-action terminal 6 observation. Do not invent hidden information or unobserved events. Return one concise 7 practical sentence. The planning payload contains goal , visible_state , and retrieved_experience . Retrieved records expose the instruction, plan, status, and advice. The planning parser returns up to six non-empty steps, using the task instruction as its default. Reflection receives stage feedback together with the actually dispatched prompts, allowing the stored advice to distinguish planned behavior from observed execution context. G.2 Persistent memory representation The artifact is a JSON object containing a record count and a list of episode records. Each record associates a task instruction with a proposed plan, the prompts dispatched to the controller, terminal status, interaction count, visible state, and advice. The memory writer keeps the latest configured number of records and replaces the artifact atomically. A read-only target run under the listed field values. 1 { 2 "environment_profile": "evolution_wood_species_grove", 3 "max_stage_steps": 450, 4 "environment": { 5 "kind": "minerl", 6 "seed": 31, 7 "per_stage_profiles": false 8 }, 9 "agent": { 10 "kind": "jarvis1_online", 11 "random_seed": 5100, 12 "memory_mode": "read_only", 13 "memory_max_records": 256, 14 "retrieval_limit": 4, 15 "skill_horizon_steps": 120 16 }, 17 "probe": { 18 "profile_policy": "chain", 19 "task_ids": [ 20 "collect_acacia_log", 21 "craft_acacia_planks" 22 ] 23 } 24 } The target collects acacia logs and crafts acacia planks while using the artifact generated by the related birch source. The chain profile remains constant within this episode. Stage limits are applied by the runner, and task success uses the catalog predicates. The source role uses its own task sequence and enables memory writing; all target roles retain the same task definition. G.5 Evaluation algorithm The following pseudocode summarizes the common orchestration contract. Source interaction, artifact persistence, environment reset, and target evaluation are separate operations. The same control flow can host parameter updates, text memory, or executable skills, provided that the permitted persistent state and input interface are declared. Card G6. Paired experience evaluation Purpose. Isolate the effect of related source experience. Input. Probe family, paired seed, base agent, matched source budget. Output. Four matched target scores and within-seed contrasts. 1 for each probe family and paired seed: 2 base = load_base_agent_state() 3 score[0] = evaluate_target(base, fresh_target_world()) 4 for condition in [related, unrelated, shuffled]: 5 state = independent_copy(base) 6 remaining = source_budget[family] 7 while remaining > 0: 8 episode = run_source_episode(state, condition, remaining) 9 update_source_artifact(state, episode) 10 remaining -= episode.environment_steps 11 artifact = freeze_and_identify(state.persistent_state) 12 target_agent = load_for_read_only_evaluation(base, artifact) 13 score[condition] = evaluate_target( 14 target_agent, fresh_target_world()) 15 save_paired_contrasts(score, source_costs, artifact_identities) At the task level, evaluation first observes the initial state, then alternates action and predicate evaluation until a terminal condition is reached. At the chain level, the runner applies the selected profile policy and records the first non-passing stage. At the experiment level, matched roles are combined within a seed before aggregation. These layers align environment execution, task success, and experience comparison at their respective units of analysis. G.6 Reproduction entry points Table G.6 identifies the small set of source components that define the benchmark. The accompanying task and chain CSV files provide compact access to the catalog, while the JSON source files retain the executable definitions. Table G3. The experiment configuration records these choices alongside the catalog snapshot. Card G.6 runs from the appendix bundle directory and resolves the catalog through the companion path map. Card G7.
