A small model’s gain. No result on a real repository. Scripted corrections, and few runs. What measurement costs. What a rollout could read. No independent replication. 8 Conclusion References A Further results License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.14216v1 [cs.SE] 09 Oct 2026 [Extension=.otf, UprightFont=*-regular, BoldFont=*-bold, ItalicFont=*-italic, BoldItalicFont=*-bolditalic] \setmathfont texgyretermes-math.otf [Scale=0.82, BoldFont=DejaVuSansMono-Bold.ttf] Cortex: Measurement-Gated Evolution and Pruning of Coding-Agent Skills and Rules Samuele Giampieri Affiliation: Independent researcher October 2026 Abstract AI coding agents such as Claude Code do not act on their training alone; they also follow text files that developers write for them. A project file describes how the code should be written, skills are short guides the agent may choose to read when it judges them relevant, and rules are notes tied to particular files, which the agent sees automatically whenever it opens one of those files. We call these files the agent’s harness . Developers add to it each time they have to correct the agent, but checking whether an addition really helps is harder than it looks: the same agent given the same task can succeed once and fail the next time, so seeing an instruction work once proves little. We present Cortex, a tool that tests changes to the harness instead of trusting them. At the end of a working session it saves any fix the session made as a task it can replay; across sessions it spots the corrections the developer keeps making, and writes one new skill or rule at a time to prevent them. It then runs the agent on those tasks several times with the new text and several times without it, and keeps the text only if it helps overall and makes no single task noticeably worse. Text already in the harness is tested the same way before it is deleted. Throughout, Cortex records whether each piece of text reached the agent, and it neither adds nor deletes text that the agent never used. We tested Cortex with Claude Haiku 4.5 on a repository built for the purpose, with a few coding conventions the model tends to break and one area with nothing to learn, kept as a comparison. A script played the developer, and Cortex was run several times from scratch. Each harness it built was then tested on new tasks it had never seen. The harnesses Cortex built made the agent follow the conventions far more often than a harness with no skills or rules, left the comparison area unchanged, and added no text that the agent must read at every step. The clearest lesson is about how advice is delivered rather than what it says: rules, which the agent sees automatically, did most of the work, while skills, which the agent must choose to open, helped only when they were offered for the files a task touched; offered on every turn, they were rarely opened. We also fed Cortex useless and harmful suggestions on purpose. It kept none of them, but the agent never opened the useless ones or the harmful skills, and the harmful rules, which did load, were tried on tasks that mostly failed without them, where Cortex reached no verdict, even when a harmful rule broke a task that passed without it. This shows that Cortex keeps no text the agent never uses, not yet that it can spot text that does damage. Finally, in this study Cortex was worth as much as the model needed correcting: under the stronger Claude Sonnet 5, which already followed most of the conventions, a single run’s harness added little, and on a real open-source project where the agent was rarely corrected, Cortex found nothing to learn. We release the tool, the evaluation lab and the data behind every number in the paper. 1 Introduction Coding agents are increasingly steered not only by their weights but by text their users edit. A project instruction file ( CLAUDE.md , or AGENTS.md [ 16 ] ), a folder of skills the agent may choose to invoke, and rules that load when the agent reads matching files [ 4 , 5 ] together make up what this paper calls the agent’s harness : the part of its behaviour a developer can change in a minute, by editing text. The agent works in turns : at each step the model reads its context , the text in front of it (the harness text that is loaded, the request and the work so far), and then acts. Harnesses grow the way documentation grows. A correction a developer has to make twice becomes a line, the line stays, and every line that is always in context is paid for on every turn of every session. Little of it is measured. Whether an instruction helps is often judged the way it was written: by someone who watched it work once. That is not evidence, because an agent’s success on a fixed task is a noisy quantity: the model samples its output, so the same agent can pass a task on one attempt and fail it on the next. Results in this paper are therefore given as a pass rate , the share of attempts that succeeded, and differences between pass rates in percentage points . In the evaluation reported here, one and the same harness, measured twice on the same tasks in separate batches of rollouts, differed by −3.3 points (95% confidence interval, or CI, [−7.3, 0.0], resampling tasks; Section 4 explains these intervals), a difference that, seen once, would pass for an effect. Recent studies report that adding skills can make an agent worse [ 54 ] , that skill gains measured on the tasks one repository supplies could not be told apart from run-to-run noise [ 26 ] , and that whether an updated harness helps depends on the model that uses it: weaker models often fail to activate, or to follow, what was added [ 31 ] . A harness curated by impression can accumulate instructions that do nothing, some that hurt, and a context bill for all of them. A growing body of work optimises or evolves agent text automatically: prompts and programs [ 25 , 1 ] , agent designs [ 18 , 66 ] , and most recently the harness itself [ 72 , 27 , 65 , 10 ] . These systems are typically optimised and evaluated against benchmarks. A developer’s problem is narrower and, in one respect, harder: one repository, its own conventions, a handful of tasks drawn from their own work, a fixed context budget, and no way to tell whether a given instruction earns its place. We present Cortex , a tool for Claude Code that treats the harness as something to measure rather than to curate ( Figure 1 ). Cortex calls each skill or rule an item , and the harness the developer is using now the live harness. It consists of three commands. /harvest runs at the end of a working session. When something in the session went from broken to working, it saves a replayable task : the broken commit, the developer’s request, and a check , a script that decides whether an attempt at the task succeeded. It also logs each correction the developer made along the way. /evolve reads the corrections that recur and writes one new skill or rule, a candidate , for one of them. It also chooses the candidate’s loading tier , which decides when its text enters the agent’s context ( Section 2 ): if the fixes behind the problem sit in one folder, the candidate loads only when the agent works there. It then runs the agent on the harvested tasks several times each, with the live harness and with the live harness plus the candidate, in disposable clones of the repository. Each attempt is a rollout , and a batch of rollouts that compares two harnesses in this way is a sweep . The candidate is kept only if it helped, fired in at least one of its rollouts (a rule loaded into the agent’s context, or a skill opened), and made no task worse beyond a set tolerance, which is zero on a task the live harness never failed; a candidate killed only for such a drop is swept again first. /prune works the other way round: it re-measures live items by removing them one at a time, and never deletes one it has not seen fire. One principle runs through both measurements: an item is credited or blamed only where it entered the agent’s context. Figure 1: The Cortex loop. /harvest turns a session that went from broken to working into a task; /evolve measures one candidate against the live harness and keeps it only if it helped, fired, and cost no task more than a small tolerance; /prune re-measures live items by removal and keeps any item it never saw fire. We evaluate Cortex in a replicated study ( Section 4 ), with Claude Haiku 4.5 as both the agent that is measured and the one that runs Cortex’s commands. The study uses a small synthetic repository with four house rules : conventions of that one project, such as reading the current time only through its own clock module, which code can break while still working, and which the model often breaks unaided. Each house rule has a family of tasks built around it; a fifth family, plain bugs with no rule to learn, is the control . A script plays the developer. The 4 independent runs , R1 to R4, each start from a fresh copy of the repository, play the same 10 rounds of scripted sessions, and let Cortex evolve a harness from them. Every harness is then measured on 30 held-out scenarios: pieces of work of the same families that no session played. The loop never saw them, so a gain on them cannot come from remembering the tasks it was shown: what it learned has to carry over to new work. The main findings are these. • It works on held-out scenarios. On the four rule families, the evolved harness beats a harness with no skills or rules by +55.0 points of pass rate (95% CI [+34.1, +74.1], permutation p = 0.0001 p=0.0001 ). The interval allows for chance in both which runs and which scenarios were measured. The control family changes by −0.8 points, and no run kept an item for it. • It adds no always-on context. Every item the loop kept has a paths field, which ties it to certain files, so that it loads only when the agent works on them. So the evolved harness adds nothing to what every turn carries: beyond the skill listing every arm shares, its only text present on every turn is the 559-character CLAUDE.md that the harness with no skills or rules has too. In the one run that measured it (R1), the evolved harness also scored 11.1 points higher on the rule families than a harness that instead appends the project’s contribution guide, the file that states the house rules, to CLAUDE.md (95% CI [0.0, +22.5]); the interval reaches zero, and the comparison crosses a batch boundary ( Section 5.4 ). • It kept nothing known to be useless or harmful. None of 20 placebo candidates (plausible advice about matters the repository does not care about) and none of 5 harmful ones was kept. The test was weaker than those counts suggest. Each candidate is first tried in a short, cheap sweep, its screen , which runs only those of the tasks the candidate was written for that the live harness does not always pass. The agent never opened the placebos or the 2 harmful skills on their screens, so none could be kept: Cortex’s scoring script refused the harmful skills and 12 placebos for never being used, and reached no verdict on the other 8 placebos, whose screens could show no gain. The 3 harmful rules did load, but harm shows only on a task that passes without the harmful item, and these screens ran on tasks chosen because the live harness had failed them, where no task could show a gain; so Cortex’s scoring script reached no verdict on them, even on the screen where a rule broke a task that passed without it ( Section 5.3 ). • Rules are loaded; skills must be chosen. Of the 18 items kept across the runs, 16 are rules. Claude Code adds a rule to the context itself, whenever the agent reads a file that matches the rule’s paths . Of a skill, only the description is listed to the agent; the body enters the context only if the agent decides to open it, and often it did not. A path-gated candidate, a skill listed only once the agent works with matching files, was listed in 66 attempts at a task, in its own sweeps and in the gate test ( Section 5.3 ), and opened in 28. An always-on candidate, a skill listed on every turn, was listed in 198 attempts, likewise in its own sweeps and in the gate test, and opened in none of them. • Its value shrinks under a stronger model. The harness of run R1, which gained +66.7 points under Claude Haiku 4.5, the model it was evolved with, gained +5.6 points under Claude Sonnet 5 (95% CI [−2.8, +13.9]). One /prune pass after the upgrade, which ran each item’s tasks 3 times with the item and 3 times without it, flagged 2 of its 4 items as removable. We also report what did not work. Only 2 of 4 known-good candidates were kept. /prune reached the expected verdict on 6 of the 8 items it was tested on, but on only 2 of the 4 planted ones, items we added to a harness with a known right answer. It kept a useless always-on skill, which the agent never opened in its own sweep, because 2 tasks passed less often when it was removed. And an always-on skill that the agent never opens got no verdict where the test asks for unmeasured , the verdict for an item that never fired: /prune ’s plan leaves such an item out, since no sweep could delete it, so the item stayed without being measured. Both results miss the margins of their hypotheses ( Sections 5.3 and 5.5 ). On a real open-source repository the agent was rarely corrected, so nothing recurred and the loop learned nothing. Finally, Cortex can consult an optional judge , an outside model that advises which candidates to try ( Section 3.7 ). It was switched off during the runs; replayed on their candidates afterwards, it did not anticipate the verdicts ( Section 5.7 ). Contributions. 1. Exposure-aware measurement semantics for harness items, where an item’s exposure is whether it entered the agent’s context in a rollout: the same rule governs adding and deleting, so that both verdicts compare the harness with and without the item only on the tasks where it entered the context, a candidate that never fired is not kept, an item that never fired is not deleted, and unknown exposure blocks the verdict ( Section 3 ). 2. A known-answer test of the acceptance pipeline : 20 placebo, 5 harmful and 4 known-good candidates run through it. It shows that a candidate that never fires is never kept; it could not test harm, and the test’s other weaknesses are reported ( Section 5.3 ). 3. Evidence on loading tiers : why an item the agent must choose fares differently under measurement from one that is simply loaded ( Sections 5.2 and 5.4 ). 4. A replicated evaluation with a control run in which /evolve is off, an A/A arm (the same harness measured twice, to show how far two measurements of one harness can differ), ablations (other harnesses, each built to answer one question, such as the evolved harness with its paths removed), a model-change study and a real-repository attempt. Every number can be regenerated offline from the released data: rows exported from the runs’ records and from Claude Code’s session records (the records themselves are not released). 5. The open-source tool and its evaluation lab , at https://github.com/samugit83/cortex : tag v1.0-eval is the system as evaluated, and tag v1.0.5 adds the lab’s data and the scripts that regenerate every number in the paper. 2 Background The harness and its loading tiers. Claude Code reads three kinds of text a developer writes [ 4 , 5 ] . A CLAUDE.md at the root of a repository holds project instructions and is read at the start of every session; recent versions of Claude Code read an AGENTS.md in its place when a repository has no CLAUDE.md , and tailoring a coding agent to a repository with such a context file is widespread practice [ 16 ] . A rule is a Markdown file in .claude/rules/ . It may carry a paths field, a list of file patterns such as shop/billing/** (every file under shop/billing/ ). A path-less rule, one without the field, is loaded at launch, like CLAUDE.md ; a path-scoped rule enters the context when the agent reads a file its patterns match, and, as Cortex’s tests found on version 2.1.276, when the request names such a file with an @ -mention. A skill is a folder in .claude/skills/ holding a SKILL.md : a short description, then a body with the instructions. Only the description is kept in context, in a listing of the available skills; the body is loaded when the skill is invoked : the agent opens it with a call to Claude Code’s Skill tool, or the user types its name as a command. A skill without paths is always-on : its description is listed on every turn. A path-gated skill, one with paths , is listed only once the agent works with matching files. Every description in the listing costs context on every turn, whether or not its skill is ever used [ 5 ] . Table 1 summarises these five loading tiers . The difference that matters most in this paper is between an item that is loaded and one that must be chosen : Claude Code itself puts a rule into the context, but a skill acts only if the agent, reading its description among the others, decides to open it. Table 1: Loading tiers in Claude Code [ 4 , 5 ] . The rows for items with paths are as Cortex verified them on version 2.1.276, the oldest it accepts; the current documentation also counts writes and edits among the triggers of a path-scoped rule. The tier, not the text, decides how often an item is paid for, and whether it is loaded (rules) or must be chosen by the agent (skills). Tier What sits in context When root CLAUDE.md the whole file every turn always-on skill its description; the body when invoked every turn path-less rule the whole rule every turn path-gated skill its description; the body when invoked after a matching file is read or written path-scoped rule the whole rule after a matching file is read or @-mentioned Tasks with a check. Coding agents are evaluated on tasks cut from real repositories: a codebase at a commit where something is broken, a request in natural language, and tests that decide whether the agent’s change fixes it. SWE-bench keeps only task instances with at least one test that fails before the reference solution, the fix the project’s developers actually merged, and passes after it [ 22 ] ; SWE-rebench extracts such tasks automatically and continuously, so that models can be scored on fresh tasks they cannot have seen [ 6 ] . Cortex keeps the format but takes its tasks from the developer’s own sessions rather than from public issues ( Section 3.3 ). One run is not a measurement. An agent’s attempt at a task is a random draw: the model samples its output, so two attempts at the same task can take different paths through the repository, and one may pass where the other fails. A task therefore has a pass rate , and a single pass or fail estimates it poorly. Three studies show how noisy one run is. On the retail tasks of τ \tau -bench, a GPT-4o agent, then the state of the art, solved about three tasks in five on a single attempt, but solved the same task in all eight of eight attempts less than a quarter of the time [ 63 ] . In the published repeated trials of a coding-agent benchmark, fewer than one task in five had a one-run result that reliably tracked an agent’s score on the whole benchmark [ 13 ] . When the skill files of three repositories were optimised automatically, the larger of two optimisers’ average gains, about five points, could not be separated from the agent’s run-to-run variance with the tasks one repository supplies [ 26 ] . Treating an evaluation as an experiment, Miller recommends two remedies [ 36 ] : sample each question more than once, so that the luck of single attempts averages out; and compare two systems through their paired, question-level differences rather than their two overall scores, so that what makes a question easy or hard for both systems cancels. Cortex does both: it runs every task k k times under the live harness and k k times under the candidate, and compares the two task by task ( Section 3.4 ). 3 Cortex Cortex changes only text: the files that make up a Claude Code harness. The model is fixed. This section describes Cortex as it stands at the git tag v1.0-eval , a named snapshot of its code, with that snapshot’s default settings. Every experiment of Section 4 was made on this version, except the development run D0, which used an earlier one. No run changed a gate’s threshold, so the rules that decide whether an item is kept are the same in every experiment. The runs changed a few other settings, none of which decides a verdict; Section 4 lists them. Section 3.1 follows the three commands from start to finish. The subsections after it give the reasons for each step: what an item costs ( Section 3.2 ), where the tasks come from ( Section 3.3 ), how a change is measured ( Section 3.4 ), when a new item is kept ( Section 3.5 ), and when an old one is deleted ( Section 3.6 ). Figure 2 collects the terms they use, for reference. Figure 2: The terms this paper uses for Cortex, in roughly the order a reader meets them, with the subsection that explains each in full. Term Meaning See harness the text files that steer the agent: CLAUDE.md , skills and rules Section 2 item a skill or a rule, the harness files Cortex measures Section 3.2 live harness the harness the developer is using now Section 3.4 loading tier when an item’s text enters the agent’s context ( Table 1 ) Section 2 task an episode /harvest saved so it can be replayed: a broken commit, the request, a check and the fix Section 3.3 check a script that exits zero when an attempt solved the task Section 3.3 quarantine set aside a task whose check no longer tells the broken state from the fixed one, or needs the fix’s own test code Section 3.3 lesson one logged line for each correction the developer made Section 3.1 theme a problem that recurs in the lessons or the failing tasks Section 3.5 candidate a new skill or rule under test, not yet live Section 3.5 rollout one attempt by the agent at one task, in a sandbox clone of the repository Section 3.4 sweep a batch of rollouts that runs each of a set of tasks k k times under each of two harnesses Section 3.4 run (of a task) one of the k k rollouts of a task under one arm of a sweep; not to be confused with an evaluation run, R1 to R4 ( Section 4 ) Section 3.4 pinned model the one model that every rollout uses, when the developer names it in Cortex’s configuration Section 3.4 base , cand the two arms of a sweep: the live harness, and the live harness with the change under test Section 3.4 exposed, fire a task is exposed to an item when the item reached the context in one of its rollouts (a rule loaded, a skill at least listed); the stricter second one, on every task Section 3.5 gate one condition a candidate must meet to be kept, computed by the scoring script score.sh ( Table 2 ); gates 2 and 3, which stop a candidate that makes a task worse, are the regression gates Section 3.5 recheck (RECHECK) a repeat sweep of the tasks that dropped, when a candidate failed only the regression gates, before its KILL is final Section 3.5 KEEP, KILL the candidate goes live; The commands are prompts that the model follows; for every step that must be exact (running a sweep, scoring it, recording a cycle), they call a command-line program, cortex , whose subcommands, such as cortex cycle or cortex scope , appear below. /harvest runs at the end of a working session and turns what happened into evidence: a replayable task when something went from broken to working, and a one-line lesson for each correction ( Figure 3 ). /evolve runs one cycle at a time: it looks in that evidence for one recurring problem, writes one skill or rule for it, and measures it against the live harness before it is kept ( Figure 4 ). /prune is meant to run monthly and after every model change: it measures what removing each item of its plan costs, one item at a time, and deletes only what costs nothing measurable ( Figure 5 ). The three figures follow each command from start to finish, including every point where it stops early; the rest of this section gives the reasons for each step. Figure 3: What /harvest does at the end of a working session. It asks two questions about the session (step 1). A : did something go from broken to working? B : did the developer correct the agent, even once? In most sessions the answer to both is no, and nothing is recorded. If the answer to A is yes, the command saves that change as a task that can be replayed later (step 2): the developer’s request, word for word; the commit where the code was still broken; the fix that made it work; and a check, a short script that says whether an attempt solved the problem. Before the task is kept, preflight tests the check itself in a throwaway copy of the repository (step 3). The check must fail on the broken code, pass once the fix is applied, and still pass when the fix’s changes to test code are left out, so that an agent is judged on the code it writes, not on reproducing the developer’s own test. A task that fails any of the three is set aside and gets one repair; if it fails again, it is deleted ( Section 3.3 ). If the answer to B is yes, the command writes one line per correction to a log of lessons : the date, the task, what the agent did, and what it should have done (step 4). A lesson is written even when the same one is already there, because /evolve counts the repeats to find the problems that recur. Finally, the command reports which items of the current harness already cover the files the fix touched (step 5). /harvest only records: it never runs the agent on a task and never writes a skill or rule, which is /evolve ’s job. The tasks it saves are used next by /evolve , to measure new candidates, and by /prune , to measure what removing an item costs. The model proposes and writes the candidate, but never decides its fate: every verdict comes from a scoring script ( Table 2 ). Steps 1 to 4 prepare the cycle and run the agent on no task; the first three can end the cycle early (grey badges). Step 1 re-runs preflight to make sure the saved tasks still tell broken code from fixed code; if too few are left, the cycle stops. Step 2 looks for one theme , a problem that recurs: a lesson logged at least 3 times, or a cause behind 2 or more failing tasks. If none clears that bar, the cycle ends as BARREN and runs no rollouts. Step 3 chooses where the candidate should load: if the fixes behind the theme sit in one folder, it becomes a rule or a skill tied to that folder; if they are spread across the repository, it becomes a skill offered on every turn. A fact the agent breaks during unrelated work becomes a line in CLAUDE.md , and a check that must always run becomes a hook , a command Claude Code runs by itself at a fixed point of a session; such a change is written and recorded in the journal , Cortex’s running log of every cycle and verdict ( .evolve/journal.md ), but not measured. Step 4 writes the candidate under a new name, outside the live harness. Steps 5 to 7 measure it: the agent attempts each task with the live harness ( base ) and with the harness plus the candidate ( cand ), each attempt in its worker’s own clone of the repository, reset and verified before every attempt ( Figure 6 ). The screen (step 5) is cheap, 2 runs per task on the theme’s tasks only; a candidate that gained nothing, or that never fired (a rule never loaded, a skill never opened), is killed here. The confirm (step 6) is stricter, 3 runs per task on every valid task, so that it also sees what the candidate might break. The candidate is kept only if it wins overall, no task collapses, no task that never failed starts failing, and it fired at least once. Because one unlucky run can look like a broken task, a candidate that failed only on such a drop gets a recheck (step 7, drawn dashed): the tasks that dropped are run again, and the candidate is killed only if the drop repeats. A sweep whose data cannot be trusted, with runs missing or invalid, or in which no task the candidate reached could show a gain, is repeated rather than decided (RERUN). Step 8 acts on the verdict: a KEEP moves the candidate into the live harness and records the confirm sweep’s scores as the new baseline, with no new rollouts; a KILL buries it in the graveyard , the folder of rejected ideas ( .evolve/graveyard/ ), with its reason, so the same idea is not proposed again unchanged. Step 9 records the cycle in the journal; after 2 cycles in a row without a KEEP, cortex cycle signals the loop to stop. It is meant to run monthly and after every change of model, since a stronger model may already do what an item teaches. Steps 1 to 3 plan the pass and run the agent on no task. Step 1 checks that the tasks are still valid, that the routing is sound (no name is both a skill and a rule, no symlink leaves the repository or dangles), and that the rollouts are not pinned to a model other than the one in use; if any check fails, the pass stops. Step 2 chooses which items to test: after a model change, every skill and rule, the largest always-on items first; otherwise, the few most in doubt. Each item is tested only on the tasks where it can load; an always-on skill, only on the tasks where earlier sweeps saw it fire, and not at all if they never did. How often an item is used helps choose what to test, but never decides a deletion. Step 3 shows the developer the plan with its expected rollouts, time and cost, and nothing runs until the developer approves it, possibly dropping some items. Steps 4 to 6 then take one item at a time: the agent attempts each of its tasks 3 times with the live harness ( base ) and without the item ( cand ), and the scoring script gives the verdict. ACCEPT: the item fired in at least one base run, and removing it lost nothing measurable, so it is deleted and buried in the graveyard. REJECT: removing it lost too many runs, made a task collapse, or made a task that never failed start failing, so it stays. UNMEASURED: the item never fired in any base run, so the test says nothing about it, and it stays; an item for a rare situation looks exactly like dead weight until that situation comes. RERUN: the data cannot be trusted, and the sweep is repeated. A deleted item is removed before the next one is measured, so every test starts from the harness as it really is. Step 7 can also move advice to a better place: an always-on skill used in only one folder can become a rule or a skill tied to that folder, and overlapping items can be merged; each such change is approved and measured on its own. Step 8 records every verdict in the journal and closes the plan, noting the model it ran on ( Section 3.6 ). 3.2 Harness items and what they cost Cortex calls each skill or rule a harness item ; the harness also holds constant files such as CLAUDE.md , which Cortex never measures. When a file enters the context decides what it costs ( Table 1 ): its price is its length multiplied by how often it is present, so Cortex counts the characters present on every turn ( CLAUDE.md , always-on skill descriptions and path-less rules) and warns above a budget (3,000 characters by default). Its objective is informally pass rate − λ ⋅ always-on context \text{pass rate}-\lambda\cdot\text{always-on context} , where λ \lambda is the pass rate a developer would give up to save one character read on every turn. Cortex never computes this as one number. It enforces it by two rules on the items it measures, skills and rules: add one only if it raises the pass rate ( Section 3.5 ); remove or narrow one only if that does not lower it ( Section 3.6 ). When /evolve decides that a theme belongs in CLAUDE.md , a setting, a hook or a tool rather than in a skill or rule, it writes the change and records it in the journal, but does not measure it: the gates apply only to skills and rules. The idea of context cost as an objective is shared with Meta-Harness and SkillReducer [ 27 , 15 ] . Whether an item is loaded or must be chosen also shaped what survived in our evaluation ( Figure 19 ). 3.3 Tasks from the developer’s own sessions A task is a replayable episode: a broken commit ( base_sha ), the developer’s original request, a check.sh that exits zero when the task is solved, and the fix.patch that proves it can be. /harvest writes one at the end of a session, and only when something went from broken to working. The request is the developer’s original words, not a cleaned-up version with hints known only afterwards. /harvest is instructed to write a check that tests not only that the bug is fixed but also each correction the developer made during the session (for example, that the linter is clean), so that an item which prevents the corrected mistake can turn a fail into a pass, and show an effect; preflight confirms that the check separates broken from fixed, not that it covers every correction. Most sessions produce no task, by design. As in the benchmarks of Section 2 , a task is only a ruler if its check separates the broken state from the fixed one. preflight runs the check in three states before every cycle and every prune pass: the broken state must fail ; the broken state plus the fix must pass ; and, when the fix edits test code, the fix without those edits must still pass (test data it adds, such as a fixture, stays). One whose environment is down, as reported by an optional script that checks its services, is skipped instead, since an outage is not a bad task. 3.4 Measurement: against the live harness, with exposure Every decision rests on a sweep : the agent runs each task k k times under two harnesses. base is the harness as it is now, re-measured in every sweep; cand is the same harness plus the one change under test (or minus it, for a removal). Both arms load every existing item, so what is measured is the change’s marginal value: a near-duplicate of an item the developer already has correctly shows no gain. The two arms’ rollouts are interleaved (for each task and each run, base and then cand ), so a slowdown, or a new model deployment in the middle of a sweep, lands on both arms alike. The harness and task definitions are snapshotted at the start. Rollouts run in parallel, one per worker , and each worker has its own clone of the repository ( Figure 6 ), reset before every rollout to the task’s broken commit with that arm’s harness; every reset is verified by running the check, which must fail. The clone never has Cortex’s own folder ( .evolve/ ) on disk: that folder holds the task store , where Cortex keeps its saved tasks with every earlier task’s fix, and the lessons and graveyard, which would give the answer away, so the clone is made without it (a sparse checkout, which leaves chosen folders out) and every reset deletes it again. It is still reachable through the clone’s git history, which is not pruned; Section 7 discusses that route. Finally, the model that plays the agent can be fixed: by default each rollout uses whatever model Claude Code is set to, but the developer can name one model in Cortex’s configuration ( pin it), so that every rollout of every sweep uses the same one. The base and cand arms take exactly the same steps, in alternation, and differ only in the harness that is installed. Once per sweep, Cortex freezes a copy of the harness and of the tasks (step 1), so that an edit made while the sweep runs cannot reach it, and gives each worker its own clone of the repository, which cannot push to the real one (step 2). Then, before every rollout, the clone is reset to the task’s broken commit and that arm’s harness is installed (step 3), and the task’s check is run once to confirm that it still fails (step 4): a task that already passes before the agent starts would measure nothing. The agent then works alone, with no human, on the task’s request, within a limit of 10 minutes (step 5). Cortex records which skills and rules entered the agent’s context during the attempt (step 6). Finally, the task’s own check decides the result, after the cached build files are deleted, since a stale cache could make old code look as if it passes (step 7). Each attempt ends in one of two ways. It is scored : a pass if the check succeeds, a fail if it does not or the agent ran out of time. Or it is invalid , because it could not run fairly: the reset failed, the task already passed, a service the task needs was down, the agent exited with an error (for example a login failure or a rate limit), the check hung, or the agent ran out of time while the machine was oversubscribed. Invalid is not the same as fail, and a sweep with even one invalid rollout is run again rather than scored. Exposure. An item can change a result only in a rollout where it entered the agent’s context. Cortex reads each rollout’s event stream , the record of every message and tool call that Claude Code emits while the agent works. From it, Cortex records for each skill whether it was visible (listed to the agent) and whether it was invoked (opened with a Skill tool call). A rule leaves no trace of its own, so Cortex records that it fired when the agent read a file its paths match, or the prompt @-mentioned one. When the stream cannot be read the value is unknown , never “did not fire”. A task is exposed to an item if the item reached the context in any of its rollouts: a rule that loaded, or a skill that was at least listed, since its description then sits in the context. An always-on skill is listed on every turn, so every task is exposed to it. On a task that was not exposed, the agent in both arms read the same text, and Cortex treats any difference between the arms as chance. Whether the item fired , a rule loaded or a skill opened, is a stricter question, which gate 5 asks ( Section 3.5 ). This one principle drives four decisions: the gates read only exposed tasks; a candidate that never fired is never kept; a removal whose item never fired is never accepted; and unknown exposure in any valid rollout blocks the verdict, so that a tooling failure cannot look like dead weight. Crediting only what fired is shared with SkillMAS [ 39 ] , and it guards against inert edits such as the never-triggered hook that DemoEvolve’s audit found in a harness chosen by self-rollout search [ 9 ] . It has been applied to deletion as well: SLIM retires a skill on a comparison with and without it over the validation tasks on which it was loaded, and only once it has been loaded often enough [ 47 ] , while Bayesian-Agent and Ratchet retire a skill only on enough evidence from the runs that used it, scoring the skill’s own outcomes rather than the difference its removal makes [ 56 , 70 ] . Cortex applies the same rule to adding and to deleting, and lets unknown exposure block either verdict. Scores. The scores measure a difference between the arms, and f f ties that difference to the item: a candidate that never fired cannot have caused its gain, and an item that never fired was not tested by its removal. 3.5 Adding an item: proposal and gates Evidence before proposals. /evolve improves the harness one cycle at a time ( Algorithm 2 ): a cycle looks for one recurring problem, writes one item meant to fix it, and tests that item before the next cycle starts. It looks for the problem in four places: the corrections the developer made to the agent, which /harvest logs as one line each; the tasks the live harness currently fails; the developer’s recent transcripts; and the graveyard , the items already tested and rejected, so that a rejected idea is not proposed again unchanged. A problem that recurs is a theme , and a cycle acts on one only when the evidence is strong enough: the theme recurs at least 3 times, or it explains 2 or more failing tasks. A single correction may be a one-off, and testing an item costs rollouts, so when no theme clears this bar the cycle is BARREN : it proposes nothing and runs no rollouts. This is an expected outcome, not a failure. When 2 cycles in a row end without a KEEP, whether barren or killed, cortex cycle signals that the loop should stop (the tasks may no longer tell a good harness from a bad one, the harness may already be good, or nothing new is being harvested), and /evolve stops and tells the developer. The developer may still start another cycle; nothing enforces the stop. When a theme clears the bar, the cycle proposes one candidate, and the evidence also chooses its tier ( Section 3.2 ) from where the fixes of the failing tasks landed. If they cluster in one directory, the candidate loads only there: a path-scoped rule when the fixes edit files that already exist, since a rule is injected whenever the agent reads a matching file; or a path-gated skill when the fixes only create new files, since a skill is also offered when a matching file is written. Its paths use the narrowest glob that covers every fix, because an item costs context each time it loads. If the fixes are spread across the repository, no directory fits, and the candidate is an always-on skill tied to a moment rather than a place, such as “before reporting done”. Two stages. A cheap screen runs the candidate at k = 2 k=2 on the theme’s currently failing tasks and stops if it gained nothing or never fired, or is rerun if it reached tasks but none could show a gain (below). It cannot show what a change breaks, because it never runs the tasks that pass; only candidates that survive it pay for the confirm , at k = 3 k=3 over every valid task. A cheap screen followed by a stricter confirmation is adapted from DarwinX [ 72 ] . How many rollouts each stage took across the evaluation is shown in Figure 17 . The gates. The confirm verdict is computed by a script, not by a model ( Table 2 ); Figure 7 shows one confirm sweep, scored again from its rollouts. A change must win something and lose nothing that matters: DarwinX’s contract of extending without breaking what is preserved [ 72 ] . The net threshold in runs mirrors SkillGen’s [ 34 ] , and the no-regression gates HarnessX’s refusal to regress any solved task and Self-Harness’s non-regressive acceptance [ 10 , 65 ] . Gates 2 and 3, the regression gates , set two standards for a drop: a task already unstable may lose one run of its 3 ( τ = 0.34 \tau=0.34 ), but a task in P P may lose none. Because at k = 3 k=3 one unlucky run on a reliable task looks exactly like a broken task, a KILL that rests only on gates 2 and 3 is not final: the tasks behind it are swept again (RECHECK), and the KILL stands only if one of them regresses again on the fresh runs; otherwise the candidate is kept. Figure 8 shows a candidate killed this way, although it won more runs than it lost. UNMEASURED keeps it too: here f f counts the valid base rollouts, and f = 0 f=0 means the item fired in none of them. Only ACCEPT deletes it, to the graveyard. The cases are read from the top, so an item whose removal cost something gets REJECT even when it never fired ( Section 5.5 ). UNMEASURED is the point: if nothing in the suite used an item, removing it changed nothing because nothing needed it , which is absence of evidence, not evidence of uselessness: a skill for a twice-a-year situation looks exactly like dead weight in between. This is the direct counterpoint to deletion rules that retire items whose measured effect is small [ 54 ] . For the same reason, usage data chooses which items to test and never decides a deletion. Figure 9: Adding and removing are one test, pointed both ways. /evolve compares the live harness with the harness plus a candidate; /prune compares it with the harness minus a live item. Both count only the tasks on which the item was in the agent’s context: a candidate that never fired is never kept, and a live item that never fired is never deleted. A pass starts as a plan: the items to test, the tasks to test each one on, and the rollouts, time and cost this will take, estimated from the past rollouts in the same repository. Nothing runs until the developer approves it. Which items go into the plan depends on whether the model has changed. If the pinned model differs from the one the last pass ran on, every item is re-tested, because a stronger model may already do what an item teaches; always-on items come first, the largest first. Otherwise the pass tests only the few items most in doubt. Either way, an item is left out when no task can load it, since its removal could only come out UNMEASURED, or when it is an always-on skill the agent never opened in earlier sweeps, since no sweep could accept its removal: it could only keep the item, as REJECT or UNMEASURED. A pass can also move an item to a cheaper tier: an always-on skill whose use is concentrated in one folder can be rewritten as a skill or a rule tied to that folder. The swap is swept like a removal, the harness with the new item in place of the old against the live one, and decided by Equation 7 . For a swap, a task is exposed when the old item was in context in a base rollout or the new one in a cand rollout, and f f counts the base rollouts in which the old item fired. The swap goes ahead only if it loses nothing measurable on those tasks and the old item fired, and the new item is made live only if it fired too. 3.7 The optional judge, Jev Cortex can consult an outside model, Jev (TypeSafe’s System One), to help it choose what to try. Jev is sent some text and a typed question, and it returns a probability for a yes-or-no question, one option from a list with its confidence, or a score on a fixed scale. It writes no text and takes no action. It is off by default, and it was off in every run of this paper, so every theme, tier, candidate and prune order reported in Section 5 was chosen without it. When it is on, Jev acts only in the proposal layer, the steps that decide which theme, candidate or order to try next: it can sort the logged lessons into themes, suggest a candidate’s tier, order a prune plan and tell the developer when a session is worth harvesting. One command, cortex scope , puts two questions to it about a candidate before a sweep is paid for. The first gives the candidate’s relevance : for each task the candidate would load on, Jev is asked whether the task is actually about the candidate’s subject, from the task’s title, request and one-line note, never the code or the fix, and the share of yes answers is the relevance. When it is below 35%, Cortex prints a warning, but it never blocks a sweep. Without Jev, Cortex reports only breadth , the share of all tasks the candidate would load on. The second, for a path-gated skill, is whether an agent doing the task, seeing only the skill’s description, would choose to open it. The tasks a candidate would load on are predicted from its paths ; once the candidate has been swept, they are the tasks where its sweeps recorded it in context. What the judge may not do. Jev may change which theme, candidate or order Cortex tries; it may never decide what a measurement found. The line is mechanical rather than a promise. The scorer, the sweep runner and preflight contain no reference to Jev, and a test in the shipped suite asserts that they do not. No Jev call runs inside a rollout sandbox, where it would become part of the harness under test. A wrong suggestion can waste rollouts, but it cannot turn a KILL into a KEEP, because the gates of Table 2 judge every candidate either way. How the judge was used in this evaluation. Only the two cortex scope questions were exercised: after the runs, they were put to each run’s candidates, at no cost in rollouts ( Section 5.7 ). Each candidate was rebuilt, from the graveyard or the live harness, in a scratch copy of its run’s repository that kept the run’s sweep records. Because every candidate had such a record, cortex scope took the tasks it would load on from the tasks where its own sweeps had recorded it in context; on those tasks, from the candidate’s text and each task’s title, request and note, never from its verdict, it estimated the candidate’s relevance and, for a path-gated skill, how often the agent would open it. 3.8 Implementation Cortex’s scripts are 6,906 lines of shell and Python in 9 files (of which 1,243 lines are the optional judge client), plus 1,341 lines of prompts that define /harvest , /evolve and /prune as Claude Code commands. The prompts do what needs judgement (writing a task, proposing a candidate, choosing a tier), and every quantity a verdict depends on is computed by the scripts. The scripts refuse to make a candidate live without a KEEP from a confirm sweep or its recheck (or an ACCEPT for a swap); burying a candidate is done by the /evolve agent, the model session that runs the command. Sweeps run in parallel, one sandbox clone per worker, as many workers as the machine’s free memory and CPUs allow. Rollouts are headless Claude Code sessions, started by a script with no one at the keyboard, with a 10-minute limit. Cortex deletes the event stream it reads from each once exposure is known, because it holds everything the agent saw; Claude Code keeps its own record of every session, outside the repository. 4 Evaluation setup The evaluation measures Cortex in a synthetic repository whose house rules a model often breaks. This section describes the repository ( Figure 10 ), what one run does ( Figure 11 ), how a run’s result is measured ( Figure 12 ), two tests with known answers, two tests of how far the results carry ( Figure 13 ), and the statistics. The lab. shopkit is a small Python toolkit for orders and invoices (a catalogue, carts, invoices, refunds, exports, reports and a command line) with no dependencies and its own unit tests. Like many real codebases, it has house rules : conventions this one project has chosen, which code can break while still working. They are written in its CONTRIBUTING.md , and its continuous-integration check, which runs the unit tests and a linter, enforces part of them. Take the rule on time: code in shop/ must read the current time only through shop.clock , never with datetime.now() or date.today() , so that tests can freeze the clock. Asked to give invoices a due date counted from today, an agent that computes it from date.today() produces code that works, yet the linter rejects it, and the reviewer replies: “Works, but CI is still red: make lint rejects datetime.now() / date.today() in shop/. We only read the time through shop.clock …” (CI here is continuous integration). A model cannot learn such a rule from its training, only from the project. It is exactly what a harness exists to teach, and a model that keeps breaking it keeps being corrected, which is the evidence Cortex learns from. Four house rules each have a family of tasks built around them ( Figure 10 ), named by a letter: A, the changelog (every change users can see gets a line in CHANGELOG.md ); B, money (amounts are integer cents, scaled only with the project’s rate helpers); C, exporters (a new exporter needs a registry entry, a row in the documentation and a golden file, a stored sample of its expected output); and E, time (the clock rule above). A fifth family, D, holds plain bugs with no house rule, so the loop has nothing to learn there: it is the control, and it can only show harm. Training and held-out scenarios. A scenario is one piece of work: a teammate’s commit that adds a failing test, and a request saying what is wanted; the due date above is one. The scenarios are split in two, the way a course keeps its exam apart from its exercises. The 26 training scenarios are the exercises: the runs play them as working sessions, the reviewer corrects the agent’s mistakes on them, and Cortex learns from those corrections. The 30 held-out scenarios are the exam: no session ever plays them, so Cortex never sees them, and they serve only to measure harnesses (the benchmark, below). The split is what lets a gain be read as learning. On a training scenario, a harness could help by recalling that one task, for instance that the due date is computed from shop.clock ; on a held-out scenario, no task it recalls holds the answer, and only what carries over to new work, such as the rule, can help. Held-out scenario HE1 (held-out scenarios are named H, the family’s letter and a number), for one, asks for the orders of the last N N days, counted back from today by default: a task no session plays, under the same rule on time. A gain on the held-out scenarios therefore shows that what Cortex learned carries over to work it has never seen, which is what a developer needs from a harness. Passing the exam also takes following the rule, not only making the test pass. Every held-out scenario of the four rule families comes with a rule-breaking fix, one that makes the scenario’s own test pass but breaks the rule: for HE1, it falls back on date.today() ; in families A and C, it is the correct fix without its changelog line, or without its documentation row and golden file. Only the rule’s part of the check can tell it apart from the correct fix. Figure 10: The lab. Top: the repository, and its five task families: each rule family is built around one house rule written in CONTRIBUTING.md , with the mistake an agent typically makes, what catches it, and the counts of training and held-out scenarios; family D, plain bugs with no rule, is the control. Bottom left: one correction from start to finish, for the rule on time. Bottom right: the training scenarios are played as sessions; the held-out scenarios are kept for the benchmark. A run. A run is one complete, unattended replay of the project’s working life ( Figure 11 ). It starts from a fresh copy of the repository and plays the 26 training scenarios as 26 working sessions, one per scenario, in 10 rounds; each family is introduced in a round of its own and returns in later ones. No one sits at the keyboard: a script types what a developer would type, and nothing in the repository is edited by hand. One session. A session begins the way work reaches a developer: a teammate’s commit adds a failing test, for a bug or for a change in what the code should do, and a headless Claude Code session, one started by the script with no one watching, is asked to deal with it. When the agent stops, a scripted reviewer plays continuous integration. It checks, in order, that the teammate’s test is unchanged, that this test now passes, that the whole suite passes, that the linter is clean, and, for family A, that the changelog gained a line. The first check that fails gets the reply written for that failure, in the same words in every run, like the reply on time above, and the agent tries again, at most 3 times. The session then ends with /harvest ( Section 3.1 ): if the session went from broken to working it saves a task, whose check also tests what the reviewer corrected, and it writes each correction down as a lesson. Because the replies are scripted, every run receives the same correction for the same mistake. The loop, after each round. After the round’s sessions, the script runs /evolve ( Figure 4 ). A cycle looks for a theme, writes one candidate, screens and confirms it, and keeps or buries it, or ends as BARREN, at no cost in rollouts, when no theme clears the bar. A sweep takes minutes and runs in the background, so the session that started it ends; when the sweep has finished, the script types /evolve again in a fresh session, which reads the result and goes on. It stops once a cycle has ended with no candidate pending, or when /evolve stops on its own; most rounds hold one cycle. The script runs /evolve in every round, even after Cortex has signalled that the loop should stop, so that every run has the same shape. What /evolve changed, a kept item and the journal, is then committed, as each session’s code and task were at the session’s end, and the next round begins. The runs. The 4 evaluation runs, R1 to R4, follow this procedure with Cortex in full; repeating it shows whether a result holds beyond a single run. A control run, C1, plays the same sessions, receives the same corrections and runs /harvest as usual, but never runs /evolve , so no skill or rule is ever added. Corrections can still fall in C1, because the agent can copy a rule from the fixes already in the code, and C1 measures how much they fall without /evolve . A development run, D0, used an earlier version of Cortex than v1.0-eval . It is reported apart and named wherever it is used ( Sections 5.1 , 5.7 and 7 ); every other number comes from the runs made at v1.0-eval . One model in every role. Every evaluation and control run used Claude Haiku 4.5 ( claude-haiku-4-5-20251001 ) through Claude Code 2.1.278, with Cortex’s optional judge, Jev, off. The same model plays every role: it is the agent that works in the sessions; the model that runs /harvest and /evolve , and so writes the tasks and proposes the candidates; and the agent in every sweep and benchmark rollout. No stronger model teaches it. The runs depart from Cortex’s defaults in the settings below, and in where the sandboxes sit on disk and how many run at once; none of them decides a verdict. The rollout model is pinned to the one the sessions use, so that every rollout uses that model (by default a rollout uses whatever model Claude Code is set to). The cap on rollouts per sweep, a guard on cost, is raised from 60 to 200, because a confirm sweep over every training task takes 156 rollouts (each of the 26 tasks 3 times under each of the two harnesses). The stop limit, the number of cycles in a row without a KEEP after which Cortex suggests stopping, is raised from 2 to 3, because the lab introduces its families on a schedule, and quiet cycles are expected before the next family arrives. And Claude Code never updates itself mid-run. Figure 11: One run, end to end. (1) The rounds, and the family of each session. (2) One session: the teammate’s commit, the agent, the scripted reviewer, whose fixed reply sends the agent back at most 3 times, and /harvest . (3) The /evolve cycle after each round’s sessions ( Figure 4 ). (4) The runs: evaluation and control share one setup; the development run is reported apart. The benchmark. After the last round, each run’s final harness sits an exam ( Figure 12 ). Each held-out scenario is committed onto the run’s final code, so that it meets the codebase as that run left it, and the commit adds only the teammate’s test: the agent gets that commit and the scenario’s request, as in a session. Each scenario also has a reference fix , a correct solution written with it, and, in the rule families, its rule-breaking fix; both stay outside the repository and serve only to validate the scenario, below. The training scenarios are replayed from the commits their sessions started from. An arm is one harness: every arm faces the same scenarios, with the same model and the same oracle, and the arms differ only in the harness installed. The two primary arms are none , the minimal CLAUDE.md that Cortex’s installer, cortex init , writes, and nothing else, and evolved , what the run kept; for short, the text also calls none “no harness”, since it has no skills or rules. Each of the others answers one question ( Figure 12 , bottom). none2 , the A/A arm, is none measured a second time, in a later batch, to show how far two measurements of one harness can differ. The rest are the ablations : kitchen is none with the whole contribution guide appended to CLAUDE.md ; flat is evolved ’s texts with every paths field removed; desc-only is evolved with each skill’s body replaced by neutral filler; accept-all is evolved plus every candidate the run buried; and ideal is written by hand: always-on skills for A and E, a rule on shop/billing/** for B, and a gated skill on shop/plugins/** for C. Every attempt, or rollout, runs in a clean sandbox, in Claude Code’s acceptEdits mode, in which file edits are accepted without asking and a command runs only if the settings already allow it, as the repository’s own allow list does for make , python3 and the read-only git commands ( git status , git diff , git log , git show ; Section 7 says what a rollout could read through them). Success is decided by the lab’s own oracle , a fixed script that judges every attempt the way the scripted reviewer does, not by the checks Cortex harvested, so that Cortex never grades its own work. It makes the reviewer’s checks in the same order and stops at the first that fails: the teammate’s test is left unchanged, that test passes, the rest of the suite passes, the linter is clean (it checks the rules of B, C and E), and, for family A, the changelog gained a line. The agent does not behave the same way twice, so each scenario is attempted several times: none and evolved run each held-out scenario 5 times and each training scenario 3 times, and the other arms run the held-out scenarios 3 times. The primary arms run interleaved, taking turns, so that a slowdown lands on both; the other arms ran afterwards, in batches of their own, so every comparison with them crosses a batch boundary. Every arm alike also carried one shared skill listing on every turn: the descriptions of Claude Code’s own bundled skills, of Cortex’s three commands, which cortex init installs in the repository, and of the skills in the user-level Claude Code configuration; the agent invoked one of the bundled skills in 5.4% of none rollouts and 5.8% of evolved ones. Because every run’s code ends differently, a held-out scenario counts in a run only if it validates on that run’s final code: its test must fail there while the linter stays clean, its reference fix must pass the oracle, and, in a rule family, its rule-breaking fix must pass its own test and be caught only by the rule’s part of the check. One did not validate (HA6, in R4), and it is excluded from that run in every arm. The primary analysis uses the complete-case set, the 23 rule-family scenarios valid in every run; the set of all valid scenarios is secondary. Figure 12: The benchmark. Tests with known answers, and of generality. Four more experiments complete the evaluation ( Figure 13 ); all ran on Claude Haiku 4.5 except where the model change says otherwise. The first two measure Cortex’s own decisions against answers known before they ran; the last two ask whether its results carry beyond the lab and its model. • The gate test asks whether the gates keep only what helps. It runs 29 candidates whose right verdict is known through the real pipeline, on a copy of C1’s final repository, which holds harvested tasks and no live item: 20 placebos, plausible advice that shares no keyword with a house rule, all written as always-on skills (10 about a coding topic, such as preferring pathlib to os.path , and 10 about a moment in the work, such as what to do after finishing an edit), which should be killed; 5 harmful items, advice that contradicts a house rule, 3 of them rules and the rest always-on skills, which should be killed; and the 4 items of ideal , which should be kept. Each is screened at k = 2 k=2 on tasks the live harness had failed (the same tasks for every placebo), and confirmed if it survives. The test’s procedure stops at the screen whenever the gain is not positive or the candidate never fired, and records that stop as a KILL; score.sh ’s own verdict is recorded beside it, and the two can differ, since score.sh returns RERUN when no task on the screen could show a gain ( Section 5.3 ). • The prune test asks whether /prune deletes only dead weight. It runs /prune on a copy of R1’s final repository, with 4 items planted beside R1’s 4 and its limit on items per pass raised to cover them all. In its first pass, /prune chose which items to test and planned R1’s own, which it should keep. A second pass was given the planted items it had left out: 2 placebo always-on skills, which it should delete; a gated skill that no task reaches, which it should skip; and an always-on skill that never fires, which it should report as unmeasured rather than delete. • The model change asks whether the harness still matters under a stronger model. It benchmarks R1’s harness with Claude Sonnet 5 ( claude-sonnet-5 ) as the agent, at k = 3 k=3 , and runs /prune on another copy of R1 with its rollouts pinned to that model, while the session that runs /prune is still Claude Haiku 4.5. Every run gained on the four rule families taken together, by different amounts (the dots in Figure 14 ), though not on every family: R3 gained nothing on money and lost on the clock ( Figure 18 ). R3 gained least: its pooled pass rate on the 23 scenarios valid in every run rose from 22.6% to 52.2%, where the other runs reached between 80.9% and 87.0%. Section 5.2 traces why. The benchmark also replayed the training scenarios, the ones the sessions had played, under none and evolved ( Section 4 ). Measured on the 22 of them in the four rule families, the gain would have been +78.8 points [+68.9, +86.7] instead of +55.0. More of that difference lies in the baseline than in the harness: without a harness the agent passed 6.4% of the training rollouts in these families and 21.5% of the held-out ones, so the training scenarios left more to gain, while the evolved harness’s own pass rate went from 85.2% to 76.5%. By family, the evolved rate went from training to held-out as follows: A from 90.3% to 97.0%, B from 88.9% to 79.2%, C from 76.4% to 51.7%, and E from 85.4% to 81.7%. It fell most for exporters, and fell there in every run. For money, the fall is R3’s, the run that narrowed its money rule ( Section 5.2 ); without it, the rate rose. For the clock, the rate held but the gain did not, because the held-out clock scenarios were easier without a harness: the agent alone passed 55.0% of their rollouts, against 10.4% of the training ones. The comparison is descriptive and tests no hypothesis: the two sets are different scenarios, attempted 3 times each against 5; a training scenario starts from the commit its session started from, not from the run’s final code; and its session’s fix is in the repository’s history, which a rollout can read ( Section 7 ). Why rollouts fail. The oracle, the lab’s own script that scores a rollout ( Section 4 ), makes the reviewer’s checks in order and stops at the first that fails, so each failed rollout has exactly one cause in Figure 15 . First, the teammate’s test, the test file the scenario starts from, must be unchanged: a rollout that edits it has moved the goalposts. Second, that test must pass: otherwise the task is not solved. Third, the rest of the test suite must still pass. Last, the house rule must hold: the linter, which checks the rules of families B, C and E, must be clean, and in family A the changelog must have gained a line. None of these rollouts failed on the rest of the suite. Without a harness, 94% of the rule families’ failed rollouts (341 of 361) passed the tests and broke the house rule: the agent solved the task and missed the convention, the failure the lab was built around. The evolved harness turned most of them into passes. Of its 108 failures, 86 still broke the rule, 43 of them in the exporter family. A rollout that changes the teammate’s test fails before anything else is checked; that happened in 9 none rollouts and 13 evolved ones, all in families C and E. H4 is that the scripted developer has to correct the agent less often in the evaluation runs, where Cortex’s items go live as they are kept, than in the control run, where /evolve is off; the count covers every session, including those before any item was kept. The evaluation runs’ sessions needed 60 corrections in 104 sessions (0.58 per session), and the control run’s 23 in 26 (0.88). The margin, fewer corrections per session than in the control run, is met, so H4 is supported. But with a single control run beside the 4 evaluation runs, a permutation test that shuffles which run is the control has too few arrangements to give p p below 0.2, so we read the difference as description, not as a tested effect. H12 is that the result of the development run, D0 ( Section 4 ), holds at v1.0-eval . Its harness, measured on the same held-out scenarios with the evaluation’s tooling, gained +42.5 points, inside the evaluation runs’ interval over every valid scenario, [+35.4, +75.0], so H12 is supported. That interval is for the mean of the 4 runs, and a single run varies more: on the same scenarios the runs’ own gains ranged from +32.5 to +66.7, and the development run’s gain lies within that range as well. 5.2 What the loop did Cycles and verdicts. In the 4 evaluation runs /evolve recorded 39 cycles ( Figure 17 ; run by run in Figure 17 ). Of these, 14 were barren, most of them after the run had kept an item for every rule family; the other 25 swept 26 candidates between them, one cycle sweeping 2. score.sh kept 18 and killed 5; for the other 3 it returned RERUN, and the /evolve agent buried them without a verdict rather than sweep them again. A recheck was needed for 3 candidates, and 2 of them were kept after it. Of the 1,818 sweep rollouts, 1,494 were spent on confirm sweeps, which only candidates that had passed a screen paid for; every confirm sweep, with the runs it won net and its worst drop on one task, is drawn in Figure 22 . What the runs learned. H9 is that independent runs learn the same families, in similar forms. It is supported: every run kept an item for each of the four rule families, and none for the control ( Figure 18 , and every kept item in Table 7 ). Every run but R3 chose the same scopes: shop/** for the changelog and the clock, shop/billing/** for money and shop/plugins/** for exporters; they differed in form only for exporters, a gated skill in two runs and a rule in the third. R3 narrowed its money and clock rules: instead of a folder pattern, their paths name a short list of individual files, so the rules load only when the agent reads one of those files. Its held-out result shows what that cost. Its first money rule covered shop/billing/** . The confirm sweep, over the 3 tasks then in the suite, won 5 runs and lost none, but exposure was unknown in 7 of its rollouts, so score.sh returned RERUN ( Section 3.4 ). The /evolve agent buried the rule and, in the next cycle, proposed a narrower one. It and a later rule name 5 files between them, and the gates kept both. They loaded in 0 of the run’s 30 held-out money rollouts, where the run’s money pass rate stayed at 26.7% in both arms; the other runs’ money rules loaded in at least 28 of 30. Its clock rule on shop/** was killed when a task the live harness passed in all its runs lost one run in the confirm and another in the recheck (gate 3). The rule that replaced it names 3 files and loaded in 10 of 30 held-out clock rollouts, and the run’s clock pass rate fell from 56.7% to 50.0%. The gates judge a candidate on the tasks the loop has harvested, where these rules did load. Nothing in them can see that a scope is too narrow for tasks the loop has not yet met. The tier rubric. H3 is that every kept item lands in a sensible tier and fires mainly in its own family’s work. The lab scored each kept item on three criteria: its form fits how it loads (a skill fired at least once, a rule has paths ); its scope is limited (it has paths , or is a skill); and it fires more often on its own family’s rollouts than on the others’. The margin was every item scoring three of three. Of the 18 kept items, 15 did, so H3 is not supported. Every item that failed is a rule on shop/** and failed only the third criterion. Rules on shop/** load on almost every task of every family (in 93% to 100% of rollouts), and the 4 that passed it did so narrowly, firing on their own family at most 1.25 points more often than on the others. Loaded or chosen. Of the 18 kept items, 16 are rules ( Figure 19 ). The other 2 are skills, each an exporter checklist gated on shop/plugins/** . A gated candidate, in its own sweeps and in the gate test, was listed to the agent in 66 rollouts and opened in 28; an always-on candidate, likewise in its own sweeps and in the gate test, was listed in 198 and opened in 0. Elsewhere such a skill was opened, but rarely: the gate test’s placebos that were planted unchanged in the prune test were listed there 1,263 times and opened 46. A rule needs no such decision: it is in the context whenever the agent reads a file it covers. The gate test and the ablations below meet the same asymmetry. Figure 19: A rule is loaded; a skill must be chosen. Claude Code injects a path-scoped rule whenever the agent reads a matching file. A skill is offered by its description, and its body enters the context only if the agent opens it: in their own sweeps and in the gate test, path-gated candidates were opened in some of the rollouts that listed them, and always-on ones in none. Of the items the loop kept, 16 are rules and 2 are path-gated skills; most candidates were rules too. 5.3 The gates against known answers The verdicts. The gate test ran 29 candidates with known answers through the real pipeline ( Section 4 ). H5 is that the gates are calibrated: they rarely keep a placebo, kill every harmful candidate, and keep at least 3 of the 4 known-good ones. None of the 20 placebos was kept; with so few candidates, the rate at which the gates keep placebos could still be as high as 17% (the upper end of a two-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% CI). None of the 5 harmful candidates was kept either, but score.sh killed only 2 of them and reached no verdict on the other 3 (below). And 2 of the 4 known-good candidates were kept, short of the 3 the margin required. H5 is not supported. Fisher’s exact test, which asks whether the known-good candidates were kept more often than the placebos, gives p = 0.022 p=0.022 . What decided them. Table 6 gives each kind of candidate’s verdicts. No placebo was opened on its screen: each was listed in all 8 candidate rollouts and invoked in none. score.sh killed 12 of them for never firing (gate 5) and returned RERUN for the other 8, whose screen tasks failed in every run of both arms, so that no gain was possible; the test’s procedure, which stops at the screen, recorded all 20 as KILLs. In all, 10 candidates (7 placebos, 2 harmful skills and 1 known-good skill) showed a positive gain on their screen although the agent never opened them, 9 of them by a single run on a single task. Gate 5, which asks that a candidate fired, turned them away, not their gain. Harm was not tested. The 2 harmful skills were never opened and fell to gate 5, like the placebos. The 3 harmful rules loaded in every candidate rollout of their screens, but a harmful item shows itself only on a task that passes without it, and their screens ran, as screens do, on failing tasks. One screen included a task that passed without the rule, and the rule broke it; score.sh still returned RERUN, because no task in that screen could show a gain. The test therefore shows that the gates never keep what never fires, not that they catch harm. In the loop itself, 2 of the 5 KILLs failed a regression gate, and 1, the clock rule of R3 above, failed nothing else. The positives. The known-good candidates split along the tier line: the rule and the gated skill were kept, and the 2 always-on skills, never opened on their screens, were lost. Do the gates add value? H6 is that they do: a harness that also keeps what the loop buried should be no better than evolved , and the margin asks that the upper end of its difference’s interval be below +5 points. accept-all , R2’s harness plus the one candidate that run buried, scored −8.9 points against evolved [−16.1, −1.7], an interval that resamples scenarios only, since the arm ran in a single run. That meets H6’s margin, though the permutation test, at p = 0.075 p=0.075 , does not by itself rule out chance. That candidate, a second clock rule, was not buried by a gate: both arms passed every run of its screen, score.sh returned RERUN, and the /evolve agent buried it as overlapping a live rule. The loss falls on families A (−13.3) and C (−17.8) more than on E (−4.4), the family the added rule is about. The rule, on shop/** , was in context in every A and C rollout, so it could have caused the loss there, but the arm also ran in a later batch, so part of the difference may be the shift between batches. The margin is met, but it rests on one burial the /evolve agent made, not on the gates, so H6 is inconclusive. 5.4 What the harness costs Figure 20: What each harness costs, in R1: pass rate on the four rule families against the characters present in every turn’s context.
