Costs are in US dollars, as Claude Code reported them for each call. In R1 to R4 a held-out rollout cost $0.121 on average with no harness and $0.149 with the evolved one, 23% more, and took 22.1 turns instead of 18.2 and 68 s instead of 57 s. The rise was largest on the exporter family (38%), smallest on the control family (5%), and 12% to 22% on families A, B and E. Under Claude Sonnet 5 the harness of R1 made a rollout cheaper, $0.205 against $0.228. Running the loop cost each evaluation run $32.76 to $128.78 in sweep rollouts, R3 the most, and $2.39 to $4.09 for the /evolve agent’s own turns, beside $10.08 to $11.78 for the scripted sessions it learned from. Where the words reached the agent. The families show the tier asymmetry again. flat passed every A, B and E rollout but 0% of C: without its paths , the exporter checklist became an always-on skill, listed in every C rollout and opened in none ( evolved passed 70% of C). ideal wrote its advice on the changelog and on the clock as always-on skills; each was listed in all 90 of the arm’s held-out rollouts and opened in none, and families A and E stayed where none left them (0% and 56%, against 0% and 57%). In R1, what mattered was not who wrote the advice but how it was offered: tied to the files a task touches, as a rule or a gated skill, it reached the agent; offered on every turn as an always-on skill, it was not opened. The description alone. H11 is that a skill’s description, the line the agent sees in the listing, carries much of the skill’s effect by itself; the margin puts “much” at 50% or more of evolved ’s gain. desc-only tests it: it keeps each skill’s description and replaces its body with neutral filler. Over the four families together it recovered 79% of evolved ’s gain [58%, 100%], but it could rewrite only 1 of R1’s 4 items; the rest are rules and kept their words. In C, the one family whose skill was rewritten, the arm recovered 16% [0%, 56%], below half. The description still got the rewritten skill opened, in 16 of 18 C rollouts, but with filler in place of its body C’s pass rate was 11%, against 70% for evolved , and its 2 passing rollouts were among the 6 that printed the replaced body through git ( Section 7 ). One rewritten skill cannot settle the question, and H11 is inconclusive. 5.5 A stronger model, and pruning The same harness under two models. Under Claude Sonnet 5, the harness of R1 has little left to do ( Figure 21 ). none ’s pass rate on the rule-family scenarios was already 88.9%, against 20.8% under Claude Haiku 4.5, and the harness raised it to 94.4%: a gain of +5.6 points [−2.8, +13.9], against +66.7 [+51.7, +80.8] under the model it was evolved with; each comes from a single run, over every scenario valid in it, so both intervals resample scenarios only. H13 is that after a model upgrade, re-measuring the harness finds items the weaker model needed that the stronger one no longer does. /prune , in one pass at k = 3 k=3 with its rollouts pinned to the stronger model, found 2 of the harness’s 4 items removable, the money rule and the exporter checklist, so H13 is supported. Its margin asks for one such item, and the money rule is one on both measures: the stronger model passed every held-out money scenario with no harness at all. Removing the changelog rule cost 5 runs; removing the clock rule cost 1, on a task the live harness had passed in every run, where losing even one run keeps an item ( Section 3.6 ). The exporter checklist that /prune removed is less certain: it still showed the largest gain on the held-out scenarios, +11.1 [−11.1, +38.9] on C, and one pass at this k k cannot tell a small effect from none. Under a stronger model, part of a harness evolved for a weaker one may be redundant, and one pass of re-measurement flagged which part, within the limits of that pass. Pruning against known answers. H10 is that /prune deletes planted useless items that fired, keeps the items that are needed, and never deletes an item that never fired; the margin asks every planted item to get its expected verdict. Under Claude Haiku 4.5, /prune kept all 4 of R1’s own items, as expected: removing any of them cost at least 9 runs net. Of the 4 planted items it matched 2 (6 of 8 overall), so H10 is not supported. It deleted one placebo always-on skill and skipped the gated skill that no task reaches, as expected. It kept the other placebo: in its sweep the agent opened it in none of the 18 rollouts that listed it, so it could not have been deleted. The placebo got REJECT rather than UNMEASURED because the conditions for REJECT are checked first ( Algorithm 3 ), and 2 tasks lost runs when it was removed. The last planted item, the always-on skill that the agent never opens, got no verdict. The margin asks for UNMEASURED, which only a sweep can return, and the plan leaves out an always-on skill that never fired in earlier sweeps, since no sweep could delete it ( Section 3.6 ); the item stayed in the harness, but without the verdict the margin asks for. No item that never fired was deleted. 5.6 A second repository H14 is that the loop also helps on a repository that nobody in this study built. On structlog the loop found nothing to learn. Its training harvested 8 tasks but only 1 lesson: in 7 of the 8 sessions the agent passed the project’s own tests and its linter, at the version the project pins, at the first attempt. Nothing recurred, every /evolve cycle was barren, and the loop kept nothing, so evolved was byte-identical to none and the benchmark on the 4 held-out tasks had nothing to compare. With the two harnesses identical, H14 is inconclusive. At this correction rate the loop had nothing to do, and the run says nothing about whether a learned harness transfers. 5.7 Predicting a verdict from a candidate’s text The judge was off in every run; its predictions were replayed afterwards on each run’s candidates, never from a verdict, but over the tasks on which each candidate’s own sweeps had recorded it in context ( Section 3.7 ), so they are not the predictions cortex scope would have made before those sweeps. H15 is that the judge’s relevance , the share of the tasks a candidate would load on that the candidate is actually about, separates the candidates that are kept from those killed on a regression gate, while breadth , the share of all tasks a candidate would load on, which needs no judge, does not. To separate means that every kept candidate scores above every killed one. On the evaluation runs, relevance did not separate the candidates score.sh kept from the 2 it killed on a regression (lowest kept 17%, highest killed 75%), and neither did breadth (8% against 58%), so H15 is not supported. So few regression kills make a thin comparison. Skipping the evaluation runs’ candidates below Cortex’s warning floor of 35% would have avoided sweeping 3 candidates that were later buried, and lost 6 that were kept. H16 is that the judge’s predicted invocation rate, how often it expects the agent to open a skill, tracks the rate measured in the rollouts; with so few skills, its margin asks only that the predictions rank the skills in the same order as the measurements. The evaluation runs kept only 2 path-gated skills, so the test also takes the 2 that the development run kept. For these 4 skills the judge predicted a higher invocation rate than was measured for 3, by up to 54 points. The rank order is preserved, which meets the letter of the margin; but 3 of the 4 predictions are tied at the top, so the order rests on the remaining skill alone, and H16 is inconclusive. 6 Related work Cortex sits among systems that write and revise the text an agent reads, studies of whether such text helps a coding agent, and the methods used to evaluate noisy agents and to build their tasks. Most of its parts have precedents; this section says where, and what differs. Evolving what an agent reads. Agents that learn from experience keep what they learn as text: reflections on a failed attempt [ 49 ] , programs admitted to a library once a model judges the task done [ 51 ] , insights kept or dropped by a model’s votes [ 73 ] , workflows induced from past trajectories [ 55 ] , and itemised playbooks grown by small edits [ 68 ] . Optimisers search over prompts and programs against a metric [ 25 , 1 ] , and over agent designs and an agent’s own code [ 18 , 66 , 42 ] . The newest systems evolve the harness around a fixed model [ 72 , 27 , 65 , 10 , 30 , 9 , 59 , 12 ] or synthesise skills from trajectories [ 34 , 3 , 37 , 61 , 50 , 45 , 53 ] ; some of them run in Claude Code itself, on public benchmarks [ 3 , 61 , 12 ] . Cortex adapts DarwinX’s contract of extending without breaking what is preserved ( Section 3.5 ), and differs from much of this work in two ways. Its tasks come from one repository and one developer, not from a benchmark. Its baseline is the live harness, measured again in the same sweep as the candidate, as HDSO’s control arm is [ 45 ] ; many systems instead compare a candidate with a score recorded earlier, such as cached outcomes without the skill [ 34 ] , the results of the current state reused until an update is accepted [ 53 ] , or the best score so far [ 50 , 59 ] . Its verdict is computed by a script, as the acceptance rules of SkillGen, SkillOpt and LiteEvo are [ 34 , 61 , 12 ] , while a model proposes what is tried, much as HarnessX’s critic chooses which candidates reach its deterministic checks [ 10 ] . In some systems a model takes part in the verdict itself: DarwinX’s promotions are adjudicated by a verifier agent [ 72 ] , and HDSO’s promotions include a review by its curator model [ 45 ] ; model judges carry known biases, such as favouring the answer shown first [ 75 ] . Noise makes these differences matter. In HarnessDev, when models evolved their own harnesses, the score of one and the same version could move by nearly five points either way, only two of sixty-four changes gained clearly beyond that noise, and the scores on the feedback tasks and on held-out tasks moved in the same direction about half the time [ 58 ] . DarwinX’s score on its training subset saturated while its held-out score did not [ 72 ] . R3’s narrowed money and clock rules are a small instance of the same gap: they loaded on the tasks the loop had harvested, but in 0 of the run’s 30 held-out money rollouts and 10 of its 30 clock ones ( Section 5.2 ). Crediting and retiring an item. That an edit can be selected without ever reaching the model is known. In DemoEvolve’s experiments, the harness that a self-rollout baseline selected was credited with a gain, yet the hook it added appeared in none of the model requests the authors inspected [ 9 ] ; and in HarnessDev’s coding domain, about one in six of the components that models wrote into their own harnesses was never observed to trigger [ 58 ] . Some systems and studies record exposure. HarnessX’s change manifests name a trace feature that must appear if an edit fired, which its critic checks after shipping [ 10 ] , and HDSO logs each request for a skill’s full text [ 45 ] . SkillMAS credits only skills that were invoked or whose steps appear in the trace, uses the credit to rank skills, and holds a new skill in a validation pool until later rounds show enough use of it [ 39 ] . Skill-Use credits a skill’s execution only once it is triggered, and measures its effect on the runs that triggered it [ 17 ] . Skill Following compares matched runs with and without skills only on the tasks where the agent retrieved one, and on coding tasks finds this effect negative for several models that appear to gain when tasks with and without retrieval are compared [ 11 ] ; a review of such designs cautions that restricting a paired comparison to the tasks where the treated run triggered a skill does not by itself identify the effect of invoking it [ 69 ] , and Cortex’s exposed tasks are likewise defined by what happened in the arm where the item exists ( Section 3.4 ). LiteEvo drops a new processor that never fires when replayed, much as Cortex refuses a candidate that never fired, and shows its curating model which deployed components never fired [ 12 ] . WikiSkill sets the question aside by placing every skill in the prompt in full [ 50 ] . SLIM decides whether to retire a skill from a comparison with and without it restricted to the validation tasks on which it was loaded, and leaves a skill alone until it has been loaded often enough [ 47 ] ; we found no system that applies the same restriction when deciding whether to add an item, or that lets unknown exposure block a verdict. Deletion rules mostly retire what looks weak: a small measured effect [ 54 ] , failure evidence from enough runs that used a skill [ 56 , 70 ] , a negligible effect of removing it on the tasks that loaded it [ 47 ] , low utility in recent calls [ 41 ] , an insight whose votes fall to zero [ 73 ] , low-utility entries once the context grows too long [ 68 ] , or a component whose edits have stopped gaining [ 59 ] . A Shapley valuation of a skill’s parts, which separates content from context cost with length-matched padding, prunes the parts of lowest value first [ 28 ] . SkillReducer, which compresses skills rather than deleting them, reads a skill that never triggers as a sign of obsolescence [ 15 ] : the opposite reading to UNMEASURED. SLIM comes closest to UNMEASURED in mechanism [ 47 ] ( Section 3.4 ); the argument behind it is made most explicitly by a study of skill retirement for physical agents after model upgrades. When clauses were deleted because the tasks that authorised an action still passed without them, safety conditions those tasks never exercised, such as consent, were left untested: an “unmeasured support gap” [ 64 ] . Its remedy is to build counterfactual tasks that exercise the condition; Cortex keeps the item and suggests harvesting a task that needs it. An analysis of why instruction files only grow makes a related point: age and rare triggering alone do not make an instruction outdated [ 8 ] . Two observations bear on /prune ’s one-at-a-time removals: of two redundant instructions, each looks removable alone [ 8 ] , and an item judged in isolation can mislead, because its effect depends on what else is loaded [ 71 , 74 ] . Context files, rules and skills. Whether repository context helps a coding agent is contested. Context files written by a model lowered task success slightly and files written by the repositories’ developers raised it marginally, neither change significant, while both raised cost, the model-written ones by about a fifth [ 16 ] ; an ablation with Claude Code and Codex on real repositories, which delivered repository guidance either always on or as topic files the agent retrieves on demand, found that the delivery strategy had no measurable effect on correctness [ 24 ] . In Claude Code, on the SWE-bench Verified tasks it solved only sometimes, randomly drawn community rule files did as well as curated ones, which the authors read as the presence of rules mattering far more than their content [ 71 ] . A comparison with and without an item can therefore reward text as such, and a placebo candidate is the control for that. Cortex’s placebos, all always-on skills, were never opened on their gate-test screens ( Section 5.3 ), so its gates never faced a placebo that loads. A repository’s guidance file, tuned with synthetic probes, raised the resolve rate of the model that tuned it; for a second model, in one run each, the guidance tuned on the first more than halved the resolve rate, and its own tuned guidance did no better than none [ 48 ] . Skill Issue, the closest in setting, optimised one skill file per repository for Claude Code on tasks mined from the repository’s history, with gains that its tasks could not separate from noise [ 26 ] ; DeltaSelect’s author tested edits to the skills and instructions of a Codex-based harness on eight tasks, one run each, and kept changes by judgement [ 13 ] . On loading, Skill-Use finds triggering a skill and following it to be separate bottlenecks, and that placing a skill’s full text in context mainly helps the agent recognise it as relevant [ 17 ] . An agent given workflows as extra actions called them in fewer than a fifth of tasks [ 55 ] . In a benchmark whose skill library grows, GPT-5-based systems, Codex among them, invoked almost none of the skills offered at the final stage; given only each task’s own skills, Codex invoked most of them, and Claude Code, counted by the files it read, about one in seven [ 23 ] . In Claude Code, on one coding task, an agent given a memory store seeded with facts relevant to the task never chose to consult it, while the same facts, injected by the harness on matching triggers such as file paths, arrived in every run [ 43 ] . Text placed in context can also hurt: on web development tasks, injecting a relevant skill lowered the average pass rate of all four models tested, and for two of them an irrelevant skill of the same length accounted for most of the loss [ 62 ] . Cortex meets the same division, between text that is loaded and text the agent must choose, inside its acceptance loop, where 16 of the 18 items kept were rules ( Section 5.2 ). The harness and the model. The benefit of an evolved harness need not grow with the model’s strength: in one study it peaked at a model of middling strength, and the strongest gained little, consistent with its already solving many of the tasks [ 31 ] . Planning acts as a scaffold for weaker coding models and mainly saves cost for stronger ones, and predefined tools help weaker models, while models fluent in the shell do as well, more cheaply, with the shell alone [ 14 ] . A harness is argued to be specific to its model [ 65 , 30 ] and to need re-adapting when the model changes [ 30 ] , although AHE’s own evolved harness, moved unchanged to other base models and to other reasoning settings of its own model, still gained on each [ 30 ] . For data agents, many layers that compensate for a model’s weaknesses are expected to be absorbed by the model, while knowledge of the environment keeps its value [ 40 ] . DarwinX notes that a behaviour the model internalises leaves the corresponding harness edit as dead weight, and that how much of a harness survives a change of model has not been measured [ 72 ] . Cortex’s items hold knowledge of the second kind, the conventions of one repository; yet under a stronger model, which already passed most rule-family scenarios unaided, the harness gained little, and one pass of re-measurement flagged 2 of its 4 items as removable ( Section 5.5 ). Measuring under noise. Run-to-run variance in agent evaluations can be as large as the improvements papers report: ten runs of each of six agent configurations on SWE-bench Verified, at two temperatures, spread their single-run scores over two to six points [ 7 ] , and a byte-identical re-run at temperature zero changed six of seventy outcomes [ 44 ] . The remedies are repeated samples and paired comparison question by question [ 36 , 52 ] , which Cortex’s sweeps apply. For accepting a change, PACE shows that accepting every prompt edit that raises the score commits many that an audit later labels false, and proposes sequential tests that remain valid whenever they are stopped [ 46 ] ; EvoPathBench finds that the selection of candidates, more than their generation, limits self-evolving agents [ 29 ] . Some loops estimate a noise band from repeated runs: RRSI does not let a gain inside it admit a coding candidate on its own [ 59 ] , and LiteEvo reverts a candidate only when it falls below the best score by more than a margin that includes the band [ 12 ] . PACE also tests its acceptor against a known answer, a harmful instruction planted for the proposer to remove, in prompt evolution on arithmetic and science questions; its other runs, like EvoPathBench’s, score real proposals on held-out data the acceptance rule never saw [ 46 , 29 ] . Irrelevant skills of matched length have served as comparison arms [ 62 , 20 ] ; we know of no study that plants placebo candidates in a coding agent’s acceptance pipeline to count how many it keeps. Tasks, and what a sandbox leaks. Cortex’s tasks follow SWE-bench’s format, with a check that fails before the fix and passes after it [ 22 ] ; benchmarks now refresh such tasks continuously [ 6 , 67 ] , and build them for training from real issues [ 38 ] or synthesise them at scale [ 60 ] . Tasks drawn from real use are recent: REAP builds them from developers’ sessions with a production coding assistant in one monorepo [ 21 ] , and SWE-Together reconstructs them from public user–agent sessions, replaying the users’ corrections through a simulated user [ 57 ] . Both serve to compare agents. Skills distilled from each developer’s own sessions have been tested by replaying that developer’s held-out sessions with a simulated developer [ 19 ] , and a user’s corrections have been compiled into rules and runtime checks for Claude Code and Codex [ 77 ] ; neither decides what to keep by a measured comparison. Cortex harvests one developer’s sessions to improve that developer’s harness, and writes the corrections into each task’s check. A task can give its answer away: in about a third of the SWE-bench instances one agent resolved, the solution was stated in the issue or its comments [ 2 ] , and the agentic benchmark checklist asks that agents be kept from the ground truth [ 78 ] . The git-history route a rollout can take ( Section 7 ) is known. Terminal-Bench requires that a task’s repository not contain its future commits [ 35 ] . Audits of agent trajectories find agents reading future fixes in the local git history, less often but still under an explicit instruction not to [ 32 ] , and single out git history as the main recurring route to passes not earned, in runs under Claude Code among others [ 33 ] . Deleting a repository’s branches and tags leaves later commits recoverable, which is why SWE-Bench Pro Verified rebuilds each repository as a single commit [ 76 ] ; Skill Issue’s sandboxes go further and remove the repository’s .git directory [ 26 ] . A related route has been noted for solutions: a tool that shows the local, uncommitted diff can reveal a solution backed out of the working copy [ 21 ] ; Section 7 reports the same route for harness items. What is new. Paired gates with a net threshold [ 34 , 45 ] , a no-regression guard [ 10 , 65 ] , context cost as an objective [ 27 , 15 ] , measured deletion [ 54 , 47 ] , retiring a skill only after enough exposure [ 47 , 70 ] , an acceptor tested against a planted known answer [ 46 ] , and the case for re-testing a harness when its model changes [ 72 , 30 ] all have precedents. To our knowledge, what this paper adds is their combination for one developer’s repository and three things we did not find elsewhere: the same exposure rule for adding an item and for deleting one, so that both verdicts compare the harness with and without the item only on the tasks where it entered the context, with unknown exposure blocking either verdict (SLIM applies such a comparison to retirement alone [ 47 ] ); a coding agent’s acceptance pipeline tested with planted placebo and harmful candidates as well as known-good ones; and Claude Code’s loaded rules and agent-chosen skills compared as tiers inside the loop that decides what to keep. AHE’s evolving agent also chooses between a system prompt that applies to every task and skills loaded on demand, but its analysis of where the gain lies does not compare the two [ 30 ] . 7 Limitations One repository, built for the purpose. The lab, its house rules, its tasks and its checks all come from the same hand, and the lab was calibrated so that the model had room to improve: before its first session, scenarios the model already solved unaided were redesigned until it broke the rule. The four house rules are ones a machine can check, and the one with the largest gain, family A’s, is checked only by whether the changelog gained a line. Of the 30 held-out scenarios, 15 were written after the development run ( Section 4 ), when the items it had kept were known; they were written from CONTRIBUTING.md and the family definitions alone, never from an evolved item. Conventions that need judgement to check are not tested at all. The results show that the loop learns conventions of this kind, in a repository of this kind; they do not show that it learns others. A small model’s gain. Every primary number is Claude Haiku 4.5’s. Under Claude Sonnet 5, the harness of R1 gained +5.6 points [−2.8, +13.9] where it had gained +66.7, because the stronger model already followed most of the house rules without a harness ( Section 5.5 ). In this study, what the loop was worth followed how often the model broke the conventions; a single harness under a single stronger model is too little to say how it varies across models. No result on a real repository. On the one repository we did not build, the agent was rarely corrected, so nothing recurred and the loop kept nothing, and its benchmark had two identical harnesses to compare ( Section 5.6 ). Whether a harness that Cortex learns in a real repository helps on tasks drawn from real work there is untested. Scripted corrections, and few runs. The developer in the lab is a script: it replies to each mistake in the same words every time, and never misreads a change or changes its mind. There were 4 evaluation runs and 1 control run, so the variation between runs rests on few runs: the bootstrap can draw only a few distinct sets of runs, and its intervals may understate how far a further run could fall, as R3 fell below the others ( Section 5.1 ). With 1 control run, a test that permutes runs cannot give H4 a p p below 0.2, so its verdict is descriptive. The loop’s confirm sweeps ran each task 3 times per arm, and the ablation arms each held-out scenario 3 times, where a single lost run can be luck; the recheck exists for that reason, and the ablations’ intervals are wide. What measurement costs. Every verdict is paid for in rollouts ( Section 5.4 ). The costs reported there are Claude Haiku 4.5’s prices on this repository’s small tasks; a larger repository, a dearer model or a larger k k would cost more. What a rollout could read. A sandbox isolates what is on disk, not what is in git. The clone keeps the repository’s history, so a rollout could find earlier tasks’ fixes in past commits, and a replayed training scenario could find the later commit that fixed it in its session. And when an item’s file is already tracked at the commit a rollout starts from, an arm that lacks the item sees git status list that file as deleted, and git diff prints its text. In the lab neither route reached a held-out scenario’s fix, which was never committed to the lab’s repository. Under Claude Haiku 4.5 the first route was rare: 2 of the 1,809 loop rollouts that could be checked printed a harvested fix or the task store. The second was not: of the 595 held-out none rollouts, 112 saw the run’s items named by git status and 2 printed an item’s text, and on the rule families the rollouts that saw the names passed less often (9.7% of 93, against 23.6% of the 382 that did not). Under Claude Sonnet 5 reading an item’s text was common, in 67 of the 168 none rollouts, held-out and training together, and in 72 of the 300 removal rollouts of /prune , but the none rollouts that read one did not pass more often than those that did not, and for the items found removable, the removal rollouts that read the removed item passed less often (28 of 35, against 110 of 115). On structlog, 1 of the 8 training sessions and 19 of the 40 benchmark rollouts read the upstream fix through git, so that run does not show an agent working unaided. A sandbox repository that holds a single commit, with the harness installed as untracked files, would close both routes. No independent replication. No one else has yet repeated the study. 8 Conclusion A coding agent’s harness is text that a developer edits by impression, and a single run of the agent is too noisy to say whether an edit helped. Cortex treats the harness as something to measure. It turns the developer’s own sessions into tasks, keeps a skill or rule only if a repeated comparison with the live harness, task by task, shows a net gain and no task that collapses, and deletes one only if removing it costs nothing measurable. One principle runs through both directions: an item is credited or blamed only where it entered the agent’s context, so a candidate that never fired is not kept, and an item that never fired is not deleted. In a replicated evaluation with Claude Haiku 4.5, in a repository built so that the model had conventions to learn, the loop learned them. On held-out scenarios it never saw, the harnesses evolved by 4 independent runs beat no harness by +55.0 points on the four rule families (95% CI [+34.1, +74.1]) and moved the control family by −0.8 points. They added no text to what the agent reads on every turn. In the run that measured it, how the advice was offered mattered more than who wrote it. A rule enters the context whenever the agent reads a file it covers, and most candidates, and 16 of the 18 items kept, were rules. A skill’s body enters only if the agent opens it: the always-on skills written by hand for the ideal arm were listed in all 90 of its held-out rollouts and opened in none, and their families stayed where no harness left them. Advice reached the agent when it was tied to the files a task touches, but not so narrowly that new tasks missed it ( Sections 5.2 and 5.4 ). The results are as clear about where the loop stops. Its gates kept none of the 20 placebos and none of the 5 harmful candidates. But on their screens the agent never opened the placebos or the harmful skills, and the screens of the harmful rules could show no gain, so the test shows that the gates never keep what never fires, not that they catch harm. Only 2 of the 4 known-good candidates were kept; the 2 always-on skills, never opened on their screens, were lost. Under Claude Sonnet 5, which already followed most of the house rules unaided, the harness of R1 gained +5.6 points (95% CI [−2.8, +13.9]) where it had gained +66.7 points under Claude Haiku 4.5. One pass of /prune at k = 3 k=3 , with its rollouts on that model, flagged 2 of the harness’s 4 items as removable, though one pass at that k k cannot tell a small effect from none. In this study, what the loop was worth followed how often the model broke the conventions. On structlog, the one repository we did not build, the agent was rarely corrected, nothing recurred, and the loop kept nothing. The positive result therefore rests on one synthetic repository with house rules a machine can check, a scripted developer and one small model. Cortex’s optional judge, replayed afterwards, did not anticipate the verdicts, on a thin comparison ( Section 5.7 ). The next steps follow from these limits. The first is a real repository whose conventions the model does break, the test this study could not run. The second is a test of harm, in which harmful candidates are swept, as in a confirm, over tasks that pass without them as well as tasks they could help, so that a gate can see what they break. The third is to run each rollout in a repository that holds a single commit, the broken state without the task store, with the harness installed as untracked files, which closes both routes by which rollouts read what their harness did not give them ( Section 7 ). The fourth is conventions that need judgement to check, which a task’s script cannot decide alone; measuring them without letting a model decide the result ( Section 3.7 ) is an open problem. Lessons left no trace the judge could see, and a small one the renderer could. Rules on were judged slightly worse. A weaker director needs the guard. 5.8 Does the memory grow? Forty-eight more reels Lessons lower the review cost; they do not keep lowering it. And they do not move the judge. 5.9 Judge reliability The absolute rubric is stable but sees little. The pairwise verdict is repeatable—and biased by position. Where judges disagree, the human agrees with the minority. A second round under the corrected gate. 6 Related work Explainer and educational video from code. Experience memory for agents. Checkers from fixes. Self-modifying agents and judge reward hacking. 7 Limitations 8 Conclusion References A The thirteen rules B Accepted lessons License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.14495v1 [cs.AI] 10 Oct 2026 Reels-RSI: Program-Level Self-Improvement for Code-Rendered Explainer Videos Wei Lin Agentic Loops X https://github.com/agentic-loops-x October 2026 • Preprint • Code, rules, lessons and the evolve report: https://github.com/agentic-loops-x/Reels-RSI Abstract Explainer videos—a worked geometry problem, why the sky is blue, how a dynasty fell—are usually one more target for pixel video generation. We argue they are a different kind of artifact: a program (script, storyboard and per-frame animation code) that a deterministic renderer turns into frames. A program can be read, diffed, tested and audited; pixels can only be watched. Reels-RSI is an open-source reel director for any agent harness; its self-improvement happens at the program level rather than in weights or prompts. Every revision pass is logged with a code snapshot; a retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons; a lesson that a static check can catch is compiled into a rule with a must-fail and a must-pass example, so the memory is unit-tested; and a rule learned today runs over everything made before it. A bounded, benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director’s playbook, kept only when blind pairwise judgments on held-out topics prefer it; nothing enters memory without a human decision. Across 111 reels—a field study, two playbook evolutions, a 2 × \times 2 memory ablation, a weaker director, a 48-reel learning curve and a judge-reliability study—we find that the rule learned in the field caught four latent defects in frames authored before it existed and none after; that rules are an audit for a strong director (eight unguarded reels, no violation) and a guard for a weaker one (thirty violations unguarded versus five); that lessons shorten revision loops but do not compound or move the judge; and that the first rewrite’s 11–1 verdict was a position bias in our vote design (judges pick the second-shown reel 62–81% of the time), masking scripts that traded thirteen facts for craft. We document four failure modes of the preference signal, which check caught each, and the fixes. Code, rules, lessons and data are public. 1 Introduction A short explainer video has a property that sets it apart from most video: nearly everything that matters in it is symbolic . The numbers in a worked problem, the labels on a map, the order of steps in a derivation, the words the narrator says—these are the content; the picture exists to deliver them. A generated clip is judged on whether its motion looks plausible [ 22 ] ; an explainer is judged on whether the shaded triangle’s area really is 0.3 ​ cm 2 0.3\,\mathrm{cm}^{2} and whether the viewer saw why. Recent systems therefore generate explainers as code —Manim programs [ 6 , 2 , 5 ] , slide decks [ 25 ] , HTML compositions—and reap exact text, real geometry and reproducible output. We take the consequence one step further. If the reel is a program, then everything we know how to do with programs applies to reels: they can be linted, diffed, tested, audited after the fact, and carried between the models that wrote them. In particular, an agent that makes reels can improve itself at the program level , by accumulating executable checks over its own output, instead of only in its prompt or its weights. This paper presents Reels-RSI and the self-improvement loop built into it. The system is engineering: a deterministic command-line pipeline (narration with per-word timings, karaoke captions, font subsetting, procedural music and sound, map data, assembly, checks, render) that any agent harness—Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, OpenCode—drives from a Markdown skill; it makes reels in Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean, Spanish and French and dubs a finished reel into another language. The contributions are what the program view makes possible on top of it: 1. A four-tier, program-level memory (§ 4 ). Every finalize pass is logged with a code snapshot (L0). A retrospective pairs each check finding with the diff that fixed it and proposes lessons , injected into the next reel’s frame briefs and scoped to the presets, aspects and modes they hold for (L1). A lesson that a static check can detect is compiled into a rule —a check(doc) function shipped with must-fail and must-pass examples, admitted only if it passes both (L2). A benchmark-gated step lets an agent rewrite the director’s playbook, kept only if blind pairwise judges prefer the result on training and held-out topics (L3). Every tier is written by a check or by a person; the model only proposes. 2. Retroactive audit, and an honest account of the guard (§ 5.4 , § 5.7 ). A rule learned from reel n n is a program that runs on reels 1 ​ … ​ n − 1 1\ldots n-1 . The rule learned during our study found four latent defects in two reels delivered and reviewed before the system existed—defects no one had noticed—and nothing in the 21 reels made under it. The run logs and a rules-off ablation then show why the zero is cheap: for this director the rules fired three times in 58 passes, and eight reels made with no rule active contain no violation. The same four topics under a weaker director carry thirty violations unguarded and five guarded: the audit is what the program view buys a strong director, the guard is what it buys a weak one. 3. A measured account of the preference signal (§ 5.5 –§ 5.9 ). One evolution round was accepted by blind pairwise judgment 11–1 on training topics and 8–4 on held-out topics while the absolute rubric did not move. Re-judging 170 times shows the rubric stable (within-reel SD 1.3) but insensitive, the pairwise verdict repeatable but leaning on a position bias: three judge models pick the second-shown reel 62–81% of the time, and our own three-vote alternation gave the candidate the extra second slot. Judged from the disadvantaged slot the round still passes, but three of eight topics are ties and the remaining margin is not significant ( p = 0.39 p=0.39 on train). Reading all sixteen scripts shows the preferred reels dropping thirteen baseline facts over six topics while adding six. We report four failure modes of the signal—a judge misreading that became a proposed lesson, a proposer writing for the sampling schedule, craft bought with facts, and our own vote design—and the check that caught each. We are explicit about scale. This is a field study of one system during its own release testing: 23 reels in the main study, 16 in the ablation, 8 under a weaker director, 48 in a learning curve, 16 in a second evolution round; one model family as director, judge and retrospective model, one evolution round, no human preference study. It establishes what the mechanisms catch and what they miss, not effect sizes. A companion benchmark for explainer-reel systems, with outcome tests on the final video, is in preparation and is deliberately kept out of this paper. 2 Explainer reels as programs Definition. In Reels-RSI a reel is a directory. SCRIPT.md holds the spoken lines, one block per frame; STORYBOARD.md holds per-frame scene, duration, transition, route and status; compositions/frames/ holds one .html composition per frame—HTML, SVG, Canvas or Three.js driven by a single paused GSAP timeline—plus optional shared kits ( assets/*.js ) and overlays; the voice, caption and music assets are derived from these by the pipeline. Rendering is deterministic: a headless browser seeks each composition’s timeline to successive frame times and FFmpeg encodes [ 3 ] . Re-running finalize on a copy of a finished reel reproduces its assembled composition byte for byte. What the program view buys. Table 1 contrasts the two routes to an explainer video. The right-hand column makes no claim about which route produces better pictures; it lists what becomes possible once the artifact is source code, and § 4 uses each line. Pixel generation Program rendering (Reels-RSI, Manim-based agents) Text and numbers sampled; may be wrong or illegible exact strings in the program Correctness check watch the video (human or VLM) read the program; the render is deterministic Targeted edit regenerate change one value, re-render one frame Learning a mistake fine-tune or re-prompt write a check over the program text Applying it to old output impossible run the check over the corpus Portability across models none the check is code; the model is irrelevant Reproducibility seed-dependent byte-identical Table 1: Two routes to an explainer video. Three layers of verification. The artifact exists at three levels—program text, assembled composition, rendered pixels—and can be checked at each, with rising cost and falling certainty. Static rules run over the program text (§ 4.3 ): exact for the pattern they encode, free to run. Dynamic checks run on the assembled composition—the renderer’s own lint, runtime, layout and contrast checks—exact for what they cover. Judged assessment lets a vision-language model score or compare sampled frames: cheap and informative, and, as § 5.5 shows, not to be trusted alone. The design principle of the loop follows from this ordering: a learned judge may rank ; admission to memory requires a deterministic check or a person. 3 Reels-RSI Director agent any harness: Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode; reads the skill reels CLI (deterministic) new ⋅ \cdot voice ⋅ \cdot packets ⋅ \cdot finalize ⋅ \cdot render fonts ⋅ \cdot captions ⋅ \cdot music ⋅ \cdot sfx ⋅ \cdot geo ⋅ \cdot dub Reel script, storyboard, frame programs, MP4 Program-level memory ( ~/.reels ) L0 run log + code snapshot per pass L1 lessons (scoped) L2 rules = check + bad/good examples L3 playbook evolution runs writes finalize logs; rules check lessons into frame briefs; skill text retro reads history; audit old reels Figure 1: Reels-RSI. The creative half (script, storyboard, frame code, review) belongs to the agent; the deterministic half is a CLI the agent calls. Memory sits beside both and is written only by checks and by human-gated acceptance. Reels-RSI (Fig. 1 ) separates the creative work from everything that must be reproducible. The skill is about 1,000 lines of Markdown: a ten-step director’s handbook with references on script and storyboard, frame construction, a quality bar, worked problems, history, visual styles and techniques. Any agent that can read files and run commands can follow it. The CLI (about 5,000 lines of Python on the standard library, a TTS client and font tools) owns narration with per-word timings, caption building with CJK-aware grouping and bilingual lines, font subsetting so the headless renderer never shows missing glyphs, procedural music beds and sound effects cut to the real narration, Natural Earth map layers, Wikimedia Commons images with credits, stroke-order data for Chinese characters, assembly, overlays, transitions, the renderer’s checks, snapshots and render. Five visual presets (deep-space, notebook, ink, atlas, chalk) each ship a design spec and a caption skin; chalk ships a drawing kit. Models are interchangeable at two seams. The director runs inside whichever agent CLI the user already has; reels make "…" launches a headless session. The judge and retrospective roles are one-shot calls, named provider:model , over an OpenAI-compatible or Anthropic HTTP API or through a logged-in agent CLI; twelve providers and custom endpoints are configured in a TOML file. Nothing in memory depends on the model that produced it. Languages. A reel’s language is detected from its script (Hangul, kana, Han, else Latin scored by stop words); the voice, caption cutting (grouped by character for Chinese and Japanese, by word otherwise), glyph source (Noto SC, JP or KR, fetched on first use) and subtitle export follow. reels dub translates a finished reel’s spoken lines and every on-screen string in one model call, re-voices each line fitted to the original line’s duration so the frames stay in step, and re-renders; the geometry lesson of § 5 exists in six languages this way. 4 Program-level self-improvement The loop has four tiers. The invariant across them: a model may propose, and only a check or a person may commit. 4.1 L0: every pass is evidence reels finalize assembles the reel and runs every check—the renderer’s lint, runtime, layout and contrast checks, then every Reels-RSI rule. Each pass appends a record to .reels/runs.jsonl (findings with codes, lines and messages; frame count; duration) and snapshots the frame sources to .reels/history/NNN/ . Renders, scores and viewer feedback ( reels feedback "the labels are too small" --frame 04 ) append to the same log. Apart from the judge’s score, no model writes this tier; it is the raw material the next tiers read. 4.2 L1: lessons, paired with the diff that earned them reels retro compiles an evidence file from the log: per pass, which findings were new and which were fixed; for every fixed finding, the unified diff between the snapshot in which it was present and the one in which it was gone, labelled with what it fixed; the viewer’s comments; the judge’s notes; and everything already known—accepted lessons and existing rules—so nothing is proposed twice. A retrospective model reads the evidence and proposes at most five lessons, each with a kind ( doc , rule , kit , taste ), a scope (director, frame, solve, history, …) and an optional when condition such as preset=chalk , aspect=9:16 or mode=solve . Lessons land in an inbox, which is inert. On accept they are injected into the briefs of every future frame worker—but only the lessons whose conditions the new reel satisfies, so a 16:9 science reel is not told how to draw chalk boxes on a portrait board. 4.3 L2: a lesson that can be checked becomes a rule A rule is a directory: rule.py exposing RULE (id, severity, lesson, fix) and check(doc) over a frame’s text, plus bad.* files that must produce a finding and good.* files that must not. reels rules test runs every rule against its examples; reels lessons accept --rule-dir refuses a rule lesson whose rule fails them. Rules run on every finalize and lint ; once admitted, the mistake cannot recur, whichever model is directing. Listing 1 shows the rule learned during the study; Appendix A lists the rest. Listing 1: The rule compiled from a lesson during the study. Its must-fail example is the original chalk-dust helper from the reel in which the defect appeared; the must-pass example adds immediateRender: false and a fade-in from zero, which is always safe. ⬇ RULE = { "id" : "visible-from-state" , "severity" : "warning" , "kinds" : [ "frame" , "overlay" , "kit" ], "lesson" : "fromTo renders its from-state at build time: a tween that starts " "visible (opacity > 0) and fades to 0 later shows the element before its cue" , "fix" : "Add immediateRender: false to the to-vars" } def check ( doc ): out = [] for idx , args in H . calls ( doc . text , "fromTo" ): if len ( args ) < 4: continue # no position: starts at t=0 anyway frm , to = args [1], args [2] a , b = num ( frm , "opacity" ), num ( to , "opacity" ) if a is not None and a > 0 and b == 0 and "immediateRender" not in to : out . append ( H . Finding ( RULE [ "id" ], RULE [ "severity" ], doc . rel , H . line_of ( doc . text , idx ), "fromTo starts visible and fades out - visible before its cue" )) return out The line between L1 and L2 is the line between advice and enforcement. A doc lesson says “labels inside coloured regions go at the region’s widest part”; a model may or may not follow it, and no one can tell afterwards whether it did. A rule says “a fromTo that starts visible and fades out without immediateRender:false is a finding”; no model can skip it, and its own examples say whether it is right. Only mistakes detectable from program text can become rules—a real limit (§ 7 ) and the reason L1 exists. 4.4 L3: the playbook rewrites itself, under a gate it cannot move reels evolve runs one round. (1) The current skill makes the four training topics of a fixed eight-topic benchmark (science, history, a worked problem, an English explainer). (2) An agent reads the baseline’s judge notes, check findings and the lesson inbox and makes at most three edits to a copy of the skill’s Markdown, explaining each in a changelog. (3) The copy makes the same topics. (4) Per topic, a vision judge sees both reels blind, three votes with the order swapped between votes; the candidate must win most votes, render at least as many reels, and lose no topic by more than ten composite points. (5) Both versions make the four held-out topics, and the candidate must win at least half the votes there. (6) A report is written with per-topic votes, the judge’s reasons and a side-by-side image of both reels; nothing changes until a person runs evolve apply . The proposer may edit only the skill text. The pipeline, the rules, the presets, the judge’s rubric and the benchmark topics are out of its reach, and it is told to record tool defects it discovers in a separate file for a developer rather than work around them in prose. 5 Field study 5.1 Setting The data are the reels Reels-RSI made during its own release testing in October 2026. Claude Code was the director (Opus for the two reels made with a human reviewer, Sonnet for the headless benchmark reels); claude-cli:sonnet was the judge and the retrospective model. Table 2 lists the corpus: two reels predate the system (made with its predecessor skill, before any rule existed); two were made from scratch with a person reviewing at three gates (plan, look-dev, final); seventeen were made headlessly from one sentence each in the benchmark and evolve runs; two are dubs. A 30-second headless reel cost $0.56–1.29 and 230–584 s of wall time (15–34 agent turns); judging a reel takes about 30 s. Dubs of the geometry reel into Spanish, French and Korean exist but were not rendered at the time of writing and are excluded. Compute. Everything in this paper was made on one laptop and one consumer subscription. The 105 headless reels across the benchmark, two evolution rounds, ablation, weaker-director and learning-curve runs cost $82.72 in metered agent time ($0.35–1.45 per 30-s reel); the two reviewed reels were made in an interactive session and the roughly 400 judge calls ran on the subscription, unmetered. No experiment needed more than one night. 5.2 Within a reel, the review loop converges Every reel reached zero check errors before render. The two reviewed reels needed 7 and 5 finalize passes; their warning counts went 5 → 12 → 2 → 2 → 1 → 1 → 1 5\rightarrow 12\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 1\rightarrow 1\rightarrow 1 and 1 → 1 → 3 → 2 → 1 1\rightarrow 1\rightarrow 3\rightarrow 2\rightarrow 1 (the rise in pass 2 is new frames being added). The headless reels needed 1–6 passes (median 2); the hardest, a history reel, went 3 , 4 , 3 , 0 3,4,3,0 errors over four passes. The two reviewed reels also exposed thirteen defects in the tool and the skill—a caption skin with 1.27:1 contrast, placeholders missing for unbuilt frames so voice and captions drifted, a map-winding rule that flagged a car outline as a polygon—each fixed in the tool rather than patched in the reel, which is the point of recording where a fix went. 5.3 Lessons Retrospectives on the two reviewed reels, and the agents’ own retrospectives after each headless reel, produced 56 proposed lessons. A person accepted 15, rejected 1 and left 40 in the inbox. Of the 15, thirteen are doc lessons (e.g. “budget 3.9 Chinese characters per second for the teaching voice, not 4.5–5”; “a mark that underlines a word rides on the text element, never on guessed coordinates”), one is a kit lesson (every reel gets a drawing kit; the chalk kit now ships with the preset) and one is a rule lesson (§ 5.4 ). Two carry when conditions ( preset=chalk , aspect=9:16 ); before conditions existed, a 16:9 deep-space reel had been handed both. The full list is in Appendix B . The rejected lesson matters more than the accepted ones. The retrospective model had turned a judge’s note—“frame 09 is rendered at the wrong aspect, 1080 × \times 640”—into “verify every frame’s render dimensions before finalizing”. The frame was 1080 × \times 1920; the judge had been shown a sample sheet downscaled until each portrait frame was about 200 pixels wide. Had lessons been accepted automatically, a false constraint would have reached every subsequent reel. The retrospective prompt now ranks evidence (check findings and viewer words above judge notes), and sample sheets are sized per aspect. 5.4 Lesson to rule, and the audit it enables In the first reviewed reel, a chalk-dust puff showed stray specks before its cue. The cause is a GSAP semantic: fromTo renders its from-state at build time, so a tween from opacity 0.9 to 0, placed later in the timeline, shows the element from the first frame. The fix is one property. The lesson became the rule of Listing 1 , with the original helper as its must-fail example. We then ran all thirteen rules over the whole corpus (Table 3 ). Over every reel with a log—92 reels, 260 finalize passes—the thirteen rules fired 25 times, 18 of them in one weak-director reel (§ 5.7 ); nine rules, visible-from-state among them, never fired while a reel was being authored. The retroactive audit is the stronger claim: it does not depend on how often a mistake is made, only on the corpus being code. 5.5 One evolution round The round ran overnight on a consumer subscription, paused once for two hours when the quota ran out, and resumed from its state file: sixteen headless reels and about forty judge calls, $12.75 in agent cost. To learn how much of it is the judge, we re-ran the judging without making any reels: the absolute rubric three times on each of the sixteen reels, the pairwise comparison three times per topic with the same judge, and once each with two other judges ( claude-cli:haiku , claude-cli:opus ); about 170 judge calls in 45 minutes. The absolute rubric is stable but sees little. Within-reel standard deviation over three re-scores has median 1.3 and maximum 2.7 on the rubric’s 20–100 scale, so the flat score in Table 4 is not noise. Averaged over re-scores the rubric puts the candidate 3.5 points ahead on the training topics (57.0 vs 60.5) and 1.9 behind on the held-out ones (59.5 vs 57.6), with per-topic differences from − 9.9 -9.9 (the poem; baseline better) to + 8.7 +8.7 (the seasons). The rubric does see the change; it does not agree with the pairwise verdict about its direction on holdout. The pairwise verdict is repeatable—and biased by position. Three repeats with the same judge gave the candidate 8 of 8 topics every time, with 10–11 of 12 training votes and 10 of 12 held-out votes. But the breakdown by position (Table 9 ) shows that the judge picked the candidate 48 of 48 times when it was shown second and 14 of 24 times when it was shown first ; over all votes it picked the second-shown reel 81% of the time, and the two other judges 67% and 62%. Our vote design—three votes, order alternating from a fixed start—gave the candidate the second slot twice per topic, which inflated its margin. Because the second-slot preference saturates (every second-shown candidate won), the informative votes are the ones where the candidate was shown first: 8 of 12 on the training topics (two-sided binomial p = 0.39 p=0.39 ) and 6 of 12 on the held-out ones ( p = 1.0 p=1.0 ), against 24 of 24 in the second slot ( p < 10 − 6 p<10^{-6} ). The absolute rubric agrees: averaged over re-scores and the eight topics the candidate is + 0.8 +0.8 points ahead, sign-flip permutation p = 0.70 p=0.70 . There is no statistically supported evidence that the rewrite is better; the round’s 11–1 was the slot. Balancing the vote count is not enough when the bias saturates—it still hands each side two free votes per topic—so the harness now judges each side only on the votes where it was shown first, its disadvantaged slot: the side with the higher first-slot win rate takes the topic, equal rates tie. Together with the flat absolute score, these support a conclusion reached elsewhere in other settings [ 12 , 24 , 7 ] : a learned judge is a useful advisor to a self-improving loop and a poor oracle . The program view lets the loop keep its oracles deterministic—rules, render checks and, in the benchmark, outcome tests on the artifact—and reserve the judge for what only taste can rank. 6 Related work Explainer and educational video from code. TheoremExplainAgent [ 6 ] and Code2Video [ 2 ] generate Manim programs with planner, coder and critic agents and judge them with LLM rubrics or a quiz; Paper2Video [ 25 ] adds pairwise comparison against human talks. ManimAgent [ 5 ] is closest to us: a Manim-writing agent with an episodic memory of success rationales and validated failure patterns grown from its own task stream, evaluated by blind human Pass@1. Its memory is prose retrieved into the prompt; ours compiles the checkable part into tested code, which is what makes retroactive audit and cross-model portability possible. CineForge [ 9 ] and VideoWeaver [ 15 ] evolve policies or skills for long-form pixel video; what they learn cannot be run over the artifact, because the artifact is not a program. Experience memory for agents. Reflexion [ 11 ] , ExpeL [ 21 ] and ACE [ 20 ] store verbal reflections, insights or an evolving playbook; our L1 and L3 belong to this family, with ACE’s incrementally curated playbook closest to evolve . Voyager [ 13 ] and ASI [ 14 ] store skills as executable programs verified by the environment; we store checks , verified by their own examples, which is what a creative task without an environment reward affords. The neuro-symbolic dual memory of Wen et al. [16] induces executable Python verifiers from failed trajectories and validates them on positive and negative pools—the same contract as our L2, in household and web environments. SkillRevise [ 10 ] revises LLM-authored skills from execution traces. Checkers from fixes. KNighter [ 17 ] synthesises static analysers from historical kernel patches, validating each against the buggy and the patched code, and found 92 long-latent Linux bugs; test-driven checker development [ 8 ] makes the same contract explicit. Our rules follow it exactly—must fail, must pass—but the corpus audited is the agent’s own past output, and the patches come from the agent’s own revision log. Self-modifying agents and judge reward hacking. ADAS [ 4 ] , the Darwin Gödel Machine [ 19 ] and GEPA [ 1 ] let an agent rewrite its scaffold or prompts under an objective score. Wahi [12] and Zhou [24] show what happens when the score is an LLM judge; Ye et al. [18] show how sensitive such loops are to variance and task order. Our evolve step is a small instance of this family with the guards those papers recommend: a frozen holdout, pairwise rather than absolute judgment [ 23 ] , a deterministic layer the proposer cannot edit, and a person at the end. 7 Limitations Scale and family. 111 reels, two evolution rounds, four topics per ablation cell, and one model family (Claude) as director, judge and retrospective model; the three judges differ in size, not provenance. No human preference study. We cannot say whether any judge’s taste matches viewers’; one author’s eye agrees with the dissenting judges on one topic, which is an anecdote. Position bias remains. Judging from the disadvantaged slot discards the saturated votes but halves the sample; under the balanced ablation design the second-shown reel was still picked 58% of the time, so small margins in pairwise verdicts carry little information. Null results at n = 4 n=4 . The ablation’s “lessons change nothing the judge sees” and “rules on are judged slightly worse” are within what position alone produces; they rule out large effects, not small ones. What rules can see. A rule checks program text. It cannot know that a topic requires naming an alliance or stating the perihelion, that a label is too small on a phone, or that a mood is wrong; those remain lessons (advice) or outcome tests (the companion benchmark). Rule provenance and precision. Twelve of thirteen rules were ported from the predecessor’s checker, each from a real failure; one lesson-to-rule path was exercised; one rule produced a false positive that the ablation exposed. Human cost. A person triaged 56 lessons and one evolve report and read sixteen scripts by hand; we did not measure how that scales. Dependencies. The free neural voices come from an unofficial endpoint; commercial use needs a licensed provider, which the pipeline supports. 8 Conclusion An explainer reel rendered from a program is a different object from a generated video, and the difference is worth more than exact text: it makes the agent’s own output something the agent, and its authors, can check, audit and learn from at the level of code. Reels-RSI turns that into a loop—log every pass, pair findings with fixes, propose lessons, compile the checkable ones into tested rules, rewrite the playbook under a gate it cannot move—and a release-testing study shows where each tier earns its place and where it does not. A rule found latent defects in reels made before it existed; the same rules were almost never needed by a strong director and caught thirty mistakes a weak one made; lessons bought fewer review passes without compounding and without moving a judge; and the preference signal that accepted the one playbook rewrite turned out to be stable, repeatable, position-biased and blind to the thirteen facts the rewrite traded for craft. Each of those findings came from running a check over artifacts that already existed—reels, scripts, logs, votes—which is the practice this paper argues for.
